Excerpts from some of the many Press opinions "The writer urges the necessity and the pleasure of spiritual intercourse with GOD."—Liverpool Mercury, April 15, 1891.

_ "Mr. Waddell writes in a pleasant and earnest style, sifting the experiences he has had in various parts of• the country with ft view to presenting something to the reader which is well worth considering.' —Warrington Examiner, June 27th, 1891.

"The papers are written from a remarkable knowledge of Scripture, and recommend themselves by their quiet earnest- ness of style."—Scotsman, March 23rd, 1891. "With this key to the character of the work, the pages which follow prove interesting reading, and reveal the author as a close and appreciative observer of nature, and one who sees sermons in stones, books in the running brooks, and good in everything."—Preston Herald, April 4th, 1801. CTIT and dried—The man who WU "withered by a glance." WEIS the milkmaid is awkward and fretful the cow generally turns pail. WIFE—" And do you love me still, dearie ?" PARADOXICAL—"What's happened to Bronson? You congratulated him very effusively." "There was reason—he has lost his grippe." VIN heard of a particularly ascetic Protestant spinster, the other day, who refused to engage a maid of excellent character because she had a Roman nose. A GENTLEMAN who had a Highland servant once asked her the time, and got this answer—" It's ten meenits past ten, an' the clock's ten meenits fast, an' it's stannin'." MRS. WINKt3 "SO you have taken another companion 'for better or for worse,' eh?" Mrs. Secondtrip—" Only for better, my dear. He can't possibly be worse than the other one was." "OUR rudder is broken, sir," said the first mate to the captain. "Nonsense! That's only imagina- tion!" "Beg your pardon, sir, but it's a stern reality." AND what do you have to amuse yourselves down your way these times ? " "Well, we had an eisteddfod last night." " Mercy 1 where did you get that awful cold? "—Boston Transcript. Two young writers were talking of their hopes, their ambitions. "If I have not made a reputation by the time I'm thirty I shall blow my brains out," asserted one. " He—" I was thinking about your eyes." She—" Why. my eyes, dear, are in my head." AN Irish corporal who now and then indulges in a " naggin " of the " crathur " was thus accosted by his captain while standing at ease, "Pat, what makes your nose so red?' " Plase, yet honour," said Pat, "I always blush when I spakes to an officer." ScENE—Riding-school. Pupil—" I thought you said that after twenty lessons of an hour each I should know how to ride ? " Riding-master—" So you would, sir, if you hadn't spent the best part of the time on the ground instead of on the • animal's back. MINISTER (to widow)—"l was at the cemetery to-day, my dear Mrs. Bentley, and I discovered that your husband's grave is quite overgrown with grass." Widow (fetching a sigh)—" Yes, I promised poor John just before he died I would see it was kept green." "How would you like some nice brandied • peaches of my own make 7 " asked a benevolent old lady of a tramp. "I don't want to put you to so much trouble, mum," replied the hardened vagabond. "You needn't mind the peaches; a little of the brandy will suit me." Mr. Tuinley (desperately)—" I admire your hand very much, Miss Vere-de-Vere." "I beg your pardon, Mr. Tumley, but we are not in Spain." Now, just throw the fish," and he dexterously caught them. "Talk about , catching fish I" he said, as he pursued his -way.

TILE story is told of a fa nous Boston lawyer that one day, after having a slight discussion with the Judge, he deliberately turned his back upon that personage, and started to walk off. "Are you trying, sir, to show contempt for the Court 1" asked the Judge sternly. "No, sir," was the reply. "I am trying to conceal it." VoitiaieD wife—" Oh, doctor, what has detained you? I sent for you at twelve o'clock; my husband is very low indeed." Doctor (complacently)—" Yes, I received, your call then, but as I had an engage- ment with another patient in the neighbourhood at six o'clock, I thought I'd make one job of it and kill two birds with. one stone." "MAMMA" said a beautiful maiden, in tender tones, this morning at breakfast, "Henry is coming round to-morrow night." "Well, what of that 2" replied mamma, with ill-concealed disappointment. "He's been milling every Sunday night for two years." "Very true, mamma, but neither of them was leap year," and a cold, hard, determined look spread over her lovely features an inch and a half thick. "I vIUOITLD infer, sir," he said to a young man, "from the Air of hauteur and easy self-possession which seem to be your distinglishing characteristics, that you have mixed much with the world and have travelled extensively ?" "Yes, sir," replied the young man graciously bending, "I have been an extensive :traveller in my time. For the past eight years I've been a brakeman on the elevated road."— New YorkEun. Corbett—" Please, sir, mine had yellow hair, blue eyes, and a tailor- made suit." ONE night aka party. Bays..:d Taylor was greatly bored by the ,persistent attempts of a guest to discuss sma-rayths. No matter into what groove the conversation,strayed. this individual was sure to drag it back to sun-myths. "laid you ever think that the name 'Smith,' so common in all countries, is derived from sun-myth '?" asked Taylor mis- chievously. "No, indeed 1" was the reply. " ,doubtedly I San-myth, Sumyth, . Smyth, Smith 1" ,Everyone laughed; and the poet was successful in banishing the threadbare subject. A FRIEND of Addiscn botaawed a thousand pounds from him. Finding himself unable to repay the loan, he was on all occasions very complacent to the poet, and would not venture to contradict him. One day the hypocrisy became so offensively palpable that Addison, losing all patience, ex- claimed, "For heaven's sake, sir, contradict me, Or pay me my thousand Frinds!" "Ole, I think it's lovely to be =reed," said young Mrs. Tocker to the lady on whom she was calling, "especially when you have a husband who is not afraid to compliment you." ."What does your husband say ? " "He said that I was getting to be a perfect Xanthippe:" "A. Xantheppe I Do you know who she was ?' Oh, yea; I asked Charley afterwards, and he told me she was the goddess of eyouth and beauty:" It is related of a certain divine, whose matri- monial relations are supposed not to have been of the most agreeable kind, that one Sabbath morn- ing, while reading to his congregation the parable of the Supper, •in which occurs the passage—" And another said, I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I go to prove them ; I pray thee have me excused. And another said, I have married a wife, and there- fore cannot come,' he suddenly paused at the end of this verse, drew off his spectacles, ind, look- ing on his hearers, said with emphasis—" The fact is, my brethren, one woman can draw a man further away from the kingdom of heaven than rk yoke of oxen." div.head: " CAPITAL " CHAT.
div.p: " CAPITAL " CHAT.

The death of Mr. Russell Lowell is as much la- mented in London as in America. Here, where he was well known, he was universally honoured. Per- haps, the feeling in his favour was accEntuated by the suspicion that he was required to leave the Court of St. James because his speeches in England were too British.

The Prince of Naples has, I am informed, definitely decided to visit several provincial towns before leaving England, among them being Birm- ingham, Manchester, Liverpool, and Leeds. The young Prince will embark at Newcastle for Bergen on the ordinary passenger steamer running betwcen the Tyne and Norway, and will pay a visit to the German Emperor at Berlin before returning to Italy.

According to advices from Kiel the improvement in the Emperor William's knee continues, and he has been walking .= the deck of the Hohenzollern. But for all that great care is still necessary. The Emperor's injury was the displacement cf the patella or knee-cap, which caused a strain of the ligaments. The knee had to be encased inplaster of Paris, but this was soon changed for a loose bandage, and on Monday morning, in the presence of Dr. Leuthold, a Kiel practitioner bandaged the knee afresh, in order to keep the knee-cap in its natural position.

In Mr. Balfeur's peaceful Ireland, 1,367 tenants have been converted into caretdkers by service of notice of ejectment at the suit of the landlord in the three months ending with June last. This is under the eviction-made-easy clause of the Land Act of 1887. Over 200 have been turned out of their hold- ings at the end of the period for which ejectment notices had been previously served. Thi3 is in ad- dition to .50 turned out under other processes of law at the landlords' suit. Evictions by creditors other than landlords have not numbered more than 18 in the samPperiod.

General Booth arrived on Monday .morning at Cape Town, on board the linior. Company's new twin- screw steamer The Scot, which has on this her maiden voyage accomplished the fastest passage ever made to the Cape. The steamer left Southamp- ton on the 25th of July and reached her destination at 4 40 a.m. on Monday, hernet steaming time being 15 days,.2 hours, and 10 minutes. Thic is 28 hours better than the Bunottar Castle's 16 days and 6 hours from Plymouth last december, and an im- provement of more than two days and nine hours over the quickest passage in July a year ago.

Speaking "broadly," the Inspector-General in Bankruptcy tell us that the insolvency of the trades which are based on commercial credit is diminish- ing, while that of the non-trading classes is station- aryor increasing. In other words,while the failures among those classes whose insolvency arises from personal extravagance, speculation, and gambling, or horn sickness, want of employment, and other accidental cau-es remain steady or increase, those arising from ordinary trading and industries are steadily diminishing under the wholesome influences of the increased stringency of our bankruptcy laws.

The member for Boston has, by legal process, changed his name, and will henceforth be known to fame as Henry Jahn Farmer-Atkinson. .It is not likely that this eccentric gentleman will drop into dullness in spite of his assumption of the double- barrelled appellative. His marked individuality, his brusque style of speech, and his ,picturesque figure will always secure him the attention of the House. There is just a danger of his overdoing his part or committing some indiscretion such as lately led him into trouble with the Speaker. In that case the House would be compelled again to deal with him in its summary way.

"Punch "thus hits off different points of view in "The Maiden and the Lockman She : What bliss it's to stay on the Lock all day Young and well-dressed and happy, And hear the men say as they glance my way, That's a nice girl, old chappie.
He:— What bosh to stay on my Lock all day, This billet I'm sorry I took it, The whole blooming day she gets in my way, I wish to the devil she'd hook it.

Mr. Dillon and Mr. O'Brien took off the gloves at Mallow on Sunday, and dealt Mr. Parnell some severe blows. The party of independent opposition, which Mr. Parnell has made his watchward, they described as independence of Mr. Gladstone and opposition to that leader; and their repudiation of Mr. Parnell was as emphatic as it was final and complete. Its effect has yet to be seen. Ido not anticipate that it will have the slightest influence upon Mr. Parnell himself. Ile has already survived some exceedingly severe blows, but goes on his way, and the only effect of the repudiation of those on whom he had placed his last lingering hopes will be to make his language in regard to them a little coarser.

Aix-la-Chapelle has its holy relics not less re- nowned than those of Treves. They are deposited in the Karl Chappelle, the Cathedral that Charle- magne built, and consist of a robe of the Virgin, the swaddling clothes of the Infant Christ, the cloth in which the body of John the Baptist was wrapped, and the linen cloth with which the Saviour was girded on the Cross. John, Patriarch of Jerusalem, is said to have bestowel these precious gifts upon .Charlemagne in the year 790. Certainly the shrine in which they are preserved dates back to the thir- teenth century. Once every seven years the relics are exhibited to the congregation of the faithful, who flock to Aix from all parts of Europe. The next opportunity will be in 1895.

The author of the" Biglow Papers " has been for ,thirty years a familar friend dear to all lovers of freedom and humanity. Those who had admired and revered Mr. Lowell as they knew him in his writings were, as a rule, a little disappointed when 7they first.encountered him in actual life. His admir- ation for English manners,customs,and institutions, and his constant intercourse with Englishmen had left.in his discourse and demeanour little that was characteristic of the writer. He seemed simply a well dressed, well mannered, well-informed man of the world, only distinguished from the mass of his congeners by the copiousness and variety of his knowledge and his confident way of settling con- troversies and c,oLunaunicating instruction.

Signor Verdi's hospital near Fiorenzuola cost in ,building £B,OOO. lie added an endowment of £40,000. He is now building in Milan a hospital for poor old artistes, which will cost him £20,000, The architect isCamillo Boito. Verdin will endow this hospital with a capital of £BO,OOO. The nm- ber of aged artists admitted will be 130; they will be taken from every province in Italy, and will be most comfortably boarded and lodged. A Genoese contemporary, in recording these benefactions, records also 'Verdi's dislike of his charitable deeds being published. " 1 don't want to be reduced to end my days in a 'hospital !" he said. "If I could manage that no one took any notice of the little good I attempt to do, I should live much more peacefully, and what little means are neces- sary for my own maintenance would be less threatened."

Savernake Hall with its beautiful forest and estates, will continue to be to Lord Ailesbury the "white elephant" which he has described it. Mr. Justice Stirling has refused him permission to sell the estates out of the family. The judgment was generally anticipated, as it would have been matter for much regret if the house, which has been the historic home of an ancient family for centuries, should have passed into other hands. At the same time, the judgment deprives Lord Iveagh of an opportunity he had much desired. Memories are very short. I find many people asking themselves w. i who is Lord Iveagh. The creation is a recent one, it s true. He is perhaps better known as Sir Edward Guinness Bart., the grandson of the great Dublin millionaire who founded his fortune in beer. Lord Iveagh is a man of immense wealth, ano it is said that if he were to pay the £750,000 he offered for Lord Ailesbury's estates ten times over he would still be left with a very fair income.

It was only sixteen years ago that people with old-fashioned notions about what they were pleased to consider " the sphere of women" were startled by hearing that Miss Martha Merington had been elected as a poor law guardian for the parish of Kensington. It was the first instance of the kind in England; but now there are no fewer than 108 lady guardians in England and Scotland, of whom the great majority have been chosen for English i parishes. Still more significant s the fact that they increase year by year in accelerating pace, last year alone having Adatlocl seventeen to the number. The

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, ATJGUST 15, 1891. FAIRY TALES. ILETITIA TITORSTON.

report of the society for promoting this movement, of which an abstract was published at the time of their last annual meeting, is now printed, and con- tains some interesting particulars. At last, says the Committee," the plea, so often urged, that it was but fair to permit women as well as men to have a share in the management of women and children, and likewise a voice in the care of the sick and the aged, seems to be fully admitted."

div.head: ACROSS THE ATLANTIC.
div.p: ACROSS THE ATLANTIC.
BY "TOWNSMAN." IX.-AMONG LIE AMERICANS.
RELIGIOUS LIFE—THE CHURCHES—THE PASTORS —GOSPEL TENEPERANCE—Y.M.C.A's.

Activity—should I not say aggression—is the chief characteristic of the religious life of the Americans. They believe in work, and push with a vigour that would startle and put to shame the easy-going people at home. From early on Sunday morning until late on Saturday night they are at work. They don't believe in a religion that seems to be concentrated in your go-to-meeting clothes, but in a religion that is of every day use. Four or five meetings on the SlLbbath,and one every night in the week, is the order of services across the Atlantic. The Americans run their churches on business , principles, and are strong in the belief that if you would have success you must just—work. They don't believe in hiding their light under a bushel, , but let everybody know what they are doing. They advertise their services as freely as they do their businesses, and, it must be added, with no little success. Their services are all well-attended, and when they get the people there the ministers or speakers just "go for" their hearers as if they meant it. The pastors are as "personal" as ever they can be, and it is truly refreshing to hear the frank outspoken declarations that emanate from the "desk." The services are made as bright and hearty as possible. The singing is lively, and there is pretty well of it. It is led by a quartette of pro- fessional vocalists, whose singing it is a treat to hear, and who are often assisted by a large choir.

div.head: "TM CHURCHES
div.p: "TM CHURCHES

are large, commodious, and comfortable buildings of brick or stone,or a combination of both materials. Sometimes the Sunday School is situated beneath the Church, but in any case, the edifices are ap- proached by a series of steps which lead to a spacious vestibule, from which entrance to the building is gained. Inside every effort is made to secure the comfort of the congregation. The seats are of the horseshoe shape, and each row is higher than the other, so that every person gets a full view of the minister. In the well of the church is placed the pastor's platform, which has no protecting rail, and which is furnished with a chair or two, and a sort of music stand on which the books are placed. Above and behind this are placed the choir stall and organ. Like the houses, the churches are heated in winter by the hot-air stoves, and as an additional aid to comfort in summer each pew is furnished with a fan. As you enter on Sun- day you are presented with a leaflet giving the en- gagements &c., of the week, and a printed sheet of hymns for the current service. At the Second Baptist Church in Chicago, a thousand persons of the artizan class attended,'and the services regularly opened and closed with the singing of the Doxology. It was a grand sight to see the great congregation • rise and sing this splendid hymn of praise.

div.head: PASTORS.
div.p: THE PASTORS.

All the pastors I heard preach were capable men who delivered very able discourses. It was notice- able that none of them used MS, and they threw themselves into their subjects with an energy that is becoming rare in England. Their feeling regard- ing the use of MS was illustrated one Sunday evening by a personal reminiscence of the Rev. Dr. Lawrence, pastor of the church above referred to. In the course of his subject dealing with the power of will, the rev, gentleman said that some time ago Ihe was alarmed to find his memory failing him. 1 He appealed to his friends for advice, and they un- animously advised him to rely upon MS. But that was against the grain, and for a whole week he struggled with himself, until he conquered, and thus avoided the use of MS. It would have been a great pity had it been otherwise, for the rev. Dr. addresses his large congregation with much free- dom, arid he interests them in a° way that would have been quite impossible had he had to keep his eye on a MS. American ministers take a leading part in the "Law and Order Committees," and un- dertake duties that would scare their English cossfreres. For instance, in one city I visited, some races were advertised to take place on Sunday. A large number of people attended, and with them two ministers, who insisted that the police should prevent the races taking place. As a resulc no races were held that day, and during the following week a public meeting was held at which the two brave pastors were thanked and commended for their action. Now, where are the ministers who will attempt to stop the glaring Sunday trading in Warrington?

div.head: GOSPEL TEMPERANCE.
div.p: GOSPEL TEMPERANCE.

In connection with a churct I attended in Bos- ton frequent gospel temperance meetings are held, and they are of a very free and easy order. Any member of the audience is at liberty to call for his or her favourite hymn, and some time is occupied in singing the hymns thus called for. Then the chairman will give an address upon a portion of scripture which is followed by more singing, and this is in turn followed by personal testimonies." Americans have great faith in the value of testi- monies, and very few meetings are held at which they are not given. It is remarkable how many speakers in these meetings speak against the use of tobacco, and express their thankfulness that they have been able to put away the "unclean thing." After the testimonies direct personal appeals were made to members of the audience to sign the pledge and these appeals were put in such a way that the people were literally compelled to sign the roll. 'There is plenty of variety at the services, and we had the pleasure . one evening of being entertained by a musical family. The family consisted of the father, two daughters, and a young son. The father played a cornet, one daughter presided at the piano, whilst the other daughter also played a cornet, and the son manipulated a trombone. It was rather strange to see a younglady handling a cornet, but it must be admitted she acquitted herself well. The family varied their instrumental performances by giving vocal selections, and their programme gave every satisfaction. YOUNG 'KEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATIONS. In almost every city there is a branch of the Young Men's Christian Association. Those I visited were well situated in suitable buildings in which there was every convenience for carrying on the work. The reading rooms were well supplied with the daily, weekly and monthly papers of that and the surrounding cities, and the libraries well ;stocked with standard works. Then there was a well furnished parlour for private meetings, and a large hall for public gatherings and services. Short meetings are held every night, and also on Sunday afternoons. At the latter services the conductors aim at variety, and at one meeting it was announced that no two meetings would be alike during the month. I attended frequent meetings, to see how they were conducted, and I found the evening meetings were ar- ranged very similar to the Gospel Temperance meetings. These gatherings were well attended, and at a Sunday afternoon service in a city not quite as large as arrington about a hundred young men attended. The meetings are arranged and conducted entirely by young men in business. I never saw a single elderly man or minister at any of the services. Great spirit and "go " characterise all the religious meetings, and not for an instant do the proceedings become so dull or monotonous as to produce soporific effects. Intense earnestness is shown by the young men, and I heard ladies from cities widely apart bear testimony to the good work that is being done in America and Canada by the agency of the Young Men's Christian Associations. The efforts of the latter are not exclusively of a religious character, for great attention is given to the physical develop- ment of the members.. Splendid gymnasia are attached to the institutions, and the wants of the , young men are catered for in a most lavish manner. In American cities the interests of young men are looked after in a way that is almost unknown in England, and the energy and push exhibited in everything the people take in hand commend them- selves to the attention of the stranger.

The United Cotton Spinners' Association has decided, at a meeting held in Manchester, to recommend the trade to take off the last advance of wages, provided a suffi- cient majority be obtained. It has also been decided to recommend the trade to stop their mills fourteen days at the earliest opportunity.

div.head: BRAVE TIN SOLDIER.
div.p: THE BRAVE TIN SOLDIER.

There were once five-and-twenty tin soldiers, who were all brothers, for they had been made out of the same old tin spoon. They shouldered arms and looked straight before them, and wore a splen- did uniform, red and blue. The first thing in the world they ever heard were the words, "Tin soldiers I" uttered by a little boy, who clapped his hands with delight when the lid of the box, in which they lay, was taken off. They were given him for a birthday present, and he stood at the table to set them up. The soldiers were all exactly alike, excepting one, who had only one leg; he had been left to the last, and then there was not enough of the melted tin to finish him, so they made him to stand firmly on one leg, and this caused him to be very remarkable. The table on which the tin soldiers stood, was covered with other playthings, but the most attrac- tive to the eye was a pretty little paper castle. Through the small windows the rooms could be seen. In front of the castle a number of little trees surrounded a piece of looking-glass, which was in- tended to represent a transparent lake. Swans, made of wax, swam on the lake, and were reflected in it. All this was very pretty, but the prettiest of all was a tiny little lady, who stood at the open door of the castle; she, also, was made of paper, and she wore a dress of clear muslin, with a narrow blue ribbon over her shoulders just like a scarf. In front of this was fixed a glittering tinsel rose, as large as her whole face. The little lady was a dancer, and she stretched out both her arms, and raised one of her legs so high, that the tin soldier could not see it at all, and he thought that she, like himself, had only one leg. "That is the wife for me," he thought; "but she is too grand, and lives in a castle, while I have only a box to live in, five- and-twenty of us altogether, that ,is no place for her. Still I must try and make her acquaintance." Then he laid himself at full length on the table . behind a snuff-box that stood upon it, so that he could peep at the little delicate lady, who continued to stand on one leg without losing her balance When evening came, the other tin soldiers were all placed in the box, and the people of the house went to bed. Then the playthings began to have their own games together, to pay visits, to have sham fights, and to give balls. The tin soldiers rattled in their box; they wanted to get out and join the amusements, but they could not open the lid. The nut-crackers played at leap-frog, and the pencil jumped about the table. There was such a noise that the canary woke up and began to talk, and in poetry too. Only the tin soldier and the dancer remained in their places. She stood on tiptoe, with her arms stretched out, as firmly as he did on his one leg. He never took his eyes from her for even a moment. The clock struck twelve, and, with a bounce, up sprang the lid of the snuff-box; but, in- stead of snuff, there jumped up a little black goblin; for the snuff-box was a toy puzzle. "Tin soldier," said the goblin, "don't wish for what does not belong to you." But the tin soldier pretended not to hear. "Very well; wait till to-morrow, then said the ' goblin. When the children came in the next morning, ' they placed the tin soldier in the window. Now, . whether it was the goblin who did it,or the draught, , is not known, but the window flew open, and out fell the tin soldier, heels over head, from the third storey, into the street beneath. It was a terrible fall; for he came head downwards, his helmet and his bayonet stuck in between the flagstones, and . his one leg up in the air. The servant-maid and . the little boy went downstairs directly to look for , him; but he was nowhere to be seen,although once . they nearly trod upon him. If he had called out, "Here I am," it would have been all right ; but he , was too proud to cry out for help while he wore a , uniform.

Presently it began to rain, and the drops fell faster and faster, till there was a heavy shower. When it was over, two boys happened to pass by, and one of them said, "Look, there is a tin soldier. He ought to have a boat to sail in."

So they made a boat out of a newspaper, and placed the tin soldier in it, and sent him sailing down the gutter, while the two boys ran by the side of it, and clapped their hands. Good gracious, what large waves arose in. that gutter ! and how fast the stream rolled on! for the rain had been very heavy. The paper boat rocked up and down, and turned itself roundsometimes so quickly that the tin soldier trembled; yet he remained firm; his coun- tenance did not change; he looked straight before him, and-shouldered his musket. Suddenly the boat shot under a bridge which formed part of a drain, and then it was as dark as the tin soldier's box.

"Where am I going now?" thought he. "This is the black goblin's fault, lam sure. Ah, well, if the little lady were only here with me in the boat, I should not care for any darkness." Suddenly there appeared a great water-rat, who lived in the drain.

"Have you a passport ?" asked the rat, "give it to ma at once." But the tin soldier remained silent and held his musket tighter than ever. The boat sailed on and the rat followed it. How he did gnash his teeth and cry out to the bits of wood and straw, "Stop him, stop him; he has not paid toll, and has not shown his pass." But the stream rushed on stronger and stronger. The tin soldier could al- ready see daylight shining where the arch ended. Then he heard a roaring sound quite terrible enough to frighten the bravest man. At the end of the tun- nel the drain fell into a large canal over a steep place, which made it as dangerous for him as a waterfall would be to us. He was too close to it to stop, so the boat rushed on, and the poor tin soldier could only hold himself as stiffly as possible, with- out moving an eyelid, to show that he was not afraid. The boat whirled lound three or four times, and then .filled with water to the very edge; nothing could save it from sinking. He now stood up to his neck in water, while deeper and deeper sank the boat, and the paper became soft and loose with the wet, till at last the water closed over the soldier's head. He thought of the elegant little dancer whom he should never see again, and the words of the song sounded in his ears--
"Farewell warrior! ever brave, Drifting onward to thy grave."

Then the paper boat fell to pieces, and the soldier sank into the water and immediately afterwards was swallowed up by a great fish. Oh how dark it was inside the fish! a great deal darker than in the tunnel, and narrower too, but the tin soldier con- tinued firm, and lay at full length, shouldering his musket. The fish swam to and fro, making the most wonderful movements, but at last he became quite still. After a while, a flash of lightning seemed to pass through him, and then the daylight appeared, and a voice cried out, "I declare here is the tin soldier." The fish had been caught, taken to the market and sold to the cook, who took him into the kitchen and cut him open with a large knife. She picked up the soldier and held him by the waist between her finger and thumb, and car- ried him into the room. They were all anxious to see this wonderful soldier who had travelled about inside a fish; but he was not at all proud. They placed him on the table, and—how many curious things do happen in the world !—there he was in the very same room from the window of which he had fallen, there were the same children, the same playthings standing on the table, and the pretty castle with the elegant little dancer at the door; she still balanced herself on one leg, and held up the other, so she wasas firm as himself. It touched the tin soldier so much to see her that he almost wept tin tears, but he kept them back. He only looked at her, and they both remained silent. Presently one of the little boys took up the tin soldier, and threw him into the stove. He had no reason for doing 90, therefore it must have been the fault of the black goblin who lived in the snuff-box. The flames lighted up the tin soldier, as he stood, the heat was very terrible, but whether it proeeeded from the real fire or from the fire of love he could not tell. Then he could see that the bright colours were faded from his uniform, but whether they had been washed off during his journey,/or from the effects of his sorrow, no one could say. He looked at the little lady, and she looked at him. Ile felt himself melting away, but he still remained firm with his gun on his shoulder. Suddenly the door of the room flew open, and the draught of air caught up the little dancer, she fluttered like a sylph right into the stove by the side of the tin soldier, and was instantly in flames and was gone. The tin soldier melted down into a lump, and the next morning, when the maid-servant took the ashes out of the stove, she found him in the shape of a little tin heart. But of the little dancer no- thing remained but the tinsel rose, which was burnt black as a cinder.

BY LOUISA BIGG. AUTHOR OF "CLARE WELSMAN," ETC.
CHAPTER XTV.

One clear spring morning the crocuses round the Firs were in full bloom, encircling the house with a golden halo. In the beds on the grassplat blue scented irises and snowdrops and hyacinths made a fair show and were haunted by a multitude of bees, their velvet coats laden with pollen. Near the breakfast-room was a bed of great Russian violets, whose perfume wafted in through the open win- dow in company with the sweet spring sunshine that streamed over the white covered table. Miss Priscy was moving hither and thither about the room, clinking the tea-cups and pouring hot water into the pot, and cutting bread and butter. She was thinking about Dillon, but not at all uneasily, for he evidently could have no intentions with re- gard to his cousin, else he would not have gone away so quietly. "And the dear child looked as bright as possible; I am thankful that after all it was my fancy, and that they did not care for each other. I am convinced it is her fate to marry Mr. Dela.field, and it is thoroughly suitable in every way." I wonder whether any girl ever fancied a mar- riage which all her friends thought "thoroughly suitable ? " Poor Miss Priscy ! she would have been astonished if she could have read her cousin's thoughts at that moment, for Detitia was standing at her window upstairs and looking at the blue sky with a heart glowing with love for her far-off hero and wondering if such joy could last. She came tripping downstairs and, kissing Miss Priscy, took her seat at the table. "I was just thinking of Robert, my love," said Miss Priscy. "And what of Robert?" asked Lmtitia with a little rippling laugh; it was a delight to her to hear him spoken of—to speak his name. "Why he ought to be on his way back, now; do you remember on which day he said he should start?"

"On the third; that was last Tuesday week." How often she had thought of the good ship speeding over the waters, the distance between her and England lessening hour by hour, and minute by minute; as Letitia worked or read she could hear the plash of the waves round the Andalusia's timbers and it made the music of her dreams at "Then he ought to be in London in a few days; I wonder if he will run down and see us,* said bliss Priscy. " I wonder if he will," answered Letitia, blush- ing and feeling rather guilty. She fetched her hat after breakfast and announced her intention of going down the village. "It is too lovely to stay indoors," she said, "and I want to see Jessie about the frock for Mrs. Pres- ton's baby, for I have not the least idea how to cut it out. lam afraid you have brought me up to be very impractical, Cousin Priscy ; why did not you teach me better T"

"There was no necessity, my love," said her cousin, placidly; "perhaps it may be as well for you to learn such things, but you will always have someone to do them for you." "But, supposing I marry a poor man," said Lmtitia, "what a shocking housekeeper I shall make."

"I trust you will never do anything of the kind," said Miss Priscy, looking as much horrified as if LeLitia had proposed to commit murder. " It is as well to be prepared for all emer- gencies," said Letitia, wickedly; "I think I shall ask cook to let me make the pudding for our dinner to-day." She ran gaily down the lawn in the sunshine and out into the lane. Here was the gate by which she and Robert had stood to watch the setting sun one wintry evening; there was the field they had crossed so often together; and in the distance she could see the glitter of the water in the pond where they had skated that first morning. How long ago that morning seemed! how dull and colourless her life had been till then! "Life is very sweet," she said to herself ; "come what will, I shall have tasted it."

She was in tune with the spring and not a shadow of care or fear crossed her mind that morning. When she reached Jessie's door, she found it wide open, and being free of the house at all times she did not stop to ring the bell, but walked straight to the breakfast-room. No one was there, so she crossed the haal and went into the dining-room. That, too, was empty, and she sat down and resolved to wait till someone appeared. There was a newspaper on the table, and she took it up to while away the time. There was a long account of an accident to one of the Royal Family's carriages which ended in some- body's ankle being sprained; the proceedings of a bribery commission then sitting in some rotten borough; a description of a new watering-place what was to heal the public of all its ills; and a multitude of advertisements. "No news" said Letitia, turning the sheet over; "how I wish Jessie would come; I think I will ring the bell." She rose to cross the room, laying the paper on the table—and then she saw it.

(Through Reuter's Agency). "Steamship Andalusia from Quebec to London. Lost with all hands. Seen on fire by Schooner Europa. Boats sent out, but no one picked up. Two hundred passengers on board." Letitia did not scream or faint. She got out of the house somehow and hurriedly wandered towards home. She could not think or feel or believe the horror, and almost lost the consciousness of her own identity. The lane and the garden and the house all looked strange to her, and when she saw Miss Priscy in the hall she stared at her and said not a word. _ _ _ _

--;:-Lietitsia-, my dearest child, what is the matter with you," cried her cousin in alarm; she thought Ltetitia had overwalked herself, or that the sun had been too warm for her. " Letty, for pity's sake speak to me !" and she took the girl's cold hand in hers. Letitia gently pushed her away and moved towards the stairs.

"He is dead," she said, in a harsh voice, "drowned in the Andalusia; she was seen on fire." Miss Priscy cried, "Oh, my God, how dreadful! It can t be true !' and burst into tears; Lmtitia put her hand to her head and went slowly up to her room, tearless.

All that day Lmtitia lay on her bed in a sort of stupor, making no response to Miss Priscys loving cares. When night came she undressed herself mechanically, and her cousin lay down beside her, but neither of them slept. When morning dawned at last, with its twittering of birds and stir of joyous spring life, Letitia fell into a heavy sleep. Miss Priscy gently rose and left the room, but even then she did not wake. Miss Priscy had her breakfast and came back and sat by the bed, full of anxious forebodings, and herself very sorrow- ful for Robert, for she had grown to love him dearly. About midday Lretitia woke. "I ought to get up," she said; "it must be late." "Are you well enough to come down, love 2" "Oh, yes," she answered faintly, and began moving about the room. Her face was miserably pale, and her long hair hung about her shoulders. Mies Priscy left her to dress, and presently she came downstairs, and sat down in the breakfast room, looking out of the window. She had put on a black dress, and wore none of her ornaments. All the house might know now that she loved Robert, and that he had loved her. It was the one thing that bore her up through those days— the remembrance that she was his, and that she had a right to mourn him. There was nothing more to live for—and morning, noon, and night her heart was bleeding for him, but she would not shame his memory by making those who loved her wretched. Once or twice it flashed across her that it could not be—that he was not dead—but she always put from her that unreasoning hope, and remembered with a dumb anguish how she had felt too happy and content. To all telegrams, to all enquiries made there was but one answer—nt news.

She watched feverishly for the postman, but no tidings came and the Andalusia was swept out of existence so swiftly and silently that in a few days, people had forgotten the very name of the ship that had gone down; there are so many calamities daily; why should we who are fed and clothe 4, vex our souls with their memory? A battle with its thousands slain—a string of trapped revolu- tionaries dragging hopeless to Siberia—a suicide for which (the world being so satisfactory) no reason can be assigned—an unwedded mother murdering her shameful child —an Andalusia lost—if we took these things to heart our daily newspaper would soon cease to be the diverting playbill that it is, and we should become lean and uncomfortable citizens of the world.

div.head: CHAPTER XV.
div.p: CHAPTER XV.
11l news spreads fast, and before the week was out the whole village had heard Of loss. The tidings were rec.:civet' hi variens ways, some of

the villagers expressing genuine pity and sorrow for the young stranger, whose bright face and manner had won upon their liking, while others regarded the fact of any man's venturing upon the sea as a direct tempting of Providence, which rendered a violent death not altogether unde- served.

"Folks will be so restless and onsettled," reflected old Mrs. Preston one day to her daughter- in-law, "if they will go a wool-gathering all over the world what can they expect? It is very dull to think as he has got drownded, but I say he should have stopped at home." And the old lady felt herself quite a superior being on the strength of having never travelled further than ten miles from her native village. "But Mr. Dillon was obliged tb go to America, mother ; you see, things could not go on if every- body stopped at home. Miss Laatitia told me it was business as took him," _

"Was there any talk of his marrying Miss Loetitia ?" broke in Mrs. Preston, who was some- what impatient of this explanation. "I never heard any talk of it," said Mary truthfully, though deceitfully, for she knew as well as if she had been told, how it was between Dillon and Letitia, but with a delicacy which many a lady might have imitated with advantage, she ignored her know- ledge. "They say she's dressed in mourning," con- tinued Mrs. Preston, going to the door, "and looks seared like, and as white as a ghost. Whatever have you given the chickens? Just look at their crops; they've been eating till they're a misery to theirselves and everybody else." "Eating won't kill them, mother; they hays only had some bits of potato. Does Miss Lmtitia gp out? Have you seen her in the village ?" "No ; it was Mary Simpkins saw her when she went to the House about clear-starching. It seems to me a deal of fuss to make about the young man if he was not going to be her husband; but gentle- folks have queer ways with them. Good-bye, my gal, I must be getting home again." And the old lady trudged home to get ready a mysterious dish entitled a "toad in the hole" for her husband's dinner.

"In mourning, and scared like, and as white as a ghost." The description of Miss Thornton went to Mary's heart, and she thought of her all the morning, and gradually her thoughts shaped them- selves into action, She went into her little hen- house and gathered together the newlaid eggs in a basket and put on the top a bunch of such flowers as grew in her cottage garden. Then she went upstairs and smoothed her pretty brown hair, and put on her best clothes and her Sunday bonnet, and set off for the Firs with her basket in her hand. She knew that there were eggs and flowers in plenty at the great house, but these were all she had to give, and she felt that Miss Thornton would understand. As she neared the house, she began to tremble with shyness, and longed to turn back, but she held bravely on and rung the bell. She had hardly done so when she heard footsteps behind her, and turning saw Lwtitia. "I have made free to bring you a few eggs, Miss," she said, flushing painfully and hardly able to restrain her tears at Luetitia's altered looks. "Thank you," said Lxtitia, "how kind of you to think of it; come in and sit down." She led the way into her little sitting-room and brought Mary some refreshments with her own hands. Neither spoke of the bad news that had come— Letitia could not, and Mary dared not—but when Mary rose to go, the tears were running down her cheeks, and the two women whose sorrow was alike clasped each other's hands with a long, tender pressure. There was something in it all that opened the floodgates of Miss Thornton's grief, and she was hardly alone when she dropped upon the sofa and hiding her face, burst into an uncon- trollable fit of weeping. Mary went out at the gate very mournfully, and just as she was turning into the lane the postman came up with a letter in his hand. lie knew Mary and stopped to speak to her, holding the letter so that she could see it. A shock ran through her frame, and her eyes were rivetted to the writing upon the envelope; surety, surely, she had seen that clear, upright hand before; it was different to other people's writing; it flashed across her that she had seen it on the envelope in her baby's hands and it was Dillon's. She grew so confused that she did not know what the letter might mean, but one thing she was suddenly impelled to do; she must take it herself .to Miss Thornton. "I will take in the letter," she said trying to speak care- lessly, "I am going back to the house.' And the postman, willing to save himself a few steps, gave it to her at once, She hid it under her jacket and hurried back to the house. • PlAiass can I see Miss Thornton again ?" she asked the servant who answered the ring, "I have something else to say to her." "Oh, yes, she is still in her boudoir; you know your way back, don't you ? " answered the maid, who happened to be busy, and Mary without wait- ing for any more went swiftly along the passages and knocked gently at Miss' Thornton's door. There was no answer, but she could hear her sobbing within; for a moment Mary hesitated, then she made bold to push the door open and go up to where Laatitia was crouching, and lay the letter in her lap. She looked up, saw the writing dimly through her tears, and faint and sick tried to tear open the envelope with her trembling fingers. At last she reached the letter, read it in a sort of stupor and then fell to the ground with a strange cry. The servants heard and came running in, and Miss Priscy followed, and they raised Lwtitia and laid her on the sofa. She had not fainted, but was In a maze of incredulous joy. "Am I dreaming? ' she cried ; "tell me, I am awake, I dreamt that Robert was alive; it says he is coming! I think I must be mad—but it says he is coming ! " and she sobbed convulsively, afraid as yet to smile. Miss Priscy, saw the letter on the floor and picked it up. "Dearest Ltitia, ' it began, "have you given me up for lost, I wonder, or have you felt that I must come back? I have been as near death as man ever was to escape and live, but I was saved as if by a miracle and landed at Liverpool this morning. Look for me to-night." "Yours, in life or death,
"ROBERT DILLON."

If he had "come coffined home ' they could not have wept more than they did for a while over that letter, and then Mary Preston went home again glad yet sorrowful, becalse so few return from the grave and the sleep of her dead was too deep for any waking.

div.head: CHAPTER XVI.
div.p: CHAPTER XVI.

It was a few days later than the time of the events described in my last chapter. Robert Dillon had come and told his strange story of how he had swum from the burning ship, and all the night had clung to a hencoop, and driven hither and thither with death always at hand. And how when he was chilled to the heart and almost gone, a merchantman had seen him, and sent a boat and rescued him. She was bound for Liverpool with a cargo of corn, and had picked up half a dozen other drowning passengers, and the boatfal of women and part of the crew, and among the saved was Simpson. No sooner was Robert hauled on deck a drenched woful object, than the poor boy knew him and with a cry of joy ran to him and fell to kissing his dripping feet, and sobbing out that this was the man who died for him.

Bad weather came on, and kept them out at sea, so that they could not make Liverpool at the expected time, and were several days over-due, but one happy morning, with swelling sails, they rode before a fair wind into port. So Robert Dillon had come home and was Lzetitia's aeknowledged lover —her betrothed whom she gladly and proudly showed to all who loved her. Many came to rejoice with her, and there were many kindly visits to pay, not forgetting Mary Preston's cottage. The lovers went there first, and then on to the vicarage. Letitia no sooner entered the drawing. room than she felt by instinct that something un- usual had happened. John Grayson was there, looking amused and perplexed; Mrs. Grayson's eyes were red; Jessie was blushing immoderately; and finally, Mr. Delafield sat there with a cup of five o'clock tea at his side, and at sight of the new corners looked as embarrassed and conscious as it was possible for so composed a gentleman to look. The moment was evidently not opportune for a lengthened call, so after a few minutes chat, they rose to go, Lwatia feeling as certain as if she had been officially informed that her admirer had con- soled himself.

"I did not know that Delafield was so intimate at the draysons," said Dil.on innocently, when they reached the open air. "I do not suppose he knew it himself till lately," answered Letitia, laughing; "I am very glad; it will be a capital match for them both." "You never told me they were engaged • what a fool he must be not to know his own mind:"

"I do not know that some other people are very wise: You used to be vexed with him because you thought he liked me, and now you are vexed with him because he does not. I have not heard they are engaged, but I am certain of it." It was quite true, and Jessie came next day and told her all about it, and could scarcely believe in her olvn happiness.

"'on emit think how good he is, Letitia," she said, with tears in her eyes; "he is going to endow the living and make John and Lizzie as rich as possible.; is it not delightful to think of it?" "I think it is all delightful," said Miss Thorn- ton, kissing her, "and he could not have done better."

"Do you really think so? I am so glad! I was afraid you would not approve it, and—per- haps you will think me silly—l always used to think he cared for you, and I used to feel so. wicked and jealous. It is wonderful that every- thing should have turned out right." Miss Priscy. was the only person not satisfied with the engage- ment, she persisted in considering that the couples were sorted wrong, though she prudently kept this opinion to herself. Mr. Delafield and Jessie are already married, and the latter is much meeker in. her silks and jewels than she was in serge and holland aprons. Mrs. Grayson has a governess, and is regaining something of her old bloom under the unlooked-for prosperity that has fallen to her' share, while the careful lines are vanishing from her husband's face.

In the spring Dillon and Lmtitia Thornton are to be married too, and they are full of high hopes, and are intent to do well, not to themselves alone, but to the world. And, being thus intent, who knows but that, groping in the twilight, they may not touch some hidden spring that may unlock, the treasure of peace and goodwill to all mankind..
THE END.

div.head: LADY AND THE SKYLARK.
div.p: THE LADY AND THE SKYLARK.
BY THOMAS MILLER. Author of " Gideon Giles," &c.

Sheltered from day's great golden eye, I saw a lovely lady stand, Watching a lark sing up the sky, Shading her fair face with her hand. "A happy life is that of thine, Dear bird of heaven," methought she said, "I would that such a path were mine, With trails of glory round me spread." Around her lay a land of flowers, O'erhung with summer's greenest bowers. Said she, "The sky is all thine own, Soar where thou wilt no bound'ry's near; For thee the heavens are open thrown, How I should like to hover there, And be as near those gates as thou, Without a fear—without a care !" A golden light fell on her brow And rippled all her wealth of hair; And on her lips sweet smiles did play• Like sunbeams round a rose in May. Said she, " I would I were that bird, I'd soar and sing o'er dale and dell." There was more music in each word That from those parted roses fell, Than ever lark rained from the sky. "Said, I "Would I were mate to thee "-- For in the soft blue of her eye There lay a sleeping ecstacy, Like perfume cradled in a flower,, And waiting its appointed hour. With jessamines, whose starry light Gleams through the green, embowering shade. Throwing their fragrance on the night,— Her wavy hair, I'd fondly braid ; And basking in her dreamy eyes Each day discover sweeter charms, And find another Paradise Within the Eden of her arms. Vain dreams ! the lark then ceased its lay While homeward she retraced her way. "Thou, from thy watch tower in the skies, Can's look down on thy speckled mate That somewhere mid the daisies lies; Would mine were such a happy fate." "And mine !" unto myself I said, "Then would I make my longing heart A pillow for thy lovely head, And pray we never more might part. As on the blossom hangs the bee Sweet flower ! So would I cling to thee." Said she: "Up in the sky so blue, Where clouds like silver mountains lie, Outstretched 'neath thy expansive view, Like thee, sweet bird, I fain would fly."' I smiled to picture one so fair, Her garments streaming in the sun, Floating with all her blown-back hair; • And so I let my fancy run, Till she seemed hovering 'mid the light Like a winged angel, in my sight.
THE ORGAN GRINDERS' PRIVILEGE.

A correspondent writing to the "Daily News says :—" Your leader note upon the subject of Italian organ grinders reminds me of the curious fact that these arch-disturbers of our domestic peace are the especial pets and port6ges of International copyright law as embodied in that courageous and far-reaching document, the Berne Convention. When the plenipotentiaries from the various con- tracting countries were assembled in solemn con- clave at Berne. it suddenly occurred to one of their number to ask what was to become of the poor organ grinders if nobody was to be permitted to appropriate composers' music without paying for it. Strange to say, this appeal appears to have awakened a sympathetic response in the breasts of that distinguished assembly; and from that day the organ grinder has become the chartered libertine of musical copyright. At this moment, for example, not a theatre or a concert room dares play a tune from Mikado,' 'Dorothy,' or The Nautch Girl,' without permission first obtained ; but the bogey— I beg pardon, the organ—man, may grind away at these or any other copyright tunes to his heart's. content; for by Article 3 of the 'Final Protocol 'it is expressly provided that the manufacture and sale of instruments for the mechanical reproduction of musicals airs shall not be considered as constitut- ing an infringement of musical copyright.' I should be sorry to deprive any plenipotentiary of a just claim to the gratitude of mankind, but surely I can hardly be mistaken in guessing that this curious in- dulgence was adopted on a suggestion of Signor Baccaria the Italian Charge d' Affaires."

div.head: FIRST FUCEI-SIA IN ENGLAND.
div.p: THE FIRST FUCEI-SIA IN ENGLAND.

Now that flower services are being held in our various churches and chapels, the following account of the introduction of the first fuchsia, which was written some 40 years ago by Mr. Sheppard, of Dublin, is worth re-production Some 60 years ago, the late Mr. Lee, of Hammer- smith, was showing some of his fine plants to a gentleman, when the latter remarked, "Well, Mr. Lee, you have not a prettier flower in all your col- lection than one 1 saw in a window in the east end of London a few days ago." Mr. Lee inquired, "Pray, what is it like ?" The gentleman said the plant was most elegant, the flowers hanging in tassels from the pendant branches, colour of the richest crimson, and in the centre a fold of deep purple, and so forth.

Mr. tee having learnt where the plant was to be found, posted off directly, and on his arrival per- ceived at once that the plant was new in this part of the world. The plant belonged to a sailor's wife and she had it in a pot in the window. He stood and admired it; then, entering the house, he said, "My good woman, this is a nice plant; I should like to buy it." " I could not sell it for money; it was brought to me from the West Indies by my husband, who has left again,and I must keep it for his sake." "But I must have it," said Mr. Lee. " But you shall not," said the sailor's wife. Here Mr. Lee emptied his pocket of gold, silver and cop- per, the stock amounting to fomething more than eight guineas." Well-a-day," said the woman," but that is a power of money; sure the plant is yours." Having got the plant safel3 deposited in his nursery, Mr. Lee's first work was to pull off every vestige of flower. Every effort was now made to multiply the plant, and by the next season Mr. Lee was the delighted possessor of 300p1ants. The two which opened first were removed to the show- house. A lady came" Why, Mr. Lee,where did you get this charming plant ? " " H'm, this is a new thing. my lady; pretty is it not?': "It's price ? " "One guinea. Thank your ladyship, said Mr. Lee. Another and another went, until at the end of the fist season Mr. Lee had 300 golden guineu in his purse, the produce of the single plant. Mr. Lee did not forget to gladden the sailor's wife by presenting her with a plant of his favourite flower. This is the way in which the first fuchsia came into Eng- land.

div.head: TIE LIGHTS HIS PIPE ONCE MORE.
div.p: TIE LIGHTS HIS PIPE ONCE MORE.

Some fifty years ago the English ship " Argos" was wrecked on a a low-lying 'key or sand Island of the Bahama group. Only one man, a sailor, was thrown safely on the beach by the waves. In his pocket was a tin tobacco-box, a pipe, and a flint and steel. Wringing the water from his clothes, he seated himself, lighted his- pipe, and with true British phlegm proceeded to consider his situation. The moral of which is that when an Englishman, having the means, refuses to smoke, he is In very bad form. For example, here is a man who says," I always enjoyed my pipe, but now I couldn't take a whiff." To be sure there was a reason, and he puts it in this way. "Up to Michaelmas, 1887," he says, "I was a strong, healthy man. About this time I began to feel bad at my stomach and had no relish for food. I had a bad taste in the mouth, and after eating I would retch and vomit until the water oozed out of my eyes; and so bad was this that my wife had to hold my head. My eves turned yellow, and I felt low, weak, and nervous. Sometimes I would break out into a sweat and then go cold and chilly. "I couldn't touch solid food, and for months I belched up sour water; and what I did eat lay heavy upon, and seemed to be dead and lifeless in my body. Feeling low and depressed, I had no enjoyment in company." " Before this Twas alwnys cheerful and enjoyed my pipe, hut now I couldn't take a whiff." "I had a craving, gnawing pain at the stomach which nothing eased for long together. I had bran poultices applied, and took different kinds of medicine, but nothing went to the spot, nothing eased me. After a time I had to give up my work, for I got so weak and nervous I couldn't hit my work iron, and my tools and things few out of my hand. "For over four months I did not have a single good night's rest. I would turn and turn in bed all night long, and my wife and I often sat up the best part of the night rather than go to bed. I went so thin that my clothes fairly hung upon me. Friends who came to see me told one another I could not get better, and even my wife said I would do no more work in this world. "For more than twelve months I had a clever doctor attending me, but his medicine did me no good; then I went to see a physlciaca at Sudbury, with the same re- sult. The doctors sounded my lungs,'but found nothing wrong, and said all my ailments:were brought on by bad digestion. "I now got weaker, and weaker, and had given up all hopes of recovery, when in the spring of 1889, a lady from London who was staying at the vicarage atOtten Belcharnp heard of my condition. She called at Mr. Goody's the medicine dealer, and told him to supply me with some Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup and she would pay for it. Very reluctantly I took the medicine, for I .had tried so many things without obtaining any benefit. However, my wife pressed me so hard that at last I began to take the Syrup. After a few doses I said to my wife, I think I feel better for this medicine,' and from that time I commenced to improve. By the time I had taken three bottles I was back at my work, as strong and well as ever—much to the surprise of everybody. " People all about said I would never get well, but I did, thank the Lord. "Now I tell everyone that Mother Seigel's Syrup saved my life. I can now eat anything, and feel so light-hearted I could jump over a five-barred gate. My neighbours all say I look ten years younger." ELIAS BrANn, shoemaker, Belchamp St. Paul, Clare, Suffolk.

The doctors who attributed Mr. Bland's illness to in- digestion and dyspepsia were quite right. All they lacked was the proper remedy. This appeared in Mother Seigel's Syrup, and now our good friend enjoys his pipe as he did in other years. If he is ever handled in that way again we may wager he won't forget what to do.
THE NEW EDUCATION ACT.

The following synapsis of the Education Act which comes in force next month has been prepared by a school manager The main object of the Act is to extinguish or reduce school fees, and where it is adopted, 10s. per annum per head in average attendance is allowed by Govern- ment. The Act leaves untouched The management of day schools. The religious rights of day schools. The 17s. 6d. limit of grant. Evening schools. The Act does not compel Any school to come under its clauses. Any school to provide free places. Any school managers May ignore the Act. May comply from September Ist, 1891. May defer compliance till August 31, 1892. May at any time change their mind. Any parent May claim a free place in a free school. May join with others in claiming free places. Age of children earning fee grant: From three years to 15 years old.

Average attendance: School must be opened 400 times in a year. Every attendance of half-timer counted as one and a half. .5 or larger decimals in average counted as 1. Attendances of children under 3 or over 15 not counted. Payment of fee grant: Quarterly, at the end of 3rd, 6th, 9th months, and close of school year. The three first quarters on average of previous year. The last quarter the balance;on the average for the current year. Section 2 (3) allows balance due and not actually paid to be included in the year's accounts to pro- vide against the 17s. 6d. limit. Managers must ascertain: (1) Gross amount of school fees. (2) Amount charged for books, &c. (3) The average attendance. These must be for the last school year which ter- minated before January Ist, 1891. Classes of schools : Class I.—Schools in which the school fees alone pre- viously charged exceed 10s. per child per year on average attendance: These may charge tne difference between the fee grant and the pence previously charged. May charge for books, slates, &c. May allow a portion of free places. N.B.—lf an excess of fee is charged the fee grant will be reduced except when joined to another poorer school, which it may help to maintain. Class ll.—Schools in which fees alone do not exceed the 10s. per child, but where fees and book charges together do exceed 10s.: These become free for fees. May charge for books, &c. Class lll.—Schoels in which fees and book charges do not exceed 10s. Must be free. Cannot charge for books. Class IV .—Ordinary new schools (opened after Janu- ary Ist, 1891). May not charge school fees. May charge for books, &c. Class V.—High grade new schools. May be authorized by the Department. If sufficient free places exist in district. If for the advantage of the district. If fees not exceeding 6d. per week be charged. But must be reported specially to Parliament, and the Department may apply all or any portion of school fees in reduction of fee grant. .Associated Schools: Managers of adjacent voluntary schools may form a Joint Committee, and, making a common fund of all their fee grants, may distribute the same among the associated schools in any proportion they may agree upon. But any sum in excess of the fee grant earned by any one school must not be entered in Form 9, or in any way affect the 17s. 6d. limit. The Joint Committee may receive and distribute voluntary contributions. May appoint visiting teachers, to teach drawing, cookery, science, &c., in the group of schools. School Boards: Will be appointed in any district where sufficient free places are not provided.
May declare their own schools free. May form amongst themselves groups of associated schools.
irARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. Mr. Balharry presided, and there were also present the Rev. G. F. Roberts,Messrs. Ratcliffe, Heaton, Davies, Hood-Wright,D. Jones, Hibbert,Owen,Clarke,Diggle, Gill, Dobson, Aukland, Turton. Humphreys, Smith, J. Houghton, Kilshall, Mather, Dignum, W. Hough- ton, Jolly, Swinton, J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), C. H. Ward (Workhouse master), and H. M. Mines (Superintendent of Padgate schools).

THE PLDGATE scalooLs. The Schools Committee reported that the health of be children was good. The Superintendent was in- structed to advertise for a mother for No. 3 home, and also for a super-numerary assistant to the homes in the place of Miss Foard. Mr. T. Pollit having declined the appointment as assistant schoolmaster the Committee now recommended the appointment of Mr. J. R. Jones to the post, and he had expressed his readiness to accept it.—The minutes were confirmed.
THE RETURNS

The CLERK said he h;aci-reCeived his usual returns from all the townships with the exception of Penketh.—Mr. Dignum said this omission on the part of Penketh would be due to the death of Mr. Wilson, the late assistant overseer. The Clerk said it was understood that was the reason.

div.head: SCHOOL FEES.
div.p: SCHOOL FEES.
The School Fees Committee reported that fees had been allowed in 37 cases. THE NEWTON RELIEVING OFFICERSHIP.-SIXTY-FIVE
APPLICATIONS.

The CLERK said he had communicated with the Ocean Accident and Guarrantee Association with regard to the circumstances which led to the dismissal of Mr. Caldwell, the relieving officer. at Newton, and said that a gentle- man from that Society had called upon him. The Local Government Board, whom the Clerk had also informed of the same circumstances, wrote that, in accordance with their usual practice in similar cases they had written to Mr. Caldwell at his last known addre9s requesting him to furnish them with an explanation within three days. They would further communicate with the Guardians; who should not proceed to the appoint- ment of a successor until thtre was 'a legal vacancy in the office. The Clerk added that there were sixty odd applications for the vacant relieving officership, and, as it would be impossible to .o through all the applications that day, he suggested that Guardians should at that meeting nominate any of the applicants they desired, and that, in addition, he list of applicants should lie at his office until next Wednesday so that in the meantitne any two Guardians might, if they wished, nominate another applicant who would then be placed on the selected list. The object of that was that careful con- sideration should be given to the merits of any candidate who might not happen to have a friend there that day. He suggested, therefore, that they pass the following resolution: "1. That a' selected list be made of candidates who are to-day nominated by a mover and seconder.-2. That to afford an opportunity for further careful exam- ination of the applications and testimonials the same lie on the table at the Clerk's office until Tuesday, August 25.-3. That any two guardians may nominate one other candidate by placing their initials to the number of such candidate, and the same shall be included in the selected list; provided that the same two guardians, after the present Board meeting nominate but one, and that such nomination be made not later than Wednesday next.-4. That on Thursday, August 20, a circular be sent to each candidate in the selected list, and that the Board will elect the relieving officer at their Board meet- ing on August 26, when selected candiates may attend if they so desire."—This resolution was adopted as sug- gested.—.A selection was then made from a printed list of applicants the total number of whom was 65. Most of these, of course, resided in Warrington, Newton, or Earlestown, but there were some who lived at more dis- tant places, such as Southport, Preston, Manchester, Runcorn, Sandbach, Ditton, and even London. In the course of some conversation Mr. Dobson jocu- larly inquired if he might propose a lady, but the reply to this query was a unanimous negative. The following is a list of the candidates who were selected, the figures given being the ages as furnished by the applicants :—Arthur Frost, High-at., Newton, 21 ; Thomas Bowes (P.C.), Earlestown, 32 ; John Hogan, 41, Marsh House-lane • J. H. J. Hampson, 11, Academy-st., 25; Michael McCoy, Newton-le-Willows ; Herbert H. Massey, 19, Dixon-st., 27; W. H. Wallington, 30, Bew- sey-road, 35 ; Joseph Williams, 293, Wargrave-road, Newton, 37 ; Thomas Unswerth, 51, Cross-lane, Earles- town; Frederick Davies, Penketh ; James C. Lawson, Birkenhead ; George Clarke, 3, Alpine-st., Earlestown, 36 ; John Insley, 9, Wellington-st., Earlestown 42 ; Thomas Kent, Wargrave, Newton; Charles Millard, Great Sankey ; George Goff, Crow-lane, Newton, 34 ; Thomas Davies, 47,Clipsley Cottages, Haydock,26 ; Wm. Turner, 3, Stamey-st., Earlestown ; 42; Frank Herbert Aukland, 15, Froghall-lane, 22 ; James Peers, 73, Well- field-st., 25 ; J. H. Graham, 296, Earle-st., Earlestown; 38; Edwin John Mitchell, 67, Bewsey--st., 42 ; Richard Bent, 146, Mill-brow, Sutton, 30 ; Philip Powlson, But- tennarket-st., 28 ; Enoch A. Hollingworth (P.C.), War- rington, 36. It was resolved that an adjourned meeting of the Board should be held next Friday for the purpose of reducing the number of selected candidates. Thefinal appointment will be made at the usual Board meeting on the Wednesday following.

WARRINGTON AND THE " FREE " EDUCATION ACT. At the invitation of the managers, a meeting of the parents of the scholars attending Trinity Day Scnools was held on Monday evening in the school- room, Mueeum-st.," to consider the Education Act recently passed, and to settle a table of fees for the future in accordance with its provisions." There was a small attendance which included the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton (chairman of the Managers' Commit- tee), (the Rev. W. E. Glenn, Mr. W. Johnson, Mr. James Bolton, &c. The Vicar presided, and referr- ing to the Act, said the object of the Government in pass- ing the measure no doubt was to relieve parents as much as pgssible from the payment of school fees for their children. They gave a specified sum for each child for that object. It was, however, not quite sufficient to pay the fees in every case, that was, the whole of the fees. In some cases there might be no fees to pay,and in other cases they might be considerably reduced, to the great advantage of the parent. The Government could not make all schools perfectly free without being guilty of a certain amount of unfairness. There were schools in which the fees were higher than in others-6d. and 9d. a week—and it would be hardly fair for the Government to say, "We will pay 6d. and 9d. for one man, while we are only willing to pay the 3d. or 4d. for another man who may happen not to be quite so well off." If they did so they would be giving twice as much to a man who was well off as they were to a man who was not so well off ,and who might only be obtaining a labourers' wages. The Government, therefore, decided, and he thought acted very wisely and fairly, to treat all alike, and give 10s. a year to the parents for each child attending school. If the parents wished to send their children to a school were high fees were charged they would get 10s. a year but they must pay the difference themselves. It was cal- culated that 10s. a year was equivalent to 21d. per week. A halfpenny a week would have to be made up in the infants' school, and 34d. in the boys' and girls' schools. The managers had given this matter very careful consi- deration. To keep these schools going they required not only the school fees and the Government grant, but pri- vate subscriptions; in fact, they received something equal to £6O or £7O a year in addition to the school pence and the Government grant. Without that support they could not afford to carry on the schools in the way they had been carried on with a fee of 3d. and 4d. a week. The managers had come to the conclusion that the best way to deal with the matter was to charge a penny each child in the infant school, but in the case of two children from the same family, they would charge nothing for the second child. It would be practically a penny a family in the infant school, and they proposed to deal with the boys' and girls' school in the same manner. They would charge a boy or girl 2d., but if two came from the same family the secoud boy would be charged a penny, but in the case of a third very likely nothing. Other proposals had been made, and one was that the infant school should be made free, and 21d. a head charged all round. That arrangement would give them all the money they wanted, but it was thought that for the present it would hardly be advisable to make the infant school altogether free. They would like to keep up the efficiency of that school to the present standard, and he felt sure that the parents would not object to pay a penny if the character of the school did not suffer. That meeting could not bind the managers, although they wished to know what the opinion of the parents was. After some conversation the following resolution was unanimously agreed to, on the motion of the Vicar, seconded by Mr. G. D. Gleave : —" That this meeting approves of the proposal to charge a penny in the infant school for each family of children, and 2d. each scholar in the boys' and girls' school, except in the case of several scholars coming from the same family, when a penny each will be charged for all after the first." PROPOSED JOINT ACTION OF SCHOOL MANAGERS. It is proposed to hold a meeting of the managers of all the elementary schools of Warrington on Monday, Sep- tember 7, at 3 p.m., at the Town Hall, "to consider what, if any,course of action may be rendered necessary by the. clause in the Education Act which enjoins the provision of free places in elementary schools." The printed notices convening the meeting is signed by the Revs. E. C. E. Carleton, J. B. Feeny, F. Slater, M. Stevenson, F. W. Sumner, F. W. Willis, and J. Yonge, who contend that it is very important joint action should be taken by the managers in the matter, and that it will be of great assistance if an effort is made to ascer- tain (a) what demand for free places is likely to exist in the district in each school, and (b) how it is proposed to

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUMTST 15, 1891.
meet the dem; nd. It is hoped that manager.; will be able to postpone any changes they may have in contem- plation until this m.i'eting has been held.
