On Wednesday Mr. Cripps, Q.C., appeared to show cause on behalf of the Chilworth Gunpowder Company, when Mr. Justice Denman suggested that the arbitrator should in his award separate the figures according to the different views held by the parties, and then the Court could be moved as to the true construction if that was found necessary. If it turned out that the arbitrator had admitted evidence which he ought not to have done, the Chilworth Company ought to pay the costs which had thereby been thrown away. The parties were unable to agree to the suggestion of the Bench, and the Judges accordingly adjourned the motion until the next sittings, and gave a direction that no further meetings of the arbitrators should be held until the matter had been .dis- posed of by the Court. HALF-YEARLY REPORT. _ _

The half-year—lii7eport of the Manchester Ship Canal I Company, just issued, states that the whole of the share , capital has now been called up. The total amount in I arrear is £30,605. The Bill Euthorising the company to raise additional loan capital, through the Corporation, to the extent of £3,000,000, received the Royal assent on the 28th ult. Since the last report 159 acres of land have been acquired, at a cost of £52,045. Of the 4,417 acres which have been purchased altogether, a considerable partion will be available for re-sale. Applications for sites suitable for works on the banks of the canal continue to be made to the directors. The construction of the works has been well advanced during the summer months. The masonry and concrete of the docks and locks will be finished by the end of the year. The deviation railway embankments are nearly completed, and the viaducts and bridges are in a very forward state. The portion of the canal from Ellesmere Port to the river Weaver will be ready for traffic shortly. Owing to the long and severe frost early in the year, the revenue from the Bridgewater Canal fell £10,750 below the average. To equalise the revenue £ll,OOO will be taken from the re- serve fund. The traffic continues to be well maintained. The subject of river pollution is receiving the serious attention of the directors, and they appeal to losal authorities and owners and occupiers of works on the banks of the various streams to co-operate with them to remedy the evil.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.

LATCHFORD AND THELWALL. The progress which has been made in constructing the embankment for the railway deviation between Latchford and Warrington has necessitated an alteration in the temporary line which is used by the Ship Canal Company. They require now to cross the ordinary line of the London and North-Western Railway in order to get their wagons through between Salford and Runcorn, and with this object, the London and North-Western Railway men were engaged on Saturday and Sunday in laying down a crossing between Latchford Station and Wash Lane. A large gang of men were employed and they were actively at work the greater part of Sunday so as to get all the fittings completed before Monday's ordinary traffic. It is stated that the cost of this operation to the Ship Canal Company, in whose interest the charge has been made, will be about £BOO, and in addition to this they will be charged 10s. for every train of wagons that crosses the London and North- Western Railway. Near the same spot progress is being made with the erection of the proposed

HIGH LEVEL BRIDGE for vehicular traffic. The foundations have been laid in concrete and one arch of the new bridge has already been erected. The road from the proposed new bridge to Ackers-lane has been for some time staked out and the required embankment is now being raised. The founda- tions have been laid for the

NEW LATCHFORD STATION which will, of course, be on the top of the embankment. 'The timbers are solidly set in concrete and bolted down so as so ensure the station at that elevated position being capable of resisting the highest pressure of wind. Men are getting on with the foundations for the swing bridge near Knutsford-road, and here too the new road which deviates from Knutsford-road with a view to crossing the swing bridge has been staked out and the intercept- ing fences taken dowr . The GREAT GIRDER BRIDGE which crosses the Canal near Latchford locks is approach- ing completion, and it is expected that, in a month or six weeks, the last rivet will be driven home. Near the bridge the foundations are laid for the hydraulic appara- tus which will be used for working the Latchford locks. The

div.head: LATCHFORD LOCKS
div.p: LATCHFORD LOCKS

are obviously approaching completion, the granite cop- ing stones being for the most part laid, and 7 ow that they are getting a finished look it is seen that the locks are a really magnificent piece of work. One of the two gates which have been in course of erection for some weeks has now been completed and placed in position, and it is expected that the second gate will be placed in position in a very short time. MOORE, &c.

At Moore, Walton, and thereabouts, the hugh devia- tion of railway bridges are becoming more and more massive, and the embankments, made of the soil scooped out by the steam navvies, completely alter the appearance of the country. At the Daresbury end of the Acton Grange railway bank the permanent way has been laid, and can now at any time be connected with the existing line. At the Warrington end the bank has been brought nearly to the London and North-western station, and, with the exception of one at Acton Grange, the bridges on the track are all but completed. IRLAM, Sze. A new station is also being built at Irlam, but this work has met with delay, being stopped by the present main road, which is to be diverted. The new aqueduct at Barton is necessitating a deal of labour, but is making good progress. At the Irwell Park cutting preparations are being made towards letting in water from the river, and at the Manchester end work is going on briskly.

div.head: WEAVER SECTION.
div.p: THE WEAVER SECTION.

People have become, generally speaking, pretty well acquainted with the Eastham end of the works and thence on to Ellesmere Port, so much attention having been directed to that section since the water was let in- to the cutting, and since the engineers and their navvies gained such a laborious victory over the difficulties that had to be faced in making good the Ellesmere gap. The progress, here, of course, is more advanced, but work also appears to be going forward at a very satisfactory rate on the other sections. From Ellesmere Port to the Weaver the cutting is nearly ready to receive the water, and it is expected that very shortly the process of lett- ing it in will be carried out. As instancing how far the 1 labour of excavating the canal generally has been corn- pleted, it may be mentioned that the only places where steam navvies are now working are at the Weaver, at a point just east of Ellesmere Port, at the site of the river Gowy, and at Holpool Gutter, and it may be said, practically speaking, the canal has been cut. Attention is being directed to the work of finishing the banks, either by stone pitching or fascine work. .RUNCORN. _

_ When the canal had been opened as far as the Weaver, the construction of the river embankment will be pushed forward in the direction of Weston Point, in order to meet the one from the Bridgewater Locks at Runcorn. Further operations that will have to be conducted in this vicinity are the construction of a coffer dam,the excava- tion of the locks, and the building of the gates. The old dock walls at Runcorn Old Quay are being taken down, in order that the stone may be used for the pur- poses of the contractors. CLAIM FOR £lOO,OOO. In the Queen's Bench Division, London, on Monday, before Justices Denman and Vaughan Williams, sitting as a divisional court,Mr. Moulton, Q.C., said he appeared on behalf of the Manchester Ship Canal Company to move for leave to revoke a submission to arbitration in respect to a claim by the Chilworth Gunpowder Company against the Manchester Ship Canal Company. The learned counsel said the only way in which the arbitration could be revoked was by an order of the court, and he submitted that the order ought to be made in this case, inasmuch as the umpire and two arbitrators were receiv- ing evidence upon a claim which was not in accordance with the claim in respect to which notice to treat was given; and the arbitration, if allowed to proceed, would entail very serious expense, and must ultimately prove abortive. It appeared that certain gunpowder magazines being situated on the line of the canal, the Canal Com- pany gave notice to treat, but it was not proceeded with immediately, standing over for the convenience of the Canal Company. In the meantime the property was sold, and the purchasers, who were informed of the notice to treat, proceeded to store gunpowder in the magazines, and the Home Office declined to allow the Canal Company to proceed with their work so long as the powder remained in the magazines. Therefore, in order to obtain possession, the Canal Company were forced to serve a fresh order on the new holders, and the parties went to arbitration on Friday last, but the arbi- trators, instead of confining themselves to the interests of the new holders, and excluding interests under which compensation was payable under the former notice to treat, were proceeding to cover the value of the whole of thein ymests, and were thus dealing with matters beyond their jurisdiction, which was clearly defined and settled by the notice to treat. This was a very important matter, as a claim amounting to something like £lOO,OOO was made. Mr. Justice Denman thought the other side ought to be present, and that the best way to treat the matter would be to grant a rule nisi, against which the other side might show cause. Mr. Moulton had no ob-

div.head: CONVICTION OF A. CHESHIRE
div.p: THE CONVICTION OF A. CHESHIRE
FARMER.

In the Queen's Bench Division on Wednesday an application was made to Mr. Justice Wills in the case of "Howe v. Burchardt:' This was a remark- able action, which occupied Mr. Justice Wills and a jury twelve days in March. Howe, a Cheshire farmer, claimed from the executor of the late Ben- jamin Ashton, a rich colliery owner, £1,375 on a cheque which he alleged Mr. Ashton gave him. Part of Howe's case was that Mr. Ashton employed ' him to take money to a mysterious French lady, and to do other things which were to be kept secret from Mr. Ashton's relatives. After a prolonged trial the jury found for the defendant, and Howe was tried at the Old Bailey for perjury. Dr. Blake Odgers, on behalf of the executors, now applied that the documents which had been used at the trial and impounded might be returned to the solicitors. They also desired that the forged cheque might not be returned to the prisoner. Mr. Justice Wills, in acceding to the application, said he should never forget the case. The documents which had be- longed to Howe would remain in the custody of the Solicitor to the Treasury, but the defendant on making an affidavit setting out which documents were his could have them. The forged cheque would also be returned to the defendant.

div.head: FRESH DISTURBANCES IN CHINA.
div.p: FRESH DISTURBANCES IN CHINA.
CATHOLIC CHURCHES DESTROYED.

SAN FRANCISCO, TIIESDAY.—Advices from Hong Kong, dated July 15th, states that the fire of discontent still smoulders in North China. Occasional riots are re- ported, and mission stations near Canton are said to have been attacked, but no particulars have been re- ceived. Two Wusuch rioters on trial voluntarily con- fessed that they had murdered two foreigners during the Wusuch riots. The two men were sent to Kuang Chi district, and executed on the sth, their heads being hung up at Wusuch as a warning. A correspondent at Tient-Sin writes as follows, under , date June 29 :—All is quiet here, and no trouble is [' anticipated. Comparative tranquillity seems to have I been restored in the Yangtse Kiang Valley. A letter of June 27 from Tsien Kiang states that the Viceroy wrote to the officials there that the residences of foreigners should be searched to see if they had any babies' or dead people's bones. The Presbyterian Mission was searched by an official while an excited crowd of natives , waited outside. The mob broke into the Roman Catholic mission building, but were ejected by the occupants, Mr. Cholfant holding the rioters at bay with a revolver. The authorities finally sent the military to the scene of the disturb- ance, and soldiers guarded the place all night. News of serious rioting was received on July 4 from the Southern part of the province. In this section the Roman Catholics hold large broperty interests, and have many fine churches and a large orphanage. Several of these were destroyed by the mob. At Fu Chen Fu the [rioters wrecked the outhouses, and entered the churches and the priests' house, and sacked everything; but did not burn the buildings. The orphanage was not touched. Soldiers were ordered to patrol the streets during the night, and to guard the property of the Roman Catholic mission. The town was left without a gunboat, which caused much uneasiness amongst the foreign residents. A telegram from Tient-Sin states that the French and British Ministers have opened negotiations with the Tsung le Yamen in regard to the claim for indemnity on account of the recent riots. The sum demanded is 6,500,000 taels.

div.head: AFFAIRS IN IRELAND.
div.p: AFFAIRS IN IRELAND.
MR. DWYER GRAY AND THE "FREEMAN'S JOURNAL."

A Dublin correspondent telegraphs that Mr. Dwyer Gray on Tuesday presented a requisition, signed by him- self as owner of nearly half the "Freeman's Journal" shares,. by Archbishop Walsh, and by several smaller shareholders, calling on the secretary of the "Freeman's Journal" Company Le summon a meeting within three weeks, to consider the policy of the paper in the present political crisis, and to take steps to change it.

div.head: NATIONAL LEA-GUE'S. FiNANCES.
div.p: THE NATIONAL LEA-GUE'S. FiNANCES.

The fortnightly meeting of the National League was held on Tuesday, at Dublin, Mr. Leamy, M.P., presiding. Mr. Harrington said for the first time since the inception of the organisation they found themselves unable to con- tinue the grants to evicted tenants. They were only now suEpending the grants until the country enabled them to renew them. Mr. Harrington said later in all proba- bility an appeal would be made immediately to place at the service of the Irish people a Nationalist daily news- paper. NEW TIPPERARY.

The butter merchants of Tipperary on Tuesday evacuated The William O'Brien Arcade in New Tipper- ary, and went back to business on the old premises on the Smith-Barry property. The monthly cattle fair on Tuesday was also held in the old place.

div.head: STRIKE ON A LIGHT. RAILWAY.
div.p: STRIKE ON A LIGHT. RAILWAY.
Two hundred men struck work on Tuesday, on the Clifden section of the Galway and Glifden Railway for an advance of 3s. per week. The manager threatens to pay them all off. MR. DILLON AT DUBLIN.

Mr. John Dillon, M.P., speaking on Wednesday, at a crowded meeting of the Irish National Federation held in Dublin, over which he presided, referred to the progress made by the Federation as a convincing proof of the need felt by the people in the present crisis for some such organisation. While he would give to every Irishman freedom of opinion, he asserted that when the great majority of the people had given their verdict on the question of the true policy every honest Irishman should either stand aside or support that majority. Some of Mr. Parnell's friends wanted to carry on their own palicy, no matter how meagre was the support accorded to it, and any practical politician would tell them that with the admission of such a principle as that no possibility would remain of promoting an independent Irish National policy. Referring to the declaration of the National League that it can no longer provide for the wants of the evicted tenants, he said it would be for the Federation to take up this duty. There cculd be no better proof than the League's lack of funds that the people had ceased to trust that organisation. He appealed to Mr. Parnell again ta consent to the release of the Paris fund for the support of the tenants, suggesting theappointment of representa- tives of both sections of the Irish party to superintend the distribution of the money. THE MURDER OF A CARETAKER.
- Two young men were arrested near Listowel, on Thurs- day night, on the charge of being concerned in the death of the caretaker, Dillane, who was found drowned near his house.

div.head: HEROIC CONDUCT OF A MINE it
div.p: HEROIC CONDUCT OF A MINE it

A striking example of a miner's heroism was re- lated at an inquest held at Frizington, on Tuesday evening, on a lad named Joseph Walker, who was killed at the Postlethwaite Iron Ore Mines, on the 3rd inst. William Walker, father of the .deceased, with his son and two other workmen, was engaged in removing some props which were supporting the roof, when the timber gave way and a large quan- tity of metal fell upon his son and the other two men. Walker found that his son had been killed, and his companions were fast in the debris. As his own lad was past help, the courageous fellow at once commenced the work of rescueing the others. The other men in adjoining workings refused to as- sist as they feared a further fall, and for an hour, with his dead son lying near, and with pieces of metal repeatedly falling about and upon him, he continued his task, so great being his danger that even one of the imprisoned men begged him to de- sist as he could not liberate them and would pro- bably loose his own life. But Walker was not to be deterred from doing his best, and he ultimately single-handed rescued both men.—The Coroner (Mr. Webster) said he could not express his admiration for the gallant conduct of Walker.

div.head: SETTLEMENT OF THE CHEMICAL TRADE DISPIITE.
div.p: SETTLEMENT OF THE CHEMICAL TRADE DISPIITE.

Another conference of the managers of the St. Helens chemical works and the represeutatives of the men affected by the dispute was held at St. Helms. on Saturday afternoon, when after some hours' discussion,'all the points in dispute were ami- cably settled. The disagreement arose out of a notice by the employers that the scales of pay were to be reduced at all the yards, and the workmen at Greenbank Works, Sutton Lodge Works, and Kurtz's Works urged that the reduction would press heavily upon them, amounting in some cases to 15s. per week, owing to the extra work they had to perform as compared with the workmen employed at the Globe Works. At an interview on Wednesday week, the firm agreed to accept the Globe prices as a stan- dard, and the executive committee of the Chemical and Copper Workers' Union, accompanied by Mr. P. J. King, president, visited the whole of the works on Thursday with the view of suggesting or accept- ing scales of payment for each separate yard, accord- ing to the facilities for the completion of work and the processes of manufacture in use. At last Satur- day's meeting the whole of the points were discussed, with the result that an agreement satisfactory to both masters and men, was arrived at. Under these circumstances work was resumed at all the chemical yards on Monday morning.

div.head: UPSON'S
div.p: UPSON'S
Extract of Soap.
LEWISHAM ELECTION.

The writ for the election of a member in place of Vis- count Lewisham, now Earl of Dartmouth, is expected to be issued on the 17th inst • Mr. Warmingham, Liberal issued his address to the Lewisham electors on Tuesday. He declares himself a supporter of Mr. Gladstone's policy and in favour of a local Legislature in Ireland for dealing with purely Irish affairs. London, too, needs Home Rule, and its affairs should be managed by the County Council, whose powers should be extended. He is also in favour of a large number of other Radical measures.

div.head: THRFE TRAINS IN COLLISION.
div.p: THRFE TRAINS IN COLLISION.

Between one and two o'clock on Wednesday morning, while a goods train was approaching Snow Hill Station, Birmingham, on the Great Western Railway, it came to a stop in the tunnel, and while the guard proceeded to the station, another goods train came in collision with and smashed the guard's van and a waggon of the first train, throwing the debris on the adjoining line. Soon after another goods train, coming in an opposite direc- tion, ran into the debris and was thrown off the line, and destroyed a considerable length of the permanent way. The line was not cleared for eight hours, and a large number of excursionists were delayed.

div.head: WALSALL ELECTION.-A LIBERAL
div.p: WALSALL ELECTION.-A LIBERAL
RETURNED.

Tuesday was devoted more, to the preparations for the contest than to public oratory. The trades union leaders, however, who have been to town for some days held several meetings on behalf of Mr. Holden, the Liberal candidate, all of which were enthusiastic. Dr. Rentoul, M.P., and Mr. E. Spencer, M.P., supported Mr. James at his last meeting on Tuesday night, which opened with manifestations and dissent, but concluded with the carrying of a resolution in his favour. The polling in the Walsall Division to fill the Parlia- mentary vacancy caused by the death of Sir Charles Forster, commenced at eight o'clock on Wednesday morning. The polling at the twenty-eight polling sta- tions proceeded steadily, and was well kept up during the day. Both candidates drove round theconstituency, and numbers of ladies were working on both sides. The result was announced late on Wednesday night, as follows : _
-Md. Holden (L) 4,899 Mr. F. James (C)

Liberal majority 539 At the election in 1886 Sir Charles Forster was unop- posed, but in 1885 the seat was contested by Mr. James, with the following result :—Sir Charles Forster, Bart. (L), 5,112; Mr. F. James (C), 3,435 ; majority, 1,677. The registered number of electors was 10,042 in 1885, and it is now 11,224.

div.head: CONGRESS OF HYGIENE.
div.p: CONGRESS OF HYGIENE.

On Monday afternoon, the prince of Wales opened the seventh annual International Congress of Hygiene and Demography at St. James's Hall, London. There was a large and distinguished gathering of English and foreign savants. The Prince,in his address,dwelt on the dangers to health which might be ascribed to the constant in- crease of our great manufactories and to over-crowding in towns. He hoped for much good to be attained by such congresses, because business prosperity ought to be made consistent with national good health. The sections of the Congress met on Tuesday. The sections, ten in number, of the Congress of Hygiene met on Tuesday morning at Burlington House and at the London University. There was a crowded attendance in each department. Lord Basing, president of the section on State Hygiene, sketched the past his- tory of the Local Government Board in the relation to the prevention of disease in municipalities. A continua- tion of its work as a department of public health was preferable to the appointment of a minister. Papers followed by Professor Simon, of Breslau, and Sir C. Cameron, of Dublin. One of the most interesting sec- tions was that on bacteriology, over which Sir Joseph Lister presided, and spoke of the discoveries of Pasteur and Koch. Sir Joseph Fayrer, president of the secticin on preventive medicine, said it was generally understood that about one-fourth of all the mortality in England was caused by preventible disease. Surgeon- General Cunningham then read a paper on the failure of quarantine as a preventive of epidemic disease. In the section on chemistry and physics in relation to hygiene, Sir Henry Roscoe, M.P., presided, and delivered the inaugural address, dealing mainly with the importance to life of a pure water supply and the advances made by communities in dealing with such matters in modern times. Dr. W. J. Russell opened a discussion on town fogs, which he stated were mainly produced by the imperfect combustion of coal, and other matters, such as dust from roads. An analysis of London fogs showed soot and dust to be the principal ingredients. In the naval and military section, Dr.' Stopford Taylor, of Liverpool, read a paper on the medical supervision of the mercantile marine and the defects of our present system. The Conference on Hygiene was resumed on Wednes- day in London, when Mr. Diggle, chairman of the Lon- don School Board, read a paper on the duty of parents and of the State to children. The importance of physi- cal educ,ation was discussed, and the subject of home lessons considered,. a resolution that such lessons should be abolished being rejected. Dr. Ransome, of Manchester, read a paper "On the heed of special measures for the pre- vention of consumption," and C. E. Paget. of Salford, on "The difference of susceptibility to diphtheria between old and new residents." Among the papers was one by Dr. Lennox Browne on the importance of improved sanitation in theatres. On Thursday, Mrs. Besant read a paper in the school section. A resolution was afterwards adopted declaring that food and clothing for destitute and neglected child- ren were necessary for their efficient education, and that where such destitution is due to the misconduct of the parents or guardians, it is the duty of the Legislature to impose penal consequences. In other sections resolu- tions were adopted in favour of the cremation of the dead and the registration of architects.

On Thursday, in the section of bacteriology, relating to tuberculosis in all its branches, Dr. Burdon Sanderson, of Oxford, read a paper sn the relation of diseases of animals to those of man. In the section of State hygiene, Sir Henry Thompson read a paper on cremation, and dealt mainly with danger from the bodies of those who had died from contagious diseases, which amounted to one-eighth of the total mortality. Mr. Gordon Smith read an interesting paper on common lodging houses, and urged reforms.

div.head: EXTRAORDINARY MARRIAGE SUIT.
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY MARRIAGE SUIT.

Mr. Justice Collins delivered judgement on Wednesday in the suit in which Mrs. Crane, otherwise Miss Cooper, sought for a decree of nullity of marriage with her cousin, which took place at St. Bride's Church, Fleet-st., London, on the ground that she was compelled to marry the respondent against her will and owing to the threats he used. His Lordship said he could not grant the prayer of the petitioner, which was therefore dismissed. He held that the allegations made by the lady in support of her petition were not proved. There was nothing to show that she was of weak will or that her cousin was of strong will and overpowered her. saving regard to the cynical behaviour of the husband, his lordship regretted coming tA the conclusion that the petition was not in law supported by the evidence.

div.head: MR. BALFOUR AT PLYMOUTH.
div.p: MR. BALFOUR AT PLYMOUTH.

Mr. A. J. Balfour, M.P., addressed a crowded meeting in the Guildhall at Plymouth on Monday, and in reply te addresses expressing confidence in the Government and in his Irish policy, said that it did not rest with one indi- vidual, with one Government, or even with a generation to solve the Irish problem. All they claimed was that they were in process of solving it, and that claim they put forward with justice. He criticised Sir William Har- court's attitude with regard to the Irish question, and maintained that the Government had accomplished much useful work during the session, proving their capacity for constructive legislation. He denied that free education was a monopoly of the Liberal party, and said that by passing the Bill the Government had saved the system of voluntary education in the country. Deal- ing with the Irish policy, he urged that local govern- ment should be given, but given with discretion, to Ireland,and he declined to admit that the recent by-elec- tions had been won on Home Rule.

Mr. Balfour laid the foundation stone of a Working Men's Club, at Plymouth, on Tuesday, and WAS subse- quently entertained to luncheon by the Plymouth Con- servative Association,presided over by the Earl of Mount Edgecumbe. Responding to the toast of the Liberal Unionist cause, which was proposed by the Earl of Mor- ley, Mr. Baltour paid a tribute to the patriotic self-sacri- fice of the Liberal Unionists. He believed that their al- , liance with the Conservative party had become a per- manent union, which neither time nor the changes of political life was likelyin any way to impair. The right hon. gentleman added that,, in his opinion, there had not been for more than fora generation any vital differences of opinion on the great questionsof the day between mode- rate Conservatives and moderate Liberals. There was more in common between the extreme men of the Union- ist party than there was between them and the Radical- Gladstonian party. Mr. Balfour shortly afterwards left Plymouth for London.

div.head: GOOD TEIIPLAI& CONVENTION..
div.p: GOOD TEIIPLAI& CONVENTION..

The half-yearly Session of No. 1 Convention of the Good Templars Order of the south-west Lan- cashire district was held in the Baptist schoolroom, Appleton, near Widnes, on Saturday last. The Ses- sion was called to order at 3.50 p.m., by Bro. Geo. Clarke, C.C.T., of Earlestown, supported by a good staff of officers; the following distinguished visi- tors were duly received and heartily welcomed, Bro. Morris Jones, D.C.T., Liverpool; Bro. J. A. Lee, D.Chap.. Liverpool; Sister M rs. Lee, Liverpool; Bros J. W. Fisk, Sister Mrs. Fisk, Mission Van Agents. After the usual opening the Audit, Credential and Press Committees were appointed. The officers re- ports for the past half-year were then,received.Bro. G.Clarke,C C.T.,in his report referred to the presence agents and the G.T. Mission Van in the district, and urged special attention and earnestness in making the meeting successful. Several lodges were a little backward but it was hoped the present crusade would give them a lift forward. Bro. Col.-Sergt. T. Mantle, C.Sec. gave a most exhaustive report,show- ing that there were 13 lodges in the Convention area with about 420 members. With one or two exceptions all the lodges were working well, some being most earnest and active and giving signs of future prosperity and progress. He indicateda large amount of public work and various other efforts for the propagation of Good Templar principles, had been car- ried out, and the prospects of the Order in our area were bright and cheerful. Bro. Thos. Frain, C. Trea., gave the financial report, and Bro. John Taylor, C.E.S., reported on matters touching temperance legislation,Stc. Bros. J. Li ndon,ami R.Kean gave a report on Credentials showing that 12 Lodges were represented, by 11 Lodge Deputies and 28 representatives, with 42 visitors, gave a total attendance of 81 members. Interesting reports of Lodges and Temples were received from representa- tives present, after which the officers for the ensuing half year were elected as follows, nearly all contested : —C.C.T. Bro. Col. Sergr. Mantle,Warrington ; C.C. Bro. P.M. Segt. Roberts, Warrington; C.E. Sept. Bro. John Taylor, Earlestown ' • C.S.J.T. Bro. R. Skaife, St. Helens C.V.T. Sister Sheatli,Warrington ; C. Sec. Bro. R. Kean, Warrington: C. Trea. Bro J. Brockl'ank, St. Helens; C. Chap. Bro. J. Vint, Ashton-in-AlakPrfield ; C.M. Bro. Brown, Hindle),; P.C.C.T. Bro. Geo"ge Clarke, Earles- town; C.A. Sec. Bro. Geo. Tomlin, Warrington ; C.D.M. Sister Hairsnape' Wigan ; C.G. Bro. J. Bate, St. Helens; G.S. Bro. Pollitt, Warrington. The last four were appointed by the Executive elect. It was resolved to hold the next monthly session in Orford Barracks. Bros. Roberts, Vent, and Brown were elected a committtee on Juvenil3 Templary. A vote of sympathy was passed with Bro. George Heyes of Golborne who had met with a serious accident, a few days pre- viously.Encouran'ing addresses followed from the -district visitors present for which they were tendered thanks. The Widnes brethren were similarly complimented for their arrangements and a most interesting and inspiring session closed at 6.15 p.m. for tea to which a largenumber did justice. It had been decided to have a procession of members in regalia and an open air demonstration in connection with the Mission Van, but the heavy showers prevented this.

A public meeting- was held in the Baptist Schoolroom, presided over by Bro. M. Jones D.C.T. Liverppol, who was supported by Bro. Geo. Clarke D.C., Bro. Lee D. Chap., Sister Mrs. Lee and Bro. and Sister Fisk, van agents. Earnest addresses were given and songs, melodies, &c. interspersed, the large audience frequently testifying their appreciation of the proceedings which closed about 9 p.m.

Licensing, WITH the approach of the period at and which Brewster Sessions are held, Tied Houses. the question of licensing and licensing law once more occupies the public mind. Hitherto licensing magistrates have been afraid to act lest they should be found to exceed their powers; but the decision in the case of SHARP V. WAKEFIELD has set them at ease in that respect; and they now know upon the authority of the highest courts of the country that they have abso- lute discretion in dealing with what are called renewals—just RS they have in dealing with an application for a new license. The form in which the issue comes before them may be different, but the issue is the same in that the justices may grant or not grant, may renew or not renew, as they deem best in the interests of the community. A great responsibility rests therefore upon them— a responsibility which they can no longer ignore. With few exceptions, they are known to be of opinion that, in this as in every other part of the country, there are far more licensed houses than are required ; and this being the case it will be a grave dereliction of duty if they do not give effect to their opinion. The weeding out process may not be pleasant; but it ought not to be shirked on that account. The magistrates in every licensing district ought, with the aid of the police, to prepare a full report of the number of houses and the character of the houses in each locality. They would in this way readily discover where the accommodation was excessive, where police super- vision could not be properly exercised, and, where from structural defects, houses were no longer suitable for licensing purposes. A report of this was prepared two years ago by the Licensing Justices of Warrington; and, ifzit were brought up to date, it would be available for guidance at the forthcoming Brewster Sessions. Another matter of moment in connection with the licensing question, is the extraordinary ten- dency to monopoly which is being developed by the tied-house system. At the Cheshire Quarter Sessions, on Saturday. there was an interest- ing discussion on an important report, pre- pared by the Special Committee, which was directed, a short time ago, to inquire into the state and effect of the law relating to licensed houses. That report contained what Mr. H. J.TOLLEMACHE, M.P., described as "a strong indictment of the whole system of tied-houses." He himself disap- proves of the report, but the only suggestion he had to make was, that they should consult the brewing interest, which is equivalent to asking the cat what should be done • with the cream. The Opinion expressed in the report is that "The tied- house generally assumes the form of a mere drink- ing shop." This must be regarded, under the cir- cumstances, as an inevitable tendency; and it is just because it is inevitable that magistrates are called upon, as guardians of the public,to set their faces against such houses. The Duke of WEST- MINSTER, in supporting the report, said They could not help seeing that a state of things had arisen which was not contemplated by the Act of 1872. This fact would seem to point to further legislation in that direction, because of course it was one great object of the Act to have a responsible holder and resident in a public-house—a mar' they could catch and punish if be behaved wrongly. Under the system in question, if the occupant of a public-house misconducted himself, there was no question of the endorsement of license, for he was at once removed by his superior, his employer the brewer. That was certainly an unsatisfactory state of things. He saw that a large proportion—speaking from memory about one half—of the public-houses in the county were tied. It was consequently a matter which required very urgent attention on the part of all concerned. If, in the opinion of His Grace, it is a serious thing that half of the licensed houses in Cheshire are tied, what is to be said of the state of affairs in Warrington where nine-tenths of the drinking shops are tied to brewers? We hear a good deal at times about depriving a publican of his living; but that is one of the worst evils of the tied-house system. The brewer has no care for the publican, and every care for his house; and the result is, as the Duke of Westminster suggested, that occupants of houses are everywhere sacrificed rather than any risk should be run of a license being endorsed. The new departure is bad therefore in every way. It puts a premium on excessive drinking; it sacrifices the publican in case of misconduct arising out of excess; and it defeats the intentions of the legislature by pre- venting endorsements:of licenses. Mr. F. GREY, in the course of the discussion,observed that there was something to be said from the beer drinker's point of view,and that was that "Anyone going in- to a tied house was compelled to drink a quality of beer the brewer chose to supply, at a price the brewer chose to ask." He added :—" One co uld not judge by a small area, but a man in his own district applied to him for a public-house, because, he said, he was keeping a tied house, and it was more than his conscience could stand, and he wanted to go where he could carry on his business in a respectable manner." It is nothing new to find that a monopoly is a mischievous thing; and it is for licensing magistrates to say whether they will countenance those monoplies, or whether they will have regard to the good of the community and discourage them in every possible way. There are far too many licensed houses—tied and free—
and, power having been given them to reduce the number, the number ought to be reduced.

WHAT is called a Congress of The Health Parliament Hygiene and Demography, but . which might more simply, if not more scientifically, be called a Health Parliament has been held in London during the present week. The PRINCE of WALES presided over the inaugural meeting on Monday, when there was an exceed- ingly large attendance, representatives being pre- sent from all parts of the world. It is gratify- ing to ordinary humanity to see the energy and enthusiasm which professors of the healing art display in collecting and classifying facts and figures relating to the births, deaths, and occupa- tions of "all people that on earth do dwell." Knowledge and personal experience have brought it home to every observant person that life is lengthened or shortened by obeying or disobeying what have come to be known as the laws of health. We have learnt much; but we have still much to learn; and, what is more, we need to make better and fuller use of our knowledge. Medical men, and especially Medical Officers o Health, are everywhere hindered by crass ignorance and ingrained stupidity. Englishmen do not, as in the days of Erasmus, cover their floors with rushes, putting clean rushes on the top of the dirty ones, thus hiding rather than removing the dirt; but they do allow courts and alleys to be narrow and, unpaved; and foul drains to go without flushing, until—so constant are the factors of disease—it can be said of a certainty of an ill-drained district that the death-rate will always be higher there than elsewhere. It is true that the average life has been considerably prolonged during the past half century, while the death-rate in England has been reduced something like twenty per cent. All this has been done under circumstances which warrant the belief that as much more canbe accom- plished, if local authorities will give due attention to "the warrens of the poor." A serious respon- sibility rests upon them in this respect ; and if the working-classes thoroughly understood their own interests they would give no votes to candid- ates for either municipal or Parliamentary honours who could not be relied upon to do their duty in matters of this kind. Speaking as President, on Monday, the PRINCE of WALES referred to his experience as a member of the Royal Commission on the Dwellings of the Working-classes. He said:—.

I learned much there of the dangers to health which marbe ascribed to the constant increase of our great manufactories, and to other industries. from which especially come the overcrowding of our towns, the building of huge factories, the pollution of our atmosphere, the accumulation of refuse, the fouling of rivers, the impurities of earth and air and water. I learned not only of these dangers, but of the immense difficulty of increasing, or even maintaining, our activity in all branches of trade without incurring heavy risks to health, more particularly in our chief centres of popula- tion. The task of averting them might have appeared hopeless, but I have rejoiced to see how much has already been done in diminishing them, and to observe how our registers bear witness to the decreasing mortality in our large towns, to the increasing average length of life in the whole population, and of many facts proving the good influence of our sanitary institutions. "The impurities of earth, air, and water" is a com- prehensive phrase; and who needs to be told that these impurities are more abundant in the town than in the country? Those who toil not neither do they spin can to a large extent escape these abominations by judicious choice of residence ; but the worker must live near his work; and that he is in this way heavily handicapped is ilemonstrated by the returns of sickness and mortality. It will always be so—more or less; and it is our duty to see to it that it is less rather than more. If there is one individual whose health and life ought to be especially protected it is the man whose days, year in and year out, are devoted to labour for the benefit of himself and others. His health is his / wealth, and it ought to be jealously guarded.

THE report of the Technical In- Technical Instruction. struction Committee of the Lan- cashire County Council is a care- fully prepared document, and the recommendations that are made seem to have been well considered. The total sum available is just over £40,000; and of this, after making provision for scholarships, ex- hibitions, &c., £29,000 are to be apportioned to various urban authorities on the basis of popula- tion and rateable value. The schedule of approxi- mate amounts gives the following figures as the grants for this district :

Ash ton-in-Maker- New ton-in-M ake r- field Billinge Garston 3OO Rainford Haydock 7O Warrington 6lO Huyton-with-Reby.....130 Widnes: 480 It will be seen that Warrington is set down for £6lO, which is rather less than the sum estimated by the local Committee, but the difference will not materially affect the carrying out of the scheme which has been laid before the Town Council. It is to be hoped, now that there can be no question as to receiving the money, that no time will be lost in proceeding to establish a Technical School. It will be a case, to a large extent, of cutting the coat accordingly to the cloth; but there is reason to believe that the County Committee will have regard to helping those who help themselves. Alder- man MusPnATT,:speaking on behalf of Widnes, in- timated that the £4BO to be granted was inade- quate,seeing that the need for technical instruction in Widnes was so great. He wanted to see a large sum down, even if there was nothing for a feW years afterwards. Warrington, with its numer- ous industries, might put in a similar plea; but it is proposed to get over the initial difficulty as to funds by borrowing £5,000, on the security of the rates, Sinking Fund being formed for re-payment of the loan in, say, 30 years. Why should not Widnes take a similar course? It is obvious that the County Council cannot make fish of one place and flesh of another without in the end doing more harm than good. Judging from the remarks which were made at the meeting of the Newton Commissioners, on Monday, the people of that dis- trict are grateful for the £lBO allotted to thew/ especially as they can see their way to immediately making good use of the money. Where first steps have to be taken, as in Warrington, there is great deal to be done before a Technical School can be got going; and where men of energy and ability, like Mr..F. MONKS, are devoting themselveg to the work, they ought to be assisted by the local authorities in every possible way. The race is not always to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, but in the contests of the future it is the unedu- cated who will suffer defeat.

CROFT HORTICULTURAL SOCIETY. The gardens entered for competition for the prizes offered for the best cultivated gardens be- longing to the above society, were judged on Satur- day, by Mr. R. Harrison, head gardener to Mr. T. J. Gillespie, J.P., of Newton. Though the weather proved unfavourable in the evening, the gardens presented a neat appearance.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

While Warrington has been talking about open- air baths, Penketh has been getting to work to construct one. The site is in a field off Station- road, and good progress is being made with it. It is time to cry— " Play up, Warrington !"

Our Warringt‘readers will do well to turn their attention to the description in another column of ‘" A Visiting Day at the Blue Coat School." It is 'racily written—with touches suggestive of Dickens —and is in every way a credit to "Blue-Boy."

Speaking at Plymouth, on Tuesday, Mr. Balfour. referred to the union of Unionists as "a union 'which neither time nor the chances nor changes of ?political life are likely in any way to impair." That zis to say such Liberal Unionists as are left are being absorbed in the Tory ranks. But are there any left? Judging from recent elections, to speak of them as a factor in politics is to —give to airy nothing A local habitation and a name.

Charles Fudge, a Ship Canal navvy, was sent to prison for three months by the Warrington magistrates, on Monday, for kicking his wife. The forgiving woman sought to make the bench believe that the story of her injuries was "all fudge," and so in a certain sense it was. She is an illus- tration of the truth of the ancient rhyme : A woman, a dog, and a rowan tree— The more you beat them the better they be.

--- What was supposed tobe a case of child murder, at Warrington,or,at any rate concealment of birth, turns out to be neither. As the child had not breathed, it appears it was no offence against the law to make a parcel of it and place it in a brook. But it is an offence nevertheless against common- feeling and commonsense; and it is to be hoped the lesson of the inquest will go home to the offenders.

Welsh miners are agitating for payment of wages weekly instead of fortnightly; but so far they are meeting with resistance. But why should a system which has been found good in other in- dustries not be good for miners? Long payments are a remnant of the truck system; and lead to " strap" and reckless buying. The employers' plea that weekly payments will mean more book- keeping is hardly worth considering. They can surely de what is done by employers in other trades.

There has been a good deal said about the suc- cess of Professor Higgins as a parachutist; but "success" seems hardly the word now that he has lost his life. It is about time the law stepped in to put an end to exhibitions the chief feature of which is danger to the performer's neck. It would of course be interfering with the liberty of the subject; but we interfere when we say a man shall not make an attempt upon his life, and when we compel an employer to fence off dangerous machinery.

--- There is to be another meeting in Warrington of managers of Elementary Schools, to determine, if possible, what course shall be taken in bringing the new Education Act into force. It is desirable that there should, as far as possible, be unity of action, so that one school may not take advantage of another. It is a pity the Government, were not a little more liberal in their experiment with Liberalism; and it is quite certain that even Tory school managers will say" Amen" to that. But no matter ; a change will be made ; " there's a good time coming boys, wait a little longer."

A correspondent who is "in the know" states that the members of the Appleton Primrose League were conveyed to and from Tatton Park, on Saturday last, and had a tea thrown in—all for a shilling ahead! How is it done? Is there not need for somebody to beware of the provisions of the Corrupt Practices Act? The Grappenhall Leaguers, who had a less distance to go, were charged 2s. each; and they feel as if they have not been well used. They are of opinion that when it is a case of angling for that odd fish known as the electoral gudgeon there should be no difference in the bait.

Mr. Aaron, of the Runcorn Board of Guar- dians, has a weakness for denouncing—in sea- son and out of season—what he calls the extravaganca of the Cheshire County Council. He was given a good deal of rope and allowed to hang himself a few weeks since; and, as this sort of hanging is not a killing matter, he wanted to repeat the performance on Tuesday; but the chairman would have no more of it. Mr. Speak- man, who is a member of the County Council, de- scribed Mr. Aaroo as a man who did "not look into details of accounts, and could not understand 'em when they were explained to him." Poor Mr. Aaron; he had better turn his attention to his old love —the gad-about sparrow.

Lymm rush-bearing has resolved itself into an ordinary pleasure fair, where the " rush" is of an altogether different kind. Rush-bearing goes a long, long way back—to the time in fact when rushes were strewn in churches at the dedication festival. The " merrie-making" which followed often included bear-baiting. We have dispensed with that; but it is quite the thing as yet in cer- tain circles to resort to man-baiting—that is prize- fighting. The thoughts of men are doubtless widened, as the poet says, with the process of the suns; but alas, and alas, that the process is so slow.

"Music hath charms to soothe the savage breast" sometimes; but it makes the breast savage when it rushes,in:the shape of cornet solos,into the ears of people who are at their sabbath devotions. It was music of this kind which resulted in a Bolton bugler being brought before the Newton magistrateslon Saturday, and dealt with for being " disorderly " at Newton on Sunday fortnight. He was reported to be one of a party in a waggonette who were successful in making the day hideous with their unwelcome noise. The bugler pleaded that "while passing the church he played a hymm" —on the cornet of course But that didn't "get him off"—he was bound over and ordered to pay •costs. When be is again in the mood for playing hymns, he would do well to try another instrument —say, the Jew's harp.

The verdict of the jury in the case of the fatality to a warehousoman at the Central Station, War- rington, was one of "Accidental Death," an opin- ion being expressed that the poor fellow had not been sufficiently warned of the shralting operations. Naturally, the Coroner emphasised the need of greater care being exercised, which led Mr. Simp- son, who represented the Railway Company, to remark that the trains would never be got off if a shunter had to go the whole length of the train to give warning. This is typical of the callous views of railway authorities. It is no use appealing to their feelings; the only way to reach them is through the pocket, and, as the Coroner hinted, this might be done next time by a '" stronger conclusion."

The pauperism of the Prescot Union is so exces- sive that Mr. Henley, Inspector of the Local Government Board, has felt himself under the necessity of calling attention to it. In Lancashire, i the number of persons n receipt of relief is one in 53; throughout England it is one in 36; but in i the Prescot Union it is one n 28. At the usual meetineof the Board, on Thursday, it was stated that the large amount of pauperism was caused through the lack of female labour; and the Chair- man observed that they were not so black as they were painted. But the paucity of female labour cannot surely be below the average of the whole country. The matter is of too grave an import to be disposed of in a summary fashion. The Board ought to institute a special inquiry.

WORLD'S CONFERENCE OF THE 1.111.C.A. It was stated at the World's Conference of the -Young Mea's Christian Associations in Amsterdam, on Thursday., that the membership of the British Association had grown from nearly 61,000 in 1888 to over 74,000 in 1891. Including auxiliaries there were now in the United Kingdom 756 centres of association work. Seventy-one of these centres own the premises which they occupy, representing a gross value of over .£366,000.

***A Daring Imposter: The Story of an Innocent Convict. A thrilling tale or American life, by Alfred It. Calhoun, will be commenced in the Examiner on Saturday next August 22nd. This finely written story aboupids in stirring incident, and healthy sentiment, and is well calculated to excite and preserve the interest of all classes of readers.

BRUNSWICK WESLEYAN BOYS' SCHOOL, RUNCORN. This school has again earned the excellent grant for drawing. Sr. AMBROSE CHURCH CEOIR, WIDNES. The members of this choir had their annual picnic on Thursday, when a pleasant day was spent at Chester.

ST. PAUL'S CHURCH, NVIDNES. This church will shortly be closed for several weeks, whilst repairs to the floor are carried out. Through dry rot having set in the wood the floor will have to be entirely relaid at a cost of about £2OO. It is only seven years since the building was erected.

BOY MISSING AT RUNCORN. A small boy named George Dollery Owen, son of John Owen, shipwright of 7, Bridge Street, Runcorn, has been missing from home since Tuesday at noon. He was seen on the canal bank at half-past one and sometime afterwards his cap was found floating on the water. The canal has been dragged without result.
A NEW WIDNES COMPANY.

The well-known firm of Messrs. Richard Johnson, Chapham, and Morris, of Widnes and elsewhere, has just been formed into a limited liability company with a capital of £lOO,OOO in £lO shares, 2,000 of which are 5 per cent. preference shares. The business will continue to be that of chemical, paint, colour, drug and provision merchants.
UNJUST SCALES AT WIDNES

At Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, Robert Har- greaves, butcher, Mersey-road, was summoned by Mr. Kilpatrick, inspector of weights of measures for having in his possession on the Bth August, a pair of scales which were 4 drachms out of balance against the pur- chaser.—ln answer to the defendant,the Inspector said he visited the defendant's shop a fortnight ago but he could not tell whether these were the scales which he then ex- amined.—The defendant was ordered to pay a fine of ss. and costs.
WIDNES IRIS!! NATIONAL LEAGUE.

The usual weekly meeting of the above League was held in the League room, St. Paul's Chambers,on Sunday afternoon, Mr. P. Whelan presiding. The Secretary read a letter from Mr. W. O'Brien M.P., thanking the Irish- men of Widnes for their generous sympathy for himself and Mr. Dillon. He would be glad if it was in his power to visit Widnes, but, unfortunately, the split at present existing among the Irish party would keep him in Ireland for some considerable time, in order to re-unite the party again. He will probably visit Widnes early in the new year. - -
