div.head: STEALING 86LBS. OF BRASS AT RUNCORN.
div.p: STEALING 86LBS. OF BRASS AT RUNCORN.

Yesterday at Runcorn Police Court, Walter Leggett, a labourer, was charged with having on the 13th ult stolen 86 pounds of brass valued at £2l 10s. the property of the Ship Canal Company. On Thursday the prisoner and two other men offered a portion of the brass for sale at Oates marine store in Grenville-st., and the police be- coming acquainted of the fact the prisoner was appre- hended by P.c.'s Crowder and Worth. The brass•con- sists of fittings belonging to a steam navvy at the Old Quay cutting.—The prisoner was remanded in order that his accomplices might be arrested. AN UNBONAFIDE TRAVELLER AT BOLD. Wm. Bradshaw, a young man, living at Lunt's Heath, was summoned to the Widnes Petty Sessions on Thurs- day to answer a charge of obtaining intoxicating liquor during prohibited hours by falsely representing himself to be a traveller.—On Sunday last, about 8 o'clock the defendant called at Bold Arms and asked for a glass of ale. He said he lived in Snig-lane, Widnes, and had walked from there that morning. The landlord, Mr. Byron, afterwards found that he only lived a mile away, and he aad therefore brought these proceedings.—A fine of 10s. and costs 12s. was imposed.
FATAL SWING BOAT ACCIDENT.

On Monday m-orning Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, held an inquest at Widnes Accident Hospital, on the body of George Baskerville, of Lugsdale-road, Widnes, who died in that institution on Friday. On the 22nd June, the deceased and a companion named Wm. Hall were in a swing boat at Runcorn Fair. They were making the boat move at a great speed when the deceased fell out and injured his spine. Despite every medical care he died as stated. A verdict of accidental death was returned,and the jury added a rider that the authori- ties ought to stop swing boats generally.

HEAVY PBNALTY ON A WIDNES PIG KEEPER. At Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, Thomas Den- sen, wheelwright, Bold, was summoned for failing to report swine fever. On Sunday, the 9th inst., Superin- tendent Noblett and Mr. Welsby, veterinary inspector for the district, visited the defendant's premises and found a pig suffering from swine fever. The top of the animal's back was rotting away through the disease. The defendant admitted that the pig had been ill for a month and he had been doctoring it for costiveness.— Edward Parr, of Bold, was summoned on a similar charge.—Superintendent Large said this defendant's pig- cote adjoined Densen's, and his animal had no doubt contracted the disease from Densen's pig.—Mr. Welsby said when he visited the place on the ninth, the pig was dead and he made a postmortem. He found that swine fever had been the cause of death. He could not have sworn to the disease without making the post-morten.— Defendant said the pig had only been ill a few days and he had no idea it was suffering from swine fever. There was no mark on the pig at all.—The Bench dismissed the case against Parr, but said Dengen's was a very serious case indeed and he would be fined £5 and costs; total £6 4s. 11d.

div.head: MEDICINE AND SCIENCE.
div.p: MEDICINE AND SCIENCE.

We notice :with pleasure the name of Edward J. Fox (eldest son of Dr. Fox) amongst the successful candidates at the recent examinations of the Pre- liminary Scientific and the Intermediate Science for the degrees of Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Science of the London University. BessiNgrrEs.—J. S. (I.l.rland, Ironmonger, 51, Bridge-st., Warrington.—Advt.

- - HONOURS FOIL A WIDNES SCHOOLMASTER. Mr. John Beattie, assistant master at Widnes National Schools, has passed the London University Matriculation Examination for the degree of Bachelor of Arts in the first division. He is now entitled to write B.A. after his name. Mr. Beattie who served his time as a pupil teacher at the schools was trained at Chester College. J. 8c W. DUTTON'S SUMMER SALE now on. Sankey Street, Warrington. —Advt.

div.head: BREWERY ON FIRE.
div.p: A BREWERY ON FIRE.

On Sunday forenoon, Mr. John Middlehurst, of Bickerstaffe-st., St. Helens, noticed a volume of smoke issuing from the brewery of Messrs. Whitley and Co., and on the premises being entered it was found that a shed containing barrel corks and work- men's clothing was on fire. The shed is near the boilers, and it is supposed that the woodwork got overheated and ignited. The flames were immedi- ately extinguished, but not before a portion of the roof had been destroyed. J.& W. BUTTON'S SUMMER SALE now on. Sankey Street, Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: WIDNES BAKERS' UNION.
div.p: WIDNES BAKERS' UNION.

A meeting of the members was held on Saturday evening urder the presidency of Mr. T. Delaney, Mr. P. Flynn (Liverpool), delivered an address and urged the bakers of Widnes to join with other trades in the town to form a trades council. It was resolved that the Widnes branch should be affiliated to the Liverpool Operative Bakers Union and Mr. Boyle was elected delegate to the Liver- pool District Council. It was announced that all the bakers in Widnes had joined the Union.
P-ItE,IIER SAFETIES, Cash or Hire.—GARLAND, Warrington —Advt.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAV, A TTGUST 15, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAV, A TTGUST 15, 1891.

LORD EGERTON ON THE GENERAL ELECTION. About 1,000 members of the Primrose League Habitations in Knutsford, Grappenhall, Altrinch am, and district attended a garden party given by Lord and Lady Egerton :of Tatton, at Tatton Park, on Saturday afternoon. Lord Egerton said they must be prepared for a general election in the course of another year, and they must support a Government which had beaten the record in regard to measures passed for the benefit of both England and Ireland. LAWN MOWERS.—Garland, 51. Bridge-st., Warrington. and at Earlestown.—Advt. FAST PASSAGE ACROSS THE ATLANTIC. A New York telegram dated Wednesday says :- "The White Star Line Steamer " Majestic," which arrived here at 3.20 a.m. to-day, has beaten the western Transatlantic record, having made the passage in five days eighteen hours and eight minutes." The " record " which the " Majestic " has broken is that made by the "Teutonic " about this time last year, when she arrived out in five days nineteen hours five minutes, the swiftest western passage ever made. It may be of interest to note that the "Majestic" has this year crossed the Atlantic, before the present voyage four times under six days. CHESTER AND THE ROYAL SHOW. Chester is anxious to have the distinction of being the place chosen for the Royal Agricultural Show of 1893, and a correspondent writes that on Satut- day the Duke of Westminster presided over a meet- ing in that city of representatives of Cheshire and North Wales in support of the movement to hold the Royal Show there. Lord Tollemache, Earl Powis, Lord Alexander Paget, and others supported the proposal, and the Duke of Westminster and Mr. Yerburgh, M.P., each promised £5OO towards the necessary fund. Over £2,000 was promised in the room. The Royal Show has not been held in Cheshire since 1858. J. Br,. W. DUTTON S SUMMER SALE now on. Sankey Street, Warrington.—Advt.

A WIDNES MAN KILLED ON THE RAILWAY. As the workmen's excursion from the Liverpool Silver and Copper Co., Ditton-road, Widnes, was returning from Blackpool, on Saturday night, a shocking aceident occurred near Kirkham Station. The train had stopped outside the station, waiting for the advance signal, when a man named Thomas Allen, Lugsdale-road,Widnes,got out on the off side of the carriage, and was knocked down by a passing express and killed. A doctor was sent for, but when be arrived he pronounced life to be extinct. There were several other passengers in the same compart- ment, but none of them seem to have noticed de- ceased witting out. Naturally the sad event caused consternation among the passengers. J. &W W. DUTTON'S SUMMER SALE now on. Sankey Street, Warrington.—Advt.

CRUELTY TO A HORSE AT CRONTON. Thomas Clarke,of Prescot was summoned to Wid- nes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, on a charge of causing a horse to be worked while in an unfit state, and John Grady, a youth, was charged with working the horse. On the 22nd July F.C. Durkin met Grady driving the horse through Cronton. The animal was drawing a cart loaded with rags and old iron. It was old and in poor condition, was suffer- ing from spavin, very lame, and had a large wound on the near foreleg. The horse was scarcely able to walk,and he ordered the youth to take it out of the shafts and put it up. Inspo,.nr Do wty, corroborated. The defendants practically admitted the offence, and Clarke was fined 10s. and costs, and Grady ss. and costs. J. W Durrotc'S Str3tAtrlt SL & now on. Sankey Street, Warringto:l.—Advt.

A RUNCORN MIN KILLED AT ST. HELENS. Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy-coroner, held an in- quest at the St. Helens Town Hall, on Saturday, on the body of Thomas Mounfield, 33 years of age, a brakesman in the employ of the London and North- Western Railway Company, who received injuries on the Ravenhead branch lines, St. Helens, on the previous Wednesday night, and died at the St. Helens Providence Hospital next morning. The deceased resided at 19, Salisbury-st., Runcorn, and on Wednesday was in charge of a goods train on the Ravenbead siding. He was superintending some shunting operations, and was about to couple up some wagons, when the wagons approaching the end of the train where he was standing were turned on to another line by some self-acting points. The buffer of the moving wagons caught deceased and "jammed" him against the end of the standing wagon. He was very badly crushed, and on being removed to the hospital he died as stated. The evi- dence showed that deceased was provided with a coupling rod, and ought not to have stood between the rails, and also that whilst engaged in shunting it was'this duty to see that the self-acting points were right for his purpose. A verdict of "Acciden- tal death" was returned by the jury. PRES'IOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

On Thursday afternoon the fortnightly meeting of the members of this Board was he1,.1 at the Workhouse, Whiston. There were present Mr. J. Burchall (chair- man), the Rev. S. A. K. Sylvester, the Rev. Dean Fine- gan, Mr. F. Stapleton-Bretherton' J.P., Messrs. J. R. Whalley, J. Mercer, J. Buckley, P. Longton, W. Tyrer, C. B. Johnson' G. Hallas, W. Lowe, W. Middlehurst, R. A. Graves, J. Ranson, J. Peover, G. Davies, J. Whalley, W. Daine, J. Kenwright, E. Birchall, J. Birchall, and Mr. Mann (clerk). AGED MARRIED COUPLES.—The Clerk read a letter from the Local Government Board, pointing out the statutory provisions with reference to the non-separation in the workhouse of husband and wife in certain cases, and it devolves on the Guardians to provide at the workhouse necessary accommodation for aged married couples, who are entitled to live together.—Mr. Sylvester moved that the subject be brought before the notice of the next Visiting Committee.—Mr. Ranson seconded the resolu- tion, which was carried. A SERIOUS MArrea.—A letter was read from the Scul- coates Union, Hull, calling attention to the serious cost incurred in connection with the maintenance of un- married pregnant women who become chargeable to the poor rates, and to the inadequacy of the law relative thereto and enclosing a resolution which they had for- warded to the Local Government Board, Saggesting that a law should be enacted enabling guardians to whom women become chargeable, or the woman herself, to recover maintenance and expenses incurred before the birth of the child from the putative father.—The Board, resolved to support the proposal. PRESCOT AND ITS POOR.—The Clerk said that he had received from Mr. Henley, the inspector from the Local Government Board, his annual return, and from this he preceived that the Prescot Union was in a very unenviable position, as 1 in every 28 persons in the Union was in receipt of relief, as against one in 53 in Lancashire and one against 36 in the whole of England and Wales.: Mr. Finegan said that in the cotton districts there were not many persons thrown out of employ and upon the rates. In Widnes they had no special labour for women, as they found employment for men only. In Preston, Burnley, and Blackburn women owing to the cotton mills often found employment and supported themselves, but in Widnes, there was no one to support the family except the man.—The Chairman said they were not as black as painted.—The subject then dropped. AN ASSISTANT OVERSEER'S DELAY.—The Clerk said he had received the monthly returns from all the assistant overseers except Mr. Parkinson, who was the overseer for Knowsley and Eccleston. It was moved that• Mr. Parkinson should be written to .and asked to send in his monthly return forthwith.—The resolution was carried. ScnooLFEES.—The Clerk submitted a form of a letter he wished to send to all managers of schools in the union intimatingthat,in consequence of the passing of the new Education Act, the Guardians would cease to pay the present school fees for either pauper or non-pauper children on and after the 31st inst., and asking what, if any, fees will be charged in the different standards, so that, should the parents of any children attending the schools be unable to pay such fees, arrangements may be made for dealing with the cases.—After some fuither discussion,it was resolved that the letter be sent to school managers. RELIEF.-The Workhouse master reported that there were 551 inmates this week against 475 in the corres- ponding week last year, and 2,822 persons had received outdoor relief against 3,070 last year. This was the principal business.

div.head: NARROW ESCAPE.
div.p: A NARROW ESCAPE.

On Saturday -a:ftet;;;; jas—t-in--al-tirming accident occurred to the Ship Canal Co.'s tug "Runcorn" at Fiddler's Ferry. This boat, and her sister tug the "Walton," were lying alongside the lightship at the above place with steam ready for the barges, when brought up from Liverpool by the larger tug "St. Winefred," when one of the forward plugs blew out and filled the engine room full of scalding steam. The engineman, Joseph Parr, fortunately was active enough, and had sufficient presence of mind, to leap through the window into the river. He thus escaped a fearful death at the expense of a scalded arm, a bruised ankle, and the wetting. It is considered to have been most fortunate that the accident did not happen a few minutes later, when she would have been under weigh, and the engine- man not so well able to avoid the dire conse- quences of hesitancy or unreadiness. Later accounts speak of Parr as doing well. RAINIITLL ASYLUM: INTEMPERANCE AND IN-

div.head: SANITY.
div.p: SANITY.

The report for 1890 on the Lancashire Lunatic Asylums which has just been issued, is a volume of 227 pages besides a number of tables. The report says the Itainhill Asylum had on March 26th, 1891, 1,611 patients, and 191 vacant beds, 929 patients being usefully employed. The patients last year averaged 1,549, and in October females had to be re- fused. The percentage of deaths was 11.52, pul- monary consumption accounting for 61 deaths. Hereditary tendency to lunacy was traced in 41.93 per cent. of the females. "In not a few cases the only cause which could be detected for the patient's insanity was the intemperance of the parents • this was so in 28 out of the 186 female cases. Although drunkards are not generally regarded as insane, it is a question whether the habitual tippler might not with advantage be considered an irresponsible being, and treated as such. Then the children of insane persons may beconie dipsomaniacs, another fact which might lead one to consider habitual i ntem- perance as a species of insanity." ENIIGELLTION.—Intending emigrants to New York. Boston Philadelphia, San Francisco, Canaria, China, Japan, Aus- tralia, or New Zealand, should take tickets (lowest rates) at the" Examiner" Office, by Cunard, Gnion. American. Aus- tralian, Oriental, and cther lines.—John Walker, agent, "Examiner ' Office, Bewsey-st.. Warrington.—.Advt. A DEAR" BIT OF A REPORT." On Monday, at the St. Helens Town Hall, Paul Cannon, 64, Glover-st., was charged with letting off fireworks, and also with doing wilful damage to the amount of £1 to property belonging to the executors of the late William James Glover. Police-constable Wilkes deposed that on Tuesday forenoon he heard a very loud report, and on going to the rear of the defendant's house he found that a deal of damage had been done. The defendant had fixed a detonator, or a dynamite cartridge, such as are used in collieries. Mr. J. 0. Swift said he appeared for the owners of the property, and 40 panes of glass had been broken. Defendant said he only fired the detonator to make "a bit of a bit of a report." and he never thought it would do any harm. lie was sorry for what had occurred, and would make good all the damage that had been done. Chief-constable Wood remarked that the detonators were very powerful explosives. The Bench considered the defendant had no malicious intent in letting off the detonator, but ordered him to pay a fine of 2s. 6d. and costs, and ..C1 as dam- ages.

div.head: OVERHEA.D RAILWAY AT LIVERPOOL.
div.p: OVERHEA.D RAILWAY AT LIVERPOOL.

Thirty lineal yards a day is reported to be the rate at which the overhead railway along the line of the docks at Liverpool is now progressing. The fact indicates that the difficulties which have taxed very considerably the skill of the engineers are now overcome. Altogether three out of the six and a half miles have now been constructed—that is, from the Hornby to the Clarence Dock, and at the present rate of progress there seems no reason why the whole work should not be completed within the twelve months which under the original con- tract still remains. The entire work is estimated to cost .£273,000. There are to be stations at about every half-mile, and the trains will each consist of two long cars, capable of carrying 112 persons. They will be worked by electric motors, and it is expected that trains in this busy district will be I run at intervals of only three minutes. Sir W. B. Forwood, presiding on Tuesday, at the sixth half- yearly meeting of the Liverpool Overhead Railway Company, said the amount received on capital ac- count was £168,035, and the amount expended in works was £143,098 ss. 10d. Satisfactory progress had been made with the work during the half-year. After careful consideration, it had been decided to adopt electricity as the means of propulsion. J. &W. DUTTON'S SUMMER SALE now on. Sankey Street. Warrington. —Advt.

It is announced in Dublin that the Prince of Wales will visit Ireland on an early date, probably to open the new Marlborough Barracks, Dublin. Baron Hirsch is reported to have sent orders to his Argentine agents to purchase land to the value of £2,000,000 sterling for Jewish colonial purposes. Two young men were sentenced to 21 days' imprison- ment, on Monday, by the Sheriff of Aberdeen for pulling out a mare's tongue. The animal was fo_stive, and they fixed a rope round her tongue, with the result that it was wrenched out. _

A gas explosion occurred early on Thursday morning at the Stirling Castle public-house, Church-st., Camber well. Richard Andrews, potman, and Wm. Telliday barman, were so badly injured that they had to be taken to the hospital. Andrews' recovery is doubtful. An excursion train for Cardiff and Newport, convey- ing the members of the Great Western Railway Widows' and Orphans' Fund, on entering Nottage .l'unnel, near Porthcawl, on Wednesday night, dashed into three horses, which were killed. The passengers escaped with a severe shaking.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

The ordinary monthly meeting of this Board was held On Tuesday in the Town Hall. The following were present—Messrs. F. H. Gossage (chairman), H. S. Timmis, D. Wright, J. Midwood, G. I. Neil, S. Sadler. J. Houghton, J. Tilley, B. Brown, R. Cook, F. Heyes, H. S. Oppenheim (clerk), J. Craik (assistant clerk), J. S. Sinclair (surveyor), J. Carr (engineer), W. Lowe (nuisance inspector), and S. Moyle (ac- countant). _ _
The minutes of the last meeting were confirmed.
THE SWING BOAT FATALITY.

The following letter was read by the Clerk, from the Deputy Coroner :—Victoria-road, Widnes, August 10th, 1891. Dear Sir,—l beg to inform you that at an inquest held to-day in reference to the death of a youth who had fallen from a swing boat at Runcorn, on the 22nd of June last, the jury made a presentiment ccndemning swing boats generally, and urging local authorities to prohibit them,owing to the number of accidents caused by them. —I am, yours faithfully, W. T. iIIISBAND.-Mr. Gossage thought something ought to be done in the matter, but he did not think the Board had authority to prohibit the use of swing boats.—The Clerk said he was of opinion that the Board could not put a stop to these things. He would, however, look the matter up, and submit a report to the next meeting. The matter was then left in the hands of the Health Committee.

div.head: GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE.
div.p: GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE.

A special meeting of this Committee was held on July 14th, Mr. Brown presiding. The engineer submitted plan showing a subsidence that had taken place at Stocks well station in No. 2 well. The Committee visited the site and inspected the works in progress by the Engineer with reference to the matter, and approved thereof. An ordinary meeting of this Committee was held on the 4th inst., Mr. Brown presiding, when accounts amounting to £512 13s. 9d. on gas account, and £545 4s. ld. on water account, total £1,057 17s. 10d., were examined and passed for payment. Reports of tests of gas on the 13th and 24th ult. was read as follows: Illuminating power equal to 1777 and 16.26 candles, free from sulphuretted hydrogen. The Engineer reported that the first of the bore holes had been sunk to a depth of 170 feet, and a second to a depth of 22 feet. An accident to the satchet gear of the boring bar during the past month had caused a week's delay to the boring operations. A certificate for the sum of £250 was submitted on account of this contract and passed. The cavity which was discovered on the Bth ult. under the foundations and behind the well wall had been filled in with Portland cement concrete. The iron cylinders forming the lower portions of the well, toge- ther with some of the brick work, had sunk down 11 inches, leaving the pumps and the whole of the well gearing dependent for support cm the suspending bolts that are secured to the girders at the top of the well. On the 24th ult., when clearing the debris out of thei cavity, previous to putting in the concrete, a second cavity, about one-fourth of the capacity of the first one, was discovered. These subsidences were doubtless due, almast entirely, to the percolation of surface water from the adjoining brook into the well. To effectively prevent this, the Surveyor recommended that the inside of the brook be lined with cast iron plates for a distance of 70 feet, and a concrete wall be sunk into the ground at the outside of the plates to prevent any water gathering in the field from passing underneath the plates into the well. The estimated cost of this scheme is £l5O. In- structions were given to the Surveyor to carry out the work according to plans submitted.—The Clerk was in- structed to advertise for tenders for the purchase of tar for a period of twelve months.

div.head: lIIGHWAY COMMIII2I3.
div.p: lIIGHWAY COMMIII2I3.

An ordinary meeting of this Committee was held on the 30th ult., Mr. Sadler presiding.—The Clerk sub- mitted an order of the High Court of Justice, Chancery Division, dated 13th June, 1891, approving the exchange with the Local Board of lands belonging to the Leigh estate. It was recommended that the tender of Roberts Bros. for the constructi9n of ventilating shafts and flushing tanks, in accordande with the plan submitted and approved, for the sum of £BB2 18s.. be accepted.— The Surveyor read the correspondence which had taken place between him and Messrs. Sayc,e and Randle with respect to certain infringements by them of the bye-laws in the erection of houses in Deacon-road. The Clerk was instructed to take legal proceedings in the matter. The Surveyor was instructed to employ James Toole, as clerk of works, in the carrying out of the improvement works now in progress, at a salary of £2 per week.

Plans for the following were submitted and approved: —Wesleyan Chapel, Derby-road; for W. div.head: HEALTH COMMITTEE.
div.p: HEALTH COMMITTEE.

At an ordinary meeting of this Committee, held on the 4th inst., Mr. Wright in the chair, a letter, dated August Ist, from Nurse McConville, resigning her position at the Infectious Diseases Hospital was read, and it was recom- mended that her resignation be accepted, and that the Clerk be instructed to advertise for a probationer for two years in the place of Nurse McConville, at a salary of £l4 for the first year and £l6 the second year.—Mr. Wright said that since the meeting of the Health Com- mittee, the probationer at the Infectious Diseases Hospital had also sent her resignation in. He proposed that her resignation be accepted, and the Clerk be instructed to advertise for two probationers. This was unanimously carried.
MEDICAL OFFICER OF HEALTH.

It was recommended that a Medical Officer be adver- tised for in place of Dr. Cooper (resigned) at a salary of £l2O per annum ; also that the Clerk be instructed to make an application to the Local Government Board to pay half the salary assigned.—Mr. J. Taylor thought the salary proposed was too great an advance on the last Medical Cffieer's, which was only £6O, and if the Local Government Board paid half his salary they would have some conttol over the Medical Officer.—Mr. Wright ex- plained that the salary was subject to certain conditions and even now their Medical Officer was under the control of the Local Government Board to a certain extent.—As Mr: Taylor did not propose an amendment the matter dropped.

NUISANCE INSPECTOR'S REPORT. The Nuisance Inspector (Mr. Love) reported that he had inspected tke common lodging houses during the month, and found them in order. Major Cross had arranged for one of the workmen to inspect and abate any nuisances that may be found at the deposit on Sundays. It was recommended that slaughter-houses belonging to the following be registered for twelve months :—P. Buller, J. Fletcher, J. Smart, R. Potter, J. Ward, and W. J. Hedley.

FINANCE COMMITTEE. An ordinary meeting of this Committee was held on the sth inst., Mr. Midwood presiding. It was recom- mended that the Clerk advertise for applications from qualified persons to fulfil the duties of chief ledger clerk in succession to the late Mr. T. H. Wilson, deceased, at a salary of £llO per annum, and that a special meet- ing of this Committee be held on the 28th inst. to con- sider the same.--Mr. Midwood proposed the adoption of the minutes, which was agreed to.

GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE. A meeting of this Committee was held on the sth inst., Mr. Wright presiding. The Clerk submitted 147 appli- cations for the office of caretaker, and the following candidates were selected to appear before a special meet- ing of the Committee: Alfred Walker, butler, Liver- pool; William H. Parsons, caretaker, Widnes; Alex. Kermack, boilerman, Widnes ; Charles Lee, gardener, Knutsford ; Thomas Whittle, caretaker,Wigan ; and Geo. McKensie, market constable, Liverpool. At a special meeting, held on the 10th inst., it was decided to ap- point Thomas Whittle, Wigan, as caretaker at the Town Hall, at a salary of £2 ss. per week.—The minutes were confirmed. This was all the business.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.
THE ASSISTA NT -OVERSEERSHIP.
Much interest is being manifested in the forth- coming appointment of an assistant-overseer for the township, to succeed the late Mr. T. H. Wilson.

TEE REV. E. S. JACKSON. The Rev. E. S. Jackson, vicar of Great Sankey, is about to undertake a voyage to Montreal, having. been appointed by the Society for Promoting Chris- tian Knowledge to act as chaplain to emigrants sailing in the Allan Company's S.S. Mongolian, leaving the Mersey on September 10th.

THE OPEN-AIE BATHS. The work in connection with the open-air plunge baths is progressing favourably. Tire site is a field off Station-road. We understand that the first annual general meeting of the shareholders of the Penketh Park Company, Limited, in which Mr. Charles E. Parker has manifested especial interest, will be held in the course of a few days. The busi- ness of the meeting will be to receive the report of the promoters, to elect directors and auditors, and "transact such business as is proper to be trans- acted at the general meeting of the Company."

A St. Petersburg tele,gram, on Saturday, states, that in order to stave off fatnine and prevent culpable specula- tion in corn, Ministers have resolved to prohibit export- ation of wheat from Russia this var. Cholera is reported to he increasing at Aleppo, sixty- live deaths having occurred. A Blackburn excursionist named Michael Hannighan was drowned while bathing at Lytham on Sunday. The price of flour was on Tuesday advanced by the Leeds Corn Millers' Association Is. 6d. per bag of eighteen stones.

A New York telegram of Tuesday reports a continu- ance of the great heat wave, the weather for the time of the year being the warmest experienced for twenty years. Scores of people have been prostrated.

div.head: ItIiNCORN BOARITOF ULTARDIKNS.
div.p: ItIiNCORN BOARITOF ULTARDIKNS.

Mr. Mclntyre presided over the fortnightly meet- ing held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Present the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. C. Reynolds J.P., A. Thomas J.P. (ex-officio), Edwards, Lewis, Afton, Baguley, Baxter, W. Weir, J. Weir, A. J. Weir, P. Hall, J. Brandreth, R. Bate, J. Whitlow, J. W. Kirkham, P. Speakman C.C., and T. Lea, and J. Ashton (clerk). Mr. J. Williams, accountant and auditor to the Cheshire County Council wrote as follows: "1 observe that the amount of rates due from your Union under the precept of May last has not yet been paid to the bank, and as we are now about to make large payments upon the order of the County Council I shall be glad if you will have a cheque for the balance remitted with the least possible delay."—Mr. Aaron said if they were all of his mind it would not be paid until the Board had a balance sheet showing how the money was spent. While on this subject he wished to explain that some six or eight, weeks ago he was speaking about County Council extravagance and waste of money. and he mentioned that the Council had appointed four surveyors at £2OO each and had increased the salary of Mr. Bull, the surveyor, from £7OO to £9OO. He further stated that Mr. Speakman had seconded the motion giving this increase. Mr. Speakman denied that he had done so, and said that he (Mr. Aaron) was not telling the truth. He now wished to defend himself and show that he had told the truth. He held in his band a copy of the "Chester Chronicle " dated February 10th. in which Mr. S. peakman's name was given as seconding the motion to increase Mr. Bull's salary. In conclusion Mr. Aaron moved that the Clerk communicate with all the Boards of Guardians in Cheshire with a view to forming a Committee to watch the county expenditure and take such action as might be deemed advisable.— The Chairman ruled that the motion was out of order. —Mr. Brandreth : Are you going to move a vote of censure on Mr. Speakman ?--Mr. Aaron: No I am not. —Mr. Brandreth : If you will, I will second it. (Laughter.)—Mr. Aaron said about 8 or 9 years ago a Committee was f )rmed to inquire into the expenditure of the Weaver Trust and did much good. The Committee he now proposed was on similar lines.—Mr. Baxter: There will be an election in a few months and then we can turn the extravagant men out.—Mr. Aaron: They may spend many thousands before February.—Mr. Speaknaau said he remembered sayin most distinctly that he did not second the resolution, and because it was there printed did not make it a fact. If it escaped his memory at the time, he did not want to go behind the fact that he voted for the increase of Mr. Bull's salary and other sala- ries in connection with the County Council. Mr. Aaron had not looked into all the details of the county accounts, neither did he seem to understand them when they were explained to him. The council budget and a full state- ment of the county business had been brought before the Board, but there was only one single thing that Mr. Aaron could talk about, and that was the Surveyor's salary. The question was whether the County Surveyor of Cheshire was worth the £9OO a year given to him. A Committee of 36 members recom- mended the increase and it was carried by the Council by a large majority. If there was any sense in what Mr. Aaron said he should be glad to cross swords with him. He was exceedingly sorry that after all he (Mr. Speakman) had said at that Board and outside the Board, Mr. Aaron did not seem capable of getting be- yond the surveyors salary. It would give him great pleasure to give the Board any information in his power as a County Councillor, but they must understand that he attended there not in his capacity as a County Coun- cillor, but as a Guardian of the poor. He wished further to state that the County Coun- cil was an administrative body like the Guardians and they worked and gave their time the same as the Guardians did 'but if they (Guardians) would spend the time to better purpose than discussing these matters it would be an advantage to the poor generally. He trusted they would have no more of it. If he had made a mistake in saying he did not second the motion he was sorry; but he made it in ignorance. He was not one of those to go back on anything he said in the least degree.—Mr. Aaron asked if inCreasing the surveyor's department from £5OO to £1,890 was doing their duty.—The Chairman said he could not allow these irregular discussions and the matter dropped. VACCINATION OFFICER.

The Clerk read an application from Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys, solicitor, Runcorn, for the position of vac- cination officer at Runcorn.—The Chairman said Mr. Coleburn would hold the office until the end of the quar- ter and the Board would probably advertise in the ordinary way.

div.head: RESIGNATIONS.
div.p: RESIGNATIONS.

The Clerk said there had not been held a meeting of the School Attendance Committee because there was not a quorum. He wished to report that G. Ward, Mr. Riley, and Mr. W. R. De Prez, attendance officers respectively for Runcorn, Frodsham, and Great Budworth dis- tricts, had sent in their resignations.

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.
On the recommendation of the Finance Committee accounts amounting to £192 Os. ld were passed for pay- ment. The balance in the treasurer's hands was £1,853 14s. 9d.
THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c.
BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT,

Mr. Alderman Beckett, C.C., chairman of the County Highway Committee, accompanied by Mr. Ball, the surveyor, made an inspection the other day of Station-road, High-st., Bridge-st., and Hal- ton-road, which the Runcorn Board of Commis- sioners desire to be declared as county main roads. Several members of the Board of Commissioners went the circuit of the roads with the visitors who made a thorough examination, and a favourable re- port would doubtless result in the wishes of our local authority being realised.

When the Alkali Union was formed the workmen in Runcorn and Widnes districts looked on with feelings of distrust, and a fear that it would not be to their advantage. What has since occurred has rather strengthened than lessened those feelings. At Weston a part of the plant has been stopped,and about 200 men thrown idle ;in Widnes one works has been totally demolished, and in others certain departments have been dispensed with; and now there is a prospect of the wages of the men being re- duced several shillings per ton in the production of a certain article. The men have had a Union for about two years, but the membership includes but a small proportion of the workers in chemical yards.

The new lists of voters are now issued and to be seen on all the Church and Chapel doors. All Liberals who are qualified to vote should see that their names are on the:lists and that their addresses and qualifications are correctly described. Should they discover any errors or omissions they should at once communicate the fact to the overseers or to the registration agent of their respective districts. All claims must be served on the overseers not later than the 20th August. It is believed that the general election will be fought on the register now being prepared.

Recently Widnes Local Board advertised for a caretaker for the Town Hall, and no fewer than 147 applications were received. The General Purposes Committee held a special meeting on Monday last to consider these applications and selected six can- didates to make a personal appearance. Eventually the choice fell upon Mr. Thomas Whittle, caretaker, of Wigan. His salary is fixed at ..C2 ss. per week. There was a number of local applicants for the ap- pointment.

For some years the tradesmen of Widnes, who have been most often called to serve their fello vs in the capacity of jurymen, have agitated for payment of their services and loss of time, but so far with- out result. A practical step was, however, taken at an inquest on Monday. The jurymen each subscribed a shilling to form the nucleus of a fund for carrying on an organised agitation, and a meeting of trades- men will shortly be called to fully consider the question. In Garston a small voluntary rate for the payment of jurors has been levied for some years and the ratepayers without murmur—nay gladly— pay the small amount demanded from them. It is desired that the Widnes overseers should act in a like manner. Mr. Husband, the deputy coroner, sympathises with the movement and will give it all the help in his power. In Runcorn each juror is paid a shilling from the county funds.

The Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, of Runcorn, has already applied to have the Catholic schools declared free under the new Education Act,and they will have the distinction of being the first free school in the town. Financially the schools will gain £l2 a year by the new arrangement. There are only about six vacant places in the schools. Widnes School Board meet to decide the question on Tuesday night, and Run- corn School Board on the Tuesday following.

In mentioning last week the departure of Mr. J. Weston from Rnncorn section of the Ship Canal, the section was described as No. 4 whereas it is No. 3, and I wish to correct any confusion that might thereby arise., The employes have not allowed the occasion to pass without displaying their appreciation of Mr. Weston's many good qualities, and regret at the severance of their rela- tioas. Through Mr. 11. Davenport, the sub-agent, the Runcorn men have presented Mr. Weston with a handsome solid 18 carat gold guard and pendant, and also half a dozen silver serviette rings and an entree dish. The Weston point portion presented him, through Mr. J. Humphreys, with a valuable gold diamond ring. The inscription upon the various articles is "Presented by the workmen and friends to John Weston, Esq., August, 1891." The gifts were suitably acknowledged by Mr. Weston, who says he deeply feels the kindness displayed, and is much gratified at the appreciation of his services. . .

The report of the Committee .appointed by the Quarter Sessions to inquire into the state of the liquor traffic in Cheshire has created quite a sensa- tion and the speeches made at the meeting at Chester on Saturday are very interesting reading. The re- port was only" received "and not adopted, and the practical result is thus far 9ail, but there is not the slightest doubt that the report and the statistics ob- tained will have their influence in future when the magistrates are dealing with the trade.

There is one reform that might be carried out with the greatest ease, and it would be tar-reaching in its effect. At present when the licensee of a house is convicted of an offence against the liquor laws. the black mark is placed against his name, and if he be the tenant of a tied house, or manager for a brewer he is quickly removed and another man i placed n his stead. The new man starts with a clean sheet and the house is at the same time cleared from all stain. It has been suggested to me by a gentleman interested in public-house property that the conviction should be recorded agaiust the house, and then whether a new tenant was put in, or the old one permitted to remain the record against the house would stand until it had been wiped out by i better and more careful management n accordance with the terms of the license. The bad houses could then be easily weeded out to the benefit of those who were carrying on a legitimate trade.

I observe that the reputation of Runcorn came in for the usual tarnishing at the magistrates meeting on Saturday. Mr. Comber picked out the town as the most drunken place in Cheshire, and based the charge upon the assertion that one in ten of the population hal been convicted of drunkenness and that the proportion of public-houses to population was one in 190. The fact is that both statements are radically wrong, and ought not to have been made in the careless and inconsiderate manner they were. The fact is that the proportion of drunken- ness is nearer one in 40 than one in ten and that the propor ion of persons to each house is one to 230. The most ar lent defender of Runcorn would not set it up as a heaven nor as the allele of angels, but the place is not so bad as it is patnted. If Mr. Comber would trouble himself to look through the police records he would find that over one half of the con- victions for drunkenness are against " birds of pass- age," and not against the inhabitants of Runcorn. The Ship Canal workers and the "floating popula- tion," are responsible for a considerable amount of the drunkenness. Perhaps Mr. Comber will ack- nowledge the inaccuracy of his figures, and in future take into account the peculiar circumstances ,of a town before he issues an unqualified condemna- tion.

By the very narrow majority of one the scheme of water supply for Frodsham was passed at the meet- ing of Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority on Tues- day last. Mr. Edwards contended that it was a wild and ill-considered scheme,but he did not bring forward any facts in support of his opinion,although he was pretty near tke mark when he said that in ninety-nine out of one hundred water schemes the estimate was largely exceeded, and perhaps he may be a prophet in this case in predicting that the cost of the present scheme will not be .£3,000 but £6,000.

One very sore ppint with Mr. Edwards is the fact that the representatives of Frodsham Lordship and the ex-officio members of t e authority were interfereing in the question, and he was very severe upon the latter, whom he said represented nobody but themselves. Magistrates may be very good and estimable men, but I am at one with Mr. Edwards in believing that they should be elected to an adminis- trative body like the Board of Guardians and not be allowed a seat independent of their fellow rate- payers.

--- Mr. E. Aaron, of Runcorn Guardians, was a most uncompromising and persistent opponent of the Counfy Council. He regards the Council as one of the most extravagant public bodies in existence, and he misses no opportunity of inveighing against- its demands. On Tuesday last he made a proposal to form a Committee composed of repre- sentatives of the various Unions in Cheshire, whose special duty it would be to strictly investigate

county expenditure, with a view to a reduction. The Chairman, however, ruled the motion out of order and it was not put to the meeting. Mr. Speakman objects to Mr. Aaron's attitude towards the Council, and there was a shirp passage between these gentlemen, which is interesting reading.
STOPPING AN ANCIENT HIGHWAY AT WARRINGTON.
THE CORPORATION ASSERTING THE PUBLIC
RIGHTS.

The Warrington Corpoiation are, we believe, at present taking action to resist an encioachment upon an ancient highway at Bank Quay. The road:. way in question leads past Litton's Mill, and it is said to have been a public highway during the last two centuries. We believe that between the late Major Litton and the late Major Cartwright, who occupied adjoining properties, there were frequent differences as to the rights of way, and since,Ar present owners of Litton's Mill, Messrs. Fairclou—gif, came into possession they have put up two posts and a chain entirely putting a stop to vehicular traffic. Messrs. Fairclough now, we believe, pro- pose to extend their warehouses so as to entirely cover the road, only leaving a sort of covered pass.. age for the use of pedestrians. The Corporation has, however,ref used to pass the plans for this extension, and have resolved to apply for an injunction to res- train Messrs. Fairclough from stopping the high- way. It will, we should think, be the general opinion of the townspeople that the Corporation are deserving of the highest commendation for resisting all encroachments on highways.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
THURSDAY.—Before his Honour Judge Ffoulkeg.

AN UNREASONABLE DELAY.—John Pemberton, glass dealer, Market-place, brought an action against Frederick Jenkins, boot and shoe dealer, Bridge-st., to recover 21. 9d. for a square of glass supplied to the de- fendant. Mr. Arthur Browne defended. The glass was ordered by Mr. Jenkins, who understood the cost price would be Is. Bd. or is. 9d. Three or four months elapsed before the glass was supplied, and a charge of 2s. 9d. was made. Mr. Jenkins declined to receive the glass having obtained a square from another dealer. His Honour, in giving judgment for the defendant, said he did noCthink the difference in price was a sufficient reason for breaking the contract, but he gave a verdict for the defendant on the ground that there had been an unreasonable delay in supplying the glass, the fulfilment of the contract having been requested several times on behalf of Mr. Jenkins.

No JURISDICTION.-Mr. A. Browne applied to his Honour for leave to issue a summons out for jurisdiction of the court for damages for a breach of contract. The matter had, he said, been before the registrar and his deputy who had referred him to the judge. The defen- dant, it appeared, wrote a letter tc, the plaintiff who lives in Warrington in which they offered certain goods for sale. The plaintiff replied by telegram offering different price which was refused, but another price was suggested and this tho plaintiff accepted also by telegram. Mr. Browne contended that that court had jurisdiction in the case, but, after reviewing certain cases, his Honour decided that there was no jurisdiction and refused the application.

div.head: FRODSHAM
div.p: FRODSHAM

ALARMING ACCIDENT AT TIM RAILWAY STATION.—A serious accident occurred to a man named Samuel Booth, residing in Runcorn mho arrived in Frodsham by the 5.55 p.m. train on Saturday. When the train stopped for passengers to alight, the man attempted to get through the door on to the six-foot, but was unable to do so, the train having again started. Booth opened the other door, and jumped on to the platform. Not being able, however, to steady himself, he fell with his back against the footboard of the carriage, and his legs'got be- tween the platform and the step. The man's dangerous position wes noticed by the guard and Porter Poole. The former sprang on to the van and applied the brake, and the latter ran to Booth's assistance, although with extreme danger to himself. He held Booth by his jacket, and in this manner kept his body from slipping on to the metals, the distance traversed being more than fifty yards before the train was brought to a standstill. Booth was with difficulty liberated, and his injuries, which are very severe, were dressed by Dr. Robinson.

div.head: LY3LM.
div.p: LY3LM.

OUTDOOR SERVICE.—The old custom of holding divine service at the foot of Lymm Cross,on Rushbearing S un- day, was duly observed last Sunday. There was a fair gathering, especially at night, when Mr. Morris, of the Manchester City Mission, delivered an address. In the afternoon, Mr. F. Keen, of Altrincham, gave a discourse. The Rev. W. Southall was present and assisted at each service. THE NEW CLOCK.—The new clock kindly presented to the parish by Miss Fox to be placed in the new tower of St. Mary's Church, was sent off from the makers on Monday, and arrived in Lymm early in the week. The process of fixing is now going on and it is anticipated that it will be completed during the coming week. Its price is upwards of £l5O. HALF-DAY EXCURSION.—The Court Rose in the Valley Dividend Society had their half-day trip to the Zoological Gardens, Belle Vue, on Monday. In the evening at dusk the spectacle of the battle of Inkermann, fought on tha sth November, 1854., was produced. It was followed by a Naval Review, showing an attack by torpedo boats upon a squadron of ironclads. The party returned in the evening, having spent an enjoyable day. " RUSHBEARING" AT LYNIM.—The real rushbearing at Lymm passed away a long time ago. Up to the last few years a cart full of rushes and bearing one of the girls of the village wended its way through the streets. Now the rushbearing takes the form of a pleasure fair. According to the young children's opinion, this is a far more enjoyable proceeding. The fair is held in one of the large fields adjoining the village, and business is conducted with great zest. The weather so far has had rather a depressing effect upon the spirits of the youngsters. THE CHURCH BELLS.—The hanging of the new bells. was completed on Monday, and they are now ready for the ringers. It had been arranged that the opening cere- mony should have taken place on the first Sunday in September, but the Rector has received notice from the Ven. Archdeacon Barber that it will be inconvenient for him to come before &ptember 12th. It has now been definitely arranged thipt the opening service will take place on that date, and a set of ringers from the neigh- bourhood of Northwich will ring out the first peal. SUNDAY SCHOOL TRIP.—On Monday the Lymm Sun- day school scholars had their annual excursion. The place visited was Blackpool, and the choice was a good one. About 800 scholars and friends left Lymm at six o'clock on Monday morning, and having arrived at Blackpool safely, at once set off for the man, and varied amusements this pleasant sea-side to affords. The day passed merrily over, and night having arrived, the scholars assembled at the Central StatAn, where a train awaited them. They arrived at Lymm about 12 o'clock, having spent the day in a most enjoyable manner. A BRAVE ACT.—On Saturday morning as a couple of boats were proceeding through Lymm by the canal, a. child on the first boat fell into the water. the father,. who was on the boat, immediately plunged in after it, but it had fallen so close to the barge that it was " sucked" under. It came up on the other side, and as the father was on the hauling side he was powerless to render aid to the little one drowning before the eyes of its agonised mother. Mr. T. Davies of the coalyard, took in the situation in a moment, leaped in without divest- ing himself of even his hat, and secured the child. He swam round the stern of the barge and gave it to its dis- tressed father, who in turn passed it to its mother. It SOOR came round after the careful attention of the thank- ful mother. _ _

LIVERPOOL NATURALISTS AT LYIIM.—The seventh field meeting of the session was held at Lymm, on Saturday. The weather of late has not been favourable for such gatherings, and only twenty-eight members attended. From Lime-st. the party went by train to Heatley Station, and from there walked to Warburton and inspected the curious old church. Then, retracing their steps to Heatley, the route lay by field paths and by the banks of the canal to Lymm, where an excellent meat tea was I prepared at the Fleece Hotel. It was intended to have spent two hours after tea botanizing round the Mere and visiting the gardens at Beechwood, the residence of Mr. Dewhurst, but the rain fell so pitilessly that this portion of the programme had to be abandoned. The following prizes were awarded :—" Orders for the day," compositte and alismacere, Mr. A. K. Batley, with twenty-one species; best bouquet Miss Fazakerly. The botanical enigma was solved, and the plant (chrysanthemum inoderum) found by Miss E. M. Wood, Mr. A. K. Bulley, Mr. Holt, and Mr. J. Mackerel!.

Sir Hector Langevin, as the outcome of the re,Sent revelations before the Parliamentary ConamittEe of the Canadian Legislature, has tendered his resignation as Minister of Public Works. The cargo of the London and North-Western Railway Company's steamer Anglesea was much damaged by fire which broke out on Saturday morning while the vessel was lyint at Dublin.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
AN UNBROTHERLY BROTHER.

James Sauce, who has often been before the magis- trates, was on Monday charged at the Warrington Police Court, with having assaulted his sister, and also with not having appeared to a summons. The sister when called upon to give evidence appeared very reluctant to do so. She admitted that he had struck her, but said he would not have done so had ho not been drunk. She made it out that he was quite an inoffensive young man when sober. Two constables had, however, seen the assault and their version of the affair was rather different. In their opinion the defendant was not drunk when he committed the assault. They had gone into the house to quieten defendant, and just as they were leaving again he jumped up and struck his sister twice violently on the face. A tine of 20s. and costs, or one month's hard labour, was imposed.
ASSAULTING A FOREMAN

At the Borough Court on Tuesday, a man named John Ward was charged with having assaulted Joseph Smith, on the 23rd June, and also with not having appeared to a summons. Mr. Percy Davies prosecuted, and he stated that the defendant had been employed at Messrs. Monks, Hall and Co., and on the day in question, the prosecutor, who is an under-foreman asked him to do seine other kind of work from that which he was at the time engaged upon, when he used some very abusive language. This was reported to the foreman, James Woolley, and as defendant said he wonld not do what Smith told him. he was discharged. Two or three hours afterwards he suddenly and unexpectedly made an assault upon Smith. He seized complainant round the neck, pulled him down and kicked him, with the result that he had to have medical aid, a,nd stop away from work for two or three days. A fine of 10s. and costs,in- eluding advocate's fee, was imposed, or in default one months' imprisonment. _

div.head: MAN WHO DOESN'T FEAR DEATH
div.p: A MAN WHO DOESN'T FEAR DEATH

Upon the name of George Patrick being called out at I the Warrington Police Court, on Tuesday morning, a I man who bore the outward appearance of a respectable -labourer, bounced into the dock in a violent fashion, and bezan to use language which Wasinterlarded with oaths to a quite unusual extent. Before he was invited to plead, he cried out, "Guilty, ye , guilty; give me two —years, if you like, I don't care for-- death ; fetch a rope, ye-lot of paupers." The charge against him was not so tragic as his language seemed to imply, as he was only indicted for having been drunk and disorderly at Market Gate, on the pre- vious evening. He had been annoying passers-by with his language, and he had been particularly offensive to a sergeant from the barracks.—He was sent to gaol for a month's hard labour. "AN INIMBIAN BIZITTE." _ -

Charles Fudge, a Ship Canal navvy,was charged at the Warrington Borough Court, on Tuesday, with having assaulted his wife, Mary Ann Fudge, in a yard off Pennell-st. From the evidence that was given,the assault appeared to have been a very brutal one. Detective- Sergeant Monoghan said that a fternoon he had been called to the place in .question he heard Mrs. Fudge screaming in the house and,on looking through the window,he saw Fudge kicking his wife. Prisoner tried to keep the door closed against theofficers, but they forced a way in and found Mrs. Fudge lying in a pool of blood. Both hus- bandand wife were under the influence of drink. Other witnesses deposed to prisoner having savagely kicked his wife before the officers were called to the scene. In answer to the mas.7,istra.tes, Fudge said he elonged to Bristol, and the Chairman remarked that he hoped he was not a type of Bristol people, for he was an inhuman brute.—He was sent to gaol for three months with hard labour.

FRUIT STEALING BY YOUTHS. At the Borough Court, on Thursday, a lad named Walter Seott, of 9, Helsby-st., was charged with steal- ing fruit that morning, from the garden at Darlington Lodge, Manchester-road. P.C. Smith said he had been on the watch early that morning in plain clothes in the garden at Darlington Lodge, belonging to Mr. Robinson, and he saw five boys robbing an apple tree. He caught defendant, and got the names of the other lads who would be summoned. Although the fruit found upon defendant was only valued at 6d., about ss. worth of damage had been done. A fine of 2s. 6d. was imposed. Tha Chief Constable said there had been so many cases of fruit stealing lately that constables were now put on duty for the purpose of catching the culprits. The Bench considered that these cases would have to be severely dealt with.

div.head: Row IN A BAKEHOUSX.
div.p: A Row IN A BAKEHOUSX.

William Read, a baker, was charged at the borough Court yesterday with having assaulted William Harvey, a grocer's assistant. Both complainant and defendant are engaged at the same place of business, and Harvey said he was sent into the bakehouse to assist Reade, when the latter told him he was putting the bread down the wrong way. He then told Reade to "shut up his mouth" and on repeating the expression Reade struck him in the mouth. He called Reade a coward and he again struck him this ame blackening his eye. A boy named Carless gave corroborative evidence. The de- fendant said Harvey had been pitching the bread about, using provoking language, and besides hit him on the head with a loaf and afterwards with a bread tin. A fine of ss. including costs was imposed. CRUELTY TO HORSES.—A BATCH OF CASES.

Several persons were charged at Warrington Police Court yesterday morning with cruelty to horses and some heavy fines were imposed. The evidence was mostly given by Inspector Dowty, of the R.S.P.C.A. Downes Varey, a horse dealer, of Liverpool, was accused of ill- _treating a.horse on the 18th July. It was stated that at the Warrington fair he was " sawing " the mouth of the horse with the reins and causing the tongue to bleed very freely. 4 fine of 20s. and costs was im- posed.—John Urnston, a carter, of 6, Mill-yard, was charged with working a horse while in an unfit state, and Sarah Hadow, a coal-dealer, was charged with caus- ing the animal to be worked. In this case. it was said that thc horse was suffering from suppurating wounds. A fine of 3s. 6d. including costs was imposed on eael: of the defendants.—lsaac Barton ,a green-grocer, of Wan, who did not appear till after his case had been dispßsed of, was fined 40s. and costs. According to evi,leace the horse, which was being worked at '"t-gate, had three or four wounds from which it pp:, red to suffer very much.—Thomas Ellam, of Pres- sed George Newsham, a horseslaughterer, from the •wn, were charged, the first-named with using a rn unfit state, and Newsham was causing it to This offence also took place at Warlington m was fined ss. 6d. and Newsham 40s. and

12th Lancers, was ordered to Strangeways to await an escort.

BREACH OF nig PEACE.—Alfred Barnes, and William Stewart, charged with fighting in Irlam-st., on the Ist August, were each bound ever in their own recognisance , of £5 and ordered to pay the costs 7s.—Annie McCone, for breach of the peace, on Friar's Green, was similarly dealt with.—John Kelly, James McGrail, and Daniel Hennessy,were charged with breach of the peace in Crown and Sceptre Yard, and were each ordered to pay 3s. 6d. costs.—John Bailey, for a breach of the peace in Ship- yard, on the Ist August, bound over for six months. OCCASIONAL LICENSE.—Mr. :Massey, of the Roebuck Inn, applied for an occasional license to sell on the Foot- ball ground, on the occasion of the Cycling Club Sports. BAD LANCRIAGE.—MichaeI Cunningham, and Anne Daley, were charged with using obscene language in Buttermarket-st., on the sth August, and they were , each fined ss. and costs.

UNLOADING LIME IN THE STR.EET.—Patrick Noon, a carter, was charged with having obstructed Bridge-st., by unloading a quantity of lime there on the 4th inst. It was stated that when the lime was deposited it flew up In clouds and filled the street to the danger and annoy- ance of passengers. It was also added that a good deal of damage had been done to tradesmen's goods, and that some compensation would probably have to be paid. The defenda.nt said he only unloaded the lime where he was told to do it. A fine of ss. including costs was im- posed. TIIESDAY.—Before Mr. R. Garnett and Alderman
Greenall.

MISCELLANEOITS.—Thomas Drury, for having been drunk'and disorderly, in Buttermarket-st. on the pre- vious day, was discharged.—James Jordan was charged with committing a breach of the peace in the Crown and Sceptre yard on the 3rd inst., and was bound over in one surety of £lO to keep the peace.—Patrick Gannon and William Gannon for breaches of the peace in a court off Fennel-st.,were fined ss. and costs each. UNWHOLESOME STRAWBERRIES.—Benjamin Tasker was summoned for exposing for sale on a cart in Mersey-st. 611bs. of strawberries which were unfit for human food. Inspectors Norman and Church proved the charge, and the former stated that this kind of fruit was mostly sold to children. A fine of 2s. 6d. including costs was im- posed. SCHOOL CASES.—The following persons were fined for neglecting to send their children regularly to school : John Flannagan, Ropwood-st., boy sent to an industrial school; James Moseley, Lovely-lane, fined 103. ; William Carrington, Oliver-st.' 2s. 6d.; John Clare, Winwick- road, 55.; Harriet Johnson, Pinner's-brow, 2s. 6d.' • William Dagnall, Warburton-st., ' , 53. • F. Pritchard Cartwright-st., 2s 6d.; William Evans, New-road, ss. ; Edward Murray, Tanner's-lane, 55.; Mary Towey, Oliver-st., 2s. 6d.•' Michael Connor, Oliver-st., 53. War- rants were issued for the apprehension of the lads in the case of John Fallon and Thomas Knoct^n.-7The cases were proved by Mr. Riley. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. John Geddes and Alderman Wright. _

Ax INconen3LE Yount —Thos. Knockton was charged with neglecting to send his child regularly to school. This case was remanded from Tuesday, as the boy was then missing from home.—Mr. Riley, school attend- ance officer, explained to the magistrates that the boy was the ringleader of the truant-players in that part of the town.—Thomas Knockton said that his boy was com- pletely beyond his control, and he would be /leased if the magistrates would send him than industrial school.— The Bench ordered the youth to be sent to St. Ann's In- dustrial School, Liverpool. DRUNK AND DISORDERLIL—Mary Ann Fudge, the wife of Charles Fudge, w 5.3 charged with being drunk and disorderly in Green's-court, on Tuesday night, and also with assaulang another woman named Bridget McCor- mick.—Sergt. Taylor stated that he went up Green's- court, and there found the prisoner making a great dis- bance, and also ill-using an old woman.—Complainant fully bore out the last statemmt, and declared that the defendant had not received the slightest provocation for the assault.—The magistrates fined her ss. and costs for being drunk and disorderly and 53. for the assault. FRlDAY—Before Alderman Harrison, and Alderman

Wright. DRUNKENNESS.—John Kennedy, drunk and disorderly, in Buttermarket-st., on the previous day, ss. including costs; John Dodd, drunk in Winwick-st., on Thursday night, ss. including costs. ASSAULT BY A WOMAN.—Anne Noon was charged with having assaulted a gir; named Ellen Sutton, and was fined 10s. including costs. ON THE "Senn."—George Drinkwater, a blacksmith on the Ship Canal at Thelwall, was charged with having neglected to maintain his wife who had become charge- able to the Union.—Mr. Shearer said the defendant had been brought there more for the purpose of getting him sober than anything else as he had been on the " spree " for some time. When at work he could earn about 365. a week. He was sent to gaol for 14 days. ASLEEP IN THE MARKET.—DanieI Crosby was fined ss. for sleeping in the Market on Thursday night.

div.head: WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL COURT.

MONDAY.—Before Major Pickmere and Mr. J. Marson. MISCELLANEOUS.—A Ship Canal navvy named Thomas Williamson, living at Acton Grange, was charged with being drunk at Rixton on Sunday. The facts of the case were stated by P.C. Schofield. The prisoner was fined ss. and costs, but, in default of payment went to gaol for seven days.—John Miller, labourer, Antrobus, was charged with having, on the Bth inst., been drunk and assaulting Constable Gibbon. James illane, another labourer, was charged with a similar offence, and also with damaging the officer's clothing. The officer said he was on duty at Antrobus on Saturday night, on the occasion of the Foresters' anniversary, when he was called to the Wheat Sheaf Inn, as the defendants were drunk and fighting. He went to separate them, and was assaulted. One of them threatened to do for him." Blane damaged witness's helmet. The defendants ad- mitted the charge of being drunk, and were fined 2s. 6d. and costs each. The charge of assault will be heard at the next Daresbury Petty Sessions.

div.head: RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS.
MONDAY.—Before Mr. James Handley and Mr. A.
Thomas.

MISCELLANEOUS.—John Dunbabin was fined 2s. 6d.and costs for being drunk. For a similar offence Robert Ridler was fined ss. and costs.—James Lamb, for com- mitting a breach of the peace, was bound over in the usual sureties; and James Johnson, Charles Allen, and Henry Collins were each fined 10s. and costs for using obscene and profane language.—For playing pitch and toss Thomas Baker, Arthur Ellis; and Thomas Riley were each ordered to pay the costs, ss. 6d.—John Dunbabin was summoned for threatening George Whitley, at Wes- ton Point; the case was dismissed. Ellen Coffey, a well- known character was sentence I to 14 days' hard labour, for indecent conduct. On a charge of +obstructing the footpath in Church-st., John Smith was fined 2s. 6d. and costs. •

_ AN UNSIISTAINED CHARCT.—Peter Deakin, was sum- moned for assaulting Ellen Acton, wife of Edward Acton of 12, Lion-st., on the 12th July. Mrs. Acton had been to the Devonshire Hotel for some beer and when return ing the defendant charged her with having used bad- expressions to his wife. She denied the accusation but he struck her on the arm and shoulder and threw the beer she was carrying upon her.—Mr. Lake for the defence said the whole matter was jealousy, arising out of the fact that a lodger named Chisholm had left Mrs. Acton and gone to Deakin's. Witnesses were called to prove that Mrs. Acton used the laguage alleged and that defendant had not assaulted her. The case was dis- missed. Mr. E. W. Humphreys was for the complain- ant.

AFRAID OF HER HUSBAND.—AIfred Pownall, was sum- moned for assaulting his wife Jane. Mr. Burton appeared for the prosecutrix. On the first inst (Saturday) defend- ant did not come home for his dinner until four o'clock and although his dinner was waiting he abused his wife and refused to give her any money. He struck her three or four times. Afterwards he went out and did not return until an hour after midnight when he threatened to cut her head off and informed his two young boys that they would see their mother's funeral in a week or two. Complainant said she was afraid of her husband. The defendant denied the offence but he was bound over to keep the peace for six months himself in £2O and two sureties of £lO each ; and also pay the costs £1 2s.

EARIASTOWN V. CREWE ALEXANDRA. The return match was played at Crewe, on Saturday. Earlestown defeated Crewe some weeks ago and as a consequence the latter got together a particularly strong eleven with the object if possible of wiping out the previous defeat. Osborne for Crewe having won the toss elected to bat, Harrison and Clare taking up the attack. In the second over Clare dismissed Osborne, and Harrison very quickly disposed of Henshall. This was only the forerunner of a series of disasten3 which hefel the whole of the home eleven, as Harrison was in his best form, and on a true wicket had very little difficulty in removing the bails of the batsmen. He retained possession of the leather throughout the innings, and for the loss of five wickets only 17 runs were scored. The rain, however, interfered with the game, and the•ball became very greasy, rend- ering it difficult te handle. As a consequence the last two men had a rather better chance, and they together contributed about 30 runs. WARRINGTON v. LEYLAND.—This return match, which was set down to be played at Leyland, on Saturday, was unfortunately spoiled by the unpropitious state of the weather, an hour and a half sufficing to bring the game to a close. This is, indeed, .to be regretted, for the first match had a like fate, Warrington on that occasion scor- ing IC9 for seven wickets, and Leyland 29 for one, when rain put a stop to the. game. Leyland on Saturday had whipped together their strongest team, Albert Ward, the Lancashire county man, figuring in their ranks. War- rington, however, were without the services of such players as Captain Adam,Cm4ain Manson, and R. Smith. Having the good fortune to win the toss, Leyland opened the batting, R. Kershaw and Smith facing Messrs. S. M. and J. J. Crosfield. The Scoring at the opening was very- slow, maiden overs being the order. Eventually Ker- shaw opened his shoulders, and in two overs from the visiting captain placed him three times through the slips to the boundary. When Smith had made five he gave a hard chance to J.J. Crosfield. At 21 Bell relieved S. M. Crosfield, but runs came a. trifle faster, if anything. Both batsmen played good cricket, but with the score at 41 Smith played on, the scoring board reading as 41-1-19.
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 15, 1891.

A. Ward coming in, soon set to work, and Kershaw being in a hitting mood, the score rose rapidly. However, at 59. S. M. Crosfield took up the bowling at Bell's end, the latter crossing over. The change worked immediately, for Kershaw, in trying to pull a ball to leg, was bowled —a bad stroke. Tinsley narrowly escaped being caught first ball, and the total had only been increased to 70, when Ward was bowled with a grand ball, which broke nearly a foot from the leg side, and took the off bail. Dewhurst was bowled first ball, and after Tinsley and Padgett had carried the score to 83, bell beat the latter with an extra fast one. Rain now came on, and Gerrard and Tinsley pnt together seven more runs when an ad- journment was made. The rain came down iu torrents after, and there being no sign of a cessation, the game was eventually abandoned, the score reading as Leyland 90 for five wickets. Score :
