RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Mr. Mclntyre presided and there were present Messrs. C. Reynolds J. 1., and A. Thomas J.P. (ex-officio), Edwards, Lewis, Aaron, J. Baguley, Baxter, W. Weir, J. Weir, P. Hall, J. Brandreth, R. Bate, J. Whitlow, J. W. Kirkham, J. Ashton (clerk), J. Farrington (nuisance inspector.)
FRODSHAN WATER SCHEME. LIVELY DISCUSSION.

At a meeting of Frodsham and Frodsham Lordship Parochial Committee held in the overseers' office, Town Hall, Frodsham, on Monday evening, there were present Messrs. As Thomas, J.P. (chairman), John Robinson, Henry Tiley, James Edwards, E. C. Collinson, Ralph Bate, James. Percival,and L. Davies. The Clerk produced a copy of the Liverpool Water Works Act, 1887, which showed that Frodsham could be supplied with water from the Vyrnwy Mains at 9d. per 1000 gallons, taking not less a quantity than 20,000 per day. The Clerk had communicated with Mr. Parry, water engineer to the Corporation of Liverpool, on the subject and that gentleman stated that in his opinena the Corporation would be willing to enter into an agreement with the Authority on terms of payment of 9d. per 1000 gallons for the first 10,000 or 15,00 D gallons a day and of 64.. per 1,000 gallons for the excess. After a long discussion Mr. Robinson proposed and Mr. Davies seconded that the scheme prepared by Mr. Timmins except as to the erec- tion of stand pipes be approved and adopted when two voted for the motion and one against and wascleclared carried. It was resolved that the necessary steps be taken to obtain the sanction of the Local Government Board to the loan required to carry out the scheme.— The Clerk informed the- authority that the estimated total cost of the Scheme was £3,000 and it was proposed to sink a well and pump the water into a reservoir at such a height that the township could be easily supplied. —Mr. Thomas moved that the minutes be adopted.—Mr. Lewis seconded.—Mr. Edwards described the scheme as a , wild goose scheme and he moved that the minutes be re-1 ferrea back to the Committee for further consideration, ' To obtain water from the Liverpool scheme would be far simpler and cost less in the end.—Mr. Brandreth seconded the amendment "for argument's. sake."—Mr. Edwards said the estimate was £3,000, but it would cost £6,000, and that Frodsham people would have a millstone , round their necks which they would never get rid of. The residents of the Lordship dealing with the township money was not good enough.—the Chairman said Mr. Thomas and Mr. Reynolds were there as representatives of the ratepayers.—Mr. Edwards: They are here by virtue of their office, they did not represent aeybody but themselves.—The Chairman : I beg your pardon.— Mr. Edwards: I beg your pardon too. They, are siin- ply ex-officio ; I know what.they. are.—The Clerk :.Taey are members of the Parochial Committee. Mr. Edwards : Certainly; but that doesn't constitute them members 01 the Sanitary Authority.—The Clerk :. Yes, it does.—Mr. Edwards: Is Mr. They a member of the Authority, then ?—The Clerk: ; but the Autho- rity has delegated its powers to the committee.—Mr. Edwards: We have not delegated our powers. The committee can simply recommend, and we pass or re- ject.—Mr.Edwards thenwent on to say that the meeting of the committee on the previous night, was a farce from beginning to end. There were four members ot Frodsham township present, and the members of the lordship said they would have nothing to do with the scheme. Dr. Robinson moved that the plans be passed, but lie could not get a seconder, and at last Mr. Davies had to be asked to second the motion. He did so, and in showing how much he know about the matter, he asked, " Where is the water to . come from ?" He ' thougut it, absurd for a man to deal. with £3,000 of public money in that way. He asked ' the Authority whether they would lend themselves to a scheme that had not been fairly considered. No mem- ber of the Committee had seen the plans for half an hour.—The Clerk: They have been at my office a fort- night or three weeks and open to anybody's inspection. —air. Edwards : But no one had inspected them. He argued that the scheme ought to be more comprehensive and include both the township and the Lordsnip.—Mr. Reynolds said a Local Government Board Inspector had decided that the Lordship did not require a water scheme. Mr. Edwards: The only question asked was by Mr. Hargreaves, who wished to know whether any of the inhabitants of the Lordship were included in the town- ship scheme, and the reply was no. The whole thing then dropped. The plan of the Lordship and the town- ship was never produced before the Inspector, but I will take good care that such a plan is produced before him. Tne boundaries between the Lordship and the township are so vague that it could hardly be told where one began and the other ended, and the people who were close to Frodsham township' were anxiously looking for this water scheme so that they might be supplied without incurring the onus and responsibility of being rated for the scheme, and bearing a portion of the burden. —Mr. Lewis: Do you contend that a water scheme is not wanted.—Mr. Edwards: No I don't contend any- thing of the kind, but I say this is an absurd, not duly considered and a wild scheme. There is no land in- cluded in the estimate, and the ultimate cost would be ateseseies s Why..-.. Mr.. Edwards : . Because it is in 99 cases out of a hundred.—Mr. Reynolds I don't think that is a reason.—Mr. Thomas said Mr. Ed- wards described the Committee as a bogus meeting (Mr„ Edwards : I have said nothing of the kind), and he took that as an insult to himself. The only objecter to the resolution was Mr. Edwards and Mr. Tiley did not vote. No member of the Lordship voted, and the minutes were perfectly correct. With regard to the expense Mr-Tim- mins was asked by himself (Mr. Thomas) whether he would complete these works for the money, and he replied that he would complete them for the £3,000 irrespective of the land. The land that would be required was about half an acre for a pumping station and well and about half an acre for a reservoir. There was only a short way-leave. Out of about 18 schemes that had been proposed for Frodsham this was the cheapest pumping scheme. The last scheme from, Newton was .estimated at about £B,OOO, and the income was estimated at about £475. The present scheme did not perhaps embrace quite as large an area, but he believed with Mr. Timmins that it would pay. As to the Vynwy Water they could not have it under 6d. per thousand gallons, if at that price, most likely it would be 9d. and they would be liable to have it cut off, at any year. Mr. Timmins had told him that in the present scheme the cost of raising the water would be about 21,..d. per 1000 gallons. It was the cheapest scheme they had ever had.—Mr. Edwards said the cost of mainten- ance was put down at £250 a year at a moderate computation. Instead of the cost being 2Ad. lie could show by figures that it would be Bd.—After some remarks by Mr. Brandreth, who advised caution in dealing with such a matter, Mr. Edwards was about to again speak when the Chairman said he was quite out of order.—Mr. Edwards: We don't want any muzzling. He went on to observe that his colleague, Mr. Heywood,. a repre- sentative of the township was also opposed to the scheme. —ln answer to Mr. Lewis, the Clerk said if the Local Government Board did not think the scheme possible the Authority could not proceed with it.—Mr. Reynolds said the Board would send down an inspector and the inhabit- ants of the township could have the thing thrashed out before him. Mr. Edwards had hinted that ex-officio guardians had no right to vote on those questions—Mr. Edwards: They are never seen here at any other time. —Mr. Reynolds: I give that a flat contradiction—it is not true. They attended at that Board and did their duty and their attendances would bear comparison with those of any other Guardian in the district. This scheme would be better if a district that would be benefitted could be mapped out, but the Lordship stood out be- cause there was such a large rateable area that would derive no benefit from it. Those parts of the Lordship that required water from this scheme could be charged at a rate that would equalise the matter.—Mr. Thomas said they could supply a certain portion of the Lord- ship.—Mr. Edwards : That is what they want.—The motion was carried by seven yetes to six.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.
CRICKET.

The sensaticn of the week in Lancashire cricket has, says the " Menchester Guardian," been provided by the disappearance of R. G. Barlow's name from the County Eleven. It was supposed at first that the omission of this famous name was only due to the desire of the two or three members who constitute the executive to try "new blood" in a match of minor importance; but when it was found that Barlow was not selected for the Somersetshire and Notts matches, the full significance of step became apparent. Barlow's name has been so con- stantly before he public for the last 21 years in connec- tion with Lancashire cricket that his exclusion from the team causes quite as much sensation as the retirement of Mr. Ilornby would occasion.

He made his first appearance in the eleven twenty-one years ago, and we can well understand that it was his alnbition to be able to say that he had played twenty- one full seasons for the county of his birth. His chreer has been such as any man might look back upon with sat- isfaction. He has represented his county wherever it has been engaged; he has been chosen for the blue ribbon of English professional cricket—namely, the distinction of playing against the leading amateurs of the day; and he has on several visits to Australia given ample proof of his sterling qualities.

Between 1881 and 1890 he scored in first-class cricket 6,781 runs, at an average of 21 per completed innings ; in the same period he captured 714 wickets at an average cost of 14 runs—only seven men capturing a larger num- ber of wickets in that period ; and he has on fifty occa- siens carried his bat right through an innings. An old servant with such a record was, one would suppose, en- titled to much consideration. We therefore find it diffi- cult to believe the common report that at the conclusion of the Yorkshire match Barlow was simply told that he " wouldn't be wanted" for the Essex engagement, and that, without any further intimation, he was left out of the first-class matches which are to be played this week.

After many inaccurate announcements it is now said that Lord Sheffield's Australian team will consist of the following :—W. G. Grace, A. E. Stoddart, 0. G. Rad- cliffe, H. Philipson, G. M`Gregor, Lohmann, Sharpe, Briggs, Peel, Attewell, Abel, Bean, and Maurice Read. A Brighton piper says this is probably the strongest all- round team that ever left England. In 1864 George Parr took out the following team :—Parr, A. Clarke, J. Jack- son, R. C. Tinley, W. Caffyn, J. Caesar, T. Lockyer, R. Carpenter, T. Haywood, George Tarrant, E. Al. Grace, and George Anderson. That team, which did not lose a match, could certainly hold its own against any that have since gone out to the colony.

It is unfortunate in many respects that the position of Surrey in the cricket world is unassailable. It de- prives the inter-county matches in the latter part of the season of much of the interest which would otherwise attach to them. By the averages, calculated up to the end of last week, Abel still retains his position as pre- mier batsman, and it is said his great ambition is to hold that place at the end of the season. To that end, it may have been noticed that he has of late bee.' playing an unusually slow and careful game, and when it has been necessary to force the play he has left that duty to some of his colleagues. His assistance to his county this season has been invaluable.

But it is satisfactory to find that Shrewsbury, who started the year with a succession of bad luck, has in the course of a month brought himself up to second place, and is running Abel very hard for premier. honours. Some of the players are not altogether satisfied, it is said, at the manner in which the rank of counties and the position of individual cricketers is calculated. But as the County Cricket Council, which was the only body which could authoritatively determine these different matters, voluntarily effaced itself, the work can be done only by the unofficial watchers of the game, who can have no particular interests to serve. At the same time, it is felt to be a pity that a recognised and representative body of cricketers cannot be charged with the settlement of these and other 'natters which are points in dispute, and it is not improbable that an attempt will be made to resuscitate the old council or to establish a similar body on somewhat wider lines.

div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.

The English footballers in South Africa still pursue their conquering career. Tha match on Tuesday between the Pietermat itzburz fifteen and the English team resulted in an easy victory for the visitors. It was witnessed by a large crowd of spectators, but the one-sided :nature of the game detracted considerably from the interest of the event. Although the home forwards occasionally made desperate efforts to rush their opponents, play was almost confined to the colonial half, and the visitors eventually won the match by 6 goals to nil.

div.head: POLLUTION OF KECKWICIC 11.12001 i.
div.p: THE POLLUTION OF KECKWICIC 11.12001 i.

The Clerk said he had received a letter from the Local Government Board, enclosing an order to the Authority to take proceedings under the Rivers Pollution Preven- tion Act, 1876, against Messrs. R. Earp and Co., with respect to their pollution of Keckwick Brook, by the discharge into it of poisonous liquors from their tannery at Preston-o'th-Hill.—The Clerk said according to the Act they would have to give Mr. Earp two months notice of the action.—Mr. Brandreth : I think we are fighting Sir Richard Brooke's cause.—The Chairman: It is un- doubtedly for this Authority to move in the matter.—Mr. J.Weir said the tannery had done a great deal of damage, and he moved that notice be given.—Mr. Aaron seconded the motion which was carried without dissent.
SUTTON WATER SUPPLY.

The Inspector reported that the agent to Aston estate had made a most generous offer to contribute the sum of £lO towards the cost of providing a better supply of water to the public pump in Sutton village. The Inspec- tor was ordered to obtain tenders for the work.

div.head: NEW HOUSES.
div.p: NEW HOUSES.
Occupation certificates for four new houses at Helsby were granted to Mr. John Musgrove, of Whitby. NUISANCE AT lIELSBY.
A nuisance was reported as existing in Take-lane, Helsby, arising from a defective main sewer,, and the Inspector applied for and obtained the assistance of a Committee to advise him on the subject.

div.head: SEWER OUTFALL 3.
div.p: SEWER OUTFALL 3.

The Inspector reported that the engineesto the Autho- rity and the chief assistant engineer to the Ship Canal Company and himself had inspected the sewer outfa,lls into the river Weaver, and found them with one excep- tion satisfactory. The proposed plan of the Company with regard to the sea flats outfall did not meet with the approval, and he had made suggestions to the engineers as to retaining of the nresent outfall, valves and tanks.— It was resolved that the attention of the engineers should be specially drawn to these suggestions.

div.head: IMPURE WATER.
div.p: IMPURE WATER.

The Inspector said he had reason to suspect the purity of the water supply to prernlses situate in the townships of Newton-by-Daresbury, and Stretton. The Inspector was instructed to submit samples for analysis.
PRESTON 8.ii,9,015. WAM, svPri.T.

The Inspector reported that he had had a most favour- able interview with one of the engineers of the Man- chester Ship Canal Company, respecting the provision of a water supply to cottage premises situate at Preston Brook. This concluded the business.
THE MURDER OF SERVANT GIRLS IN

-VIENNA. ATTEMPTED SUICIDE OF THE AGEUSED. A Renter's telegram from Vienna says :—Last Tuesday night the woman Schneider who, with her husband, wts arrested on suopicion of murdering servant girls whom they enticed away on pretence of procuring them situa- tions, sprang out of a window on the third floor of the gaol in which she was confined, and sustained such frightful injuries that recovery is hopeless. Fiash dis- coveries tending t& implicate the woman and her hus- band in other murders than those previously reported have been made.
THE FATAL ACC/DENT AT A. WARRINGTON STATION. ADJOURNED INQUEST AND VERDICT.

The inquest on the body of William Buckley () an employe of the Cheshire Lines Committee,which was adjourned from the previous Tuesday, was re- sumed on Tuesday morning, at the White Hcrt Hotel,Sankey-st., before Mr. W. T. 1-142.aband, deputy coroner. It will be remembered that the deceased was employed as a warehouseman in,the goods de- partment at the Central Station, and\ en the after-- noon of the Ist inst.(Saturday) was engaged "sheet- ing" a wagon,and in order to do his wol* was stand- ing on the metals close to one of the buffers of the wagon. Suddenly the train was movedrand Buck- ley was so seriously crushed between the buffers that he died shortly after his admission to the In- firmary. Mr. Simpson, superintendent of railway police,watched the case for the Cheshire Lines Cora- mittee.—At the request of a juror, the evidence given on the prsvious occasion by Saml. Storey and Peter Knight was read by the Coroner. Thomas Burgess, warehouse labourer, said he did not hear the engine whistle, nor did he hear anyone call "Look out, warehouse," because he was underneath the stage. He heard the noise of the buffers, however. That was the only signal of the shunting he got.—The Coroner: Have you ever complained that sufficient warning was not given to you? Witness: I always get warning, that is right enough.—The Coroner: What sort of warning? Witness: "Look out, warehouse."—The Coroner: And the only warning you got on this occasion was the bumping of the wagons ? Witness said that was so. —A Juror: Do you know any man who within in the last three or four months has caught his foot in a bad rail in the warehouse.—Witness : No, sir.—The Juror said he should like the Coroner to see the rail.—The Coroner: Twelve men are sufficient surely without me seeing it ! Continuing witness, said he had never seen the bad rail. Further questioned, he said the rules were not read to him when he joined the company. The workmen , were always told to be careful when crossing the metals. It was reported that another man was inmed on the day in question by the same train. He had been off duty since the deceased was killed. The men were supposed to have proper warning given them while at work.—A Juror remarked, after looking at the book of rules andregulations, that it contained' no direct instructions to shooters, and he asked the witness what number of hours he worked each week.—Witness : Over 70 hours, I think.—The Juror: You don't know what time the deceased put in.—Witness: No, sir.—The Juror Is it not a fact that you men have to work for nine days out of ten, from six in the morn- ing till eleven at night ?—The Coroner: Do you think that has anything to do with the death of the deceased? —The Juror: Yes, I should think so, if a man has worked 78 hours.—The Coroner : I rule that it has nothing to do with the cause of death, with the accident. The matter is simple as daylight. I think you are going into all sorts of absurd notions apart from the inquiry. The deceased was crushed between the buffers of two waggons.—A Juror : Then there is no necessity to hold; an inquest.—The Coroner : Yes, there is.—Another ' Juror: Do I understand that we are asking unnecessary questions F— The Coroner : I will tell you when unnecessary questions are asked. I was referring to the hours of labour. I thought that was not pertinent to the hiquiry.—The Juror: I should think it was.—The Coroner : Well, Tam the judge.—The Juror: If a man is over-worked it is evident he will be sleepy, and if he is sleepy he is not capable of filling his employment. George Wilson, general labourer, said he heard the whistle from the engine. He jumped on to the stage,and when he turned he saw the deceased between the buffers. Witness had just time to get out of the way ; the de- ceased had not. There was not a whistle from the engine before the waggons bumped.—By Mr. Simpson : He was " sheeting " between the waggons on the afternoon in question. After he heard the engine whistle he got up from the ground on the stage from between the waggons. He had ample time to do so. If he had ample time the man standing against the buffers on the off side also had time.—By the jury : He heard a whistle frqm.the_foreman porter, and the engine. He heard no shout.

Peter Knight and Samuel Storey were recalled and questioned in a somewhat similar manner by the j4ry. The last-named said he believed another man was hurt on the day in question, and he was now able to walk about.—A Juror: It seems strange that the man who is able to walk about has not been brought here to give evi- dence. It is very serious, and looks as if the company do not wish the thing to be thoroughly investigated. The Coroner : The company have nothing to do with the ordering of the evidence.—Police-Inspector Bowen said that was the first time he had heard a second man was hurt on the afternoon in question. He had warned no fewer than six witnesses to be present.—Mr. Simpson said he was unaware till that morning of the second acci- dent to which reference had been made.—The Coroner asked the jury if they would again adjourn the inquiry, for another week to enable the injured man to be sum- moned.—The Jury, however, decided not to call him,

The Coroner Weil summed up the evidence, and -re- marked that he thought the jury had exhausted the question three times over. It was a very stupid act on the part of the deceased to get between the buffers, but he thought it might be taken for granted that the engine did whistle. There seemed to have been a certain amount of carelessness on the pal t of the deceased, and he did not see that the jury could return any other ver- dict except one of accidental death. There was a little bit of carelessness on the part of the persons who had charge of the train, as well as on the part of deceased,, but everyone knew that railway men were very careless. They got so accustomed to danger that they did all sorts of outrageous things, and he was constantly holding inquests on men who had been killed owing to their own carelessness. The same remarks applied to pitmen and others.

The jury were then left by themselves to consider their decision, and after a discussion of about ten minutes they returned a verdict of "Accidental death,'," but added that sufficient warning had not beengiven to the deceased.—The Coroner (to Mr. Simpson),: WilL you please see that the shunters have orders not to move the trains while shunters are between the • waggons Simpson: I will lay the matter before our people but if a shunter has to go the whole length of the train we shall never be able to get them off.—The Coroner If a similar thing occurs again, and sufficient warning is not given, I am afraid the jury will have to come to a stronger conclusion.—A Juror said a, presentment had been made to the effect that a horn should be provided to be sounded when waggons were about to be shunted. —Another juryman thought a bell would be more suit- able.—The Coroner I think something will be done. I don't think we shall meet with a case of this kind again. The inquiry then terminated. It will be remembered that two jurymen who had been summoned to attend failed to put in an appear- ance at the opening of the inquiry on the previous Tuesday, and the Coroner, at the close of the proceedings, said he would take time to consider whether he would fine them. They were in attendance on Tuesday morning, and the Coroner, addressing them, said : I had to consider the question of a fine. I don't think I will say anything about the matter now. You had better be more punctual next time. The men thanked the Ccroner and left the room.

div.head: RAILWAY MYSTERY AT WIDNES.
div.p: A RAILWAY MYSTERY AT WIDNES.

About LI p.m. on Saturday, Joseph Lowe, signal- man at Tanhouse Station, Widnes, on the Cheshire Lines Railway, heard groans from the direction of the station, and informed Mr. Patten, the station. master. The latter at once made an inspection and found a man lying between the platform and the metals suffering Horn serious injuries to various parts of the body. He was identified as Thomas Eastwood, 30 years of age, of 34, Moss-st. He was at once conveyed to the Accident Hospital, and attended by Dr. Hudson,but death occurred on Sum- day morning. The inquest was held on Monday by Mr. W. T. Husband, and evidence was given to the effect that deceased called at the Commercial H3tel, Ann-st., West, about 1.0 p.m. on Saturday night, He was them somewhat under the influence of drink and left in a few minutes to go home. He would have to pass the railway station, and it was sup- posed that he had been walking along the platform towards Messrs. Sullivan's works where he was em- ployed, and had fallen on to the line and injured his leg and other parts of his body. 31.1r,Patten had examined the engine of the train that had passed the station previous to deceased being found and he could find no traces of the accident. A verdict of "Accidental death "was returned.

The German Government is placed by this unexpected step in a very difficult position. The Ger- man poor live principaNy on rye, ST. The railway tariff for the trans- port grain is being everywhere reduced.

LICENSING IN CHESHIRE.
THE DUKE OF WESTIIINSTER ON TIED HOUSES.

A special court of quarter sessions for Cheshire was held at Chester Castle, on Saturday, to discuss a somewhat drastic report dealing with licenses, tied houses,the bon-fide trayelier,and kindred questions, prepared by a sub-committee of the court which was appointad two or three months ago. His Honour Judge Sir Horatio Lloyd presided, and among the large number of county justices present were the Duke of Westminster (Lord Lieutenant), Lord Tollemache, Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P. ; Mr. H. J. Tollemache, M.P. ; Mr, James Tomkinson (vice- &airman of the county council), and Colonel C. 11. Prance-lbyhurst (chairman of the standing joint committeo. The report under discussion found, among other important conclusions, as follows : "There are 51 !.(YWllships in the county where the licensed houses, bg they one or more, are tied houses, and where tha. is no free house. There are out of a total number of 482 townships, as many as 196 townships, with a popula- tion of 26,772, in which there ig Do licensed house. Of these, three townships have IV? popula- tion, a fourth has only eight persons, the Itlrgest has 850. Of 1,629 licensed houses, as many as 712 have no beds for travellers, nor any accommodation for the supply of refreshments other than drink. In the 14 licensing divisions in the years 1887, 1888, 1889, and 1890, the number of convictions for drunkenness, &c., were 2,224, 2,396, 3,106, and 3,117 respectively, showing a regular annual increase, and an increase in the last over the first year of 40 per cent." The report also showed that in some town- ships the proportion of tied to free licensed houses was very large. For instance, in }Toole they are 8 V? 1; 'rodsham, 12 to 2; Barntons 7to 1; Left- *kb, 9to I. Northwich, 24 to 2; Wharton, 13 to 4; Runcorn, 66 to 16; Weston, 6 to 1; Dialey, 9 to 1; and Great Neston, 10 to 2. The report winds up as follows:—" In concluding this report we desire to express our conviction that the main agency to 'which we must look for the regulation and im- provement of public-houses is effective police supervision, and that the one indispensable condi- tion of effective control by the police is magisterial support. All the evidence which has been taken before successive committees of both Houses of Parliament goes to establish the connection between drunkenness and the excessive multiplication of public-houses, as well as the demoralising character and influence exercised by the lower class of public- houses." Mr. C. S. Roundell, chairman of the committee, in moving the adoption of the report, said the report might possibly be considered a strong report, but then the facts were strong, and if, when the facts ' were so overwhelming strong. the committee had come to weak or half-hearted conclusions they would have stultified themselves. (Hear, hear.) The Duke of Westminster said that it was ad- mitted that the magistrates of the country had done their duty on the whole well, and of late years there had been very little increase in the number of licenses, notwithstanding a very large increase of population; but there was a feeling ex- pressed by Lord Aberdare and others that though the magistrates had done a good deal they might have done more under the powers they possessed. This had been emphasised by recent law decisions In the High Court, and now they found that, al- though they were not aware of it previously, they had very much more power than they were supposed to have before. The question of tied houses was pro- minently dealt with, and they could not but see that a state oi things had arisen of late years which was not contemplated by the!Act of 1872, and which called for further legislation, because, of course, it was the one great object to have a responsible holder, and resident in each house—a man that one could catch and punish if he behaved wrongly. In the case of tied houses there was no question of en- dorsement of license, but the offending tenant was t once removed by his superior employer the brewer. This was a very unsatisfactory state of things, and one which held to a very large extent in the county, because he saw from the reports that about one half, he believed, of the houses in the country were tied houses. It was a matter, there- fore, which required very urgent consideration on the part of all concerned, and especially with regard to the transfer of licenses,that due attention should be given to the circumstances under which the transfers were applied for. There was one recom- mendation with regard to removals of licenses in their last report of a year ago in which it was re- commended that the opinion of localities should be consulted—that in the case of publicans removing from one place to another, the people of the locality to which the removal was destined should be con- sulted by the magistrates before any decision was arrived at with regard to the propriety or otherwise of giving effect to the removal. A system of late years had grown up that the publican insisted, whether rightly or wrongly, that he had an interest in his business, and a right to continue his license unless there was some very strong objection or fault found with the management of the house. Under these circumstances it seemed to him whether it would not be fair, honest, and simple, in refusing a liaense renewal to give, say, twelve months' notice of such intention on the part of the magistrates. lie thought that would be worth consideration. Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., said he should like to know whether the magistrates could not at once.; ask the owners of public-houses to close the second or back entrances, which the police described as hindrances to their work. Ile had ascertained that in more than in one instance houses which were described as free in the report were practically not free, for, if they did not belong to brewers' or brewers' companies, several of them belonged to brewers' travellers, and were no more free than the former. Mr. T. Comber said that from the statistics in the report he gathered that in the districts where public houses were most numerous drunkenness was most prevalent. In Runcorn in four years' one person out of every ten of the population had been con- victed of drunkenness, and in Leftwich one out of every twelve. These were the two districts in which public-houses were thickest. In Runcorn there was one public-house for every 90 persons, and in Left- wich one public-house for every 79. Mr. H. J. Tollemache, MT., said the committee had been wise in not making any direct recommen- dations, as each magistrate had ,an individual res- ponsibility upon him which no recommendation of any committee could override. He (Mr.Tollemache) thought that this criticism of tied houses was too sweeping. For his own part, he did not disapprove of these tied housEs. After further discussion, the report was unani- mously adopted.

THE DRINKING FACILITIES
OF RUNCORN.

The return of licensed houses in the County of Chester, prepared at the instigation of the magis- trates, Cias just been published, and a contributor has extracted therefrom the following interesting details with respect to Runcorn and neighbour- hood :

THE RUNCORN LICENSING DISTRICT consists of the following townships: Aston, Aston Grange, Clifton, Halton, Norton, Runcorn, Sutton, Stockham, and Weston. The townships of Aston, Aston Grange, Clifton, Norton, and Stockham con- tain no licensed house or houses. In the township of Halton there are seven licensed houses, two of them being fully licensed, and five are beorhouses. The two fully licensed houses are returned as "free " houses (though one is leased to a firm of brewers). The five beerhouscs are all tied houses. Six of the total number are either leased to or owned by brewery firms, the remaining one belonging to the Norton estates. The two fully licensed houses have beds and accommodation for supplying refreshment to travellers, and also possess stables far horses. Three of the beer houses also have beds and refresh- ment accommodation. Two of the houses have neither beds nor refreshment accommodation, and basing the calculation on the census of 1881 there is a licensed house for every 191 persons in the town- ship. The total number of licensed houses in

The five fully licensed houses have also back entrances which are used in connection with the houses by the public. Two of the fully licensed houses have beds and refreshment accom- modation for travellers; one has refreshment ac- commodation for travellers, but no beds; two have neither beds nor refreshment accommodation. It is noted that ; in the great majority of cases that beds, refresh- j ments,or other accommodation are seldom supplied. Taking the census basis of 1881, there was a public- house to ever 230 persons, and basing it cu the 1891 census there is a licensed house_ to every 244 per- sons. In the

RUNCORN LICENSING DISTRICT there are 44 fully licensed houses, and 53 beer- houses, four of which have wine licenses and two are provision shops with off beer licenses. The whole have seven day licenses and 85 of the total number are either owned by or leased to brewery firms, brewers, beer merchants or brewers' agents. In the licensing district there are in addition 4 licenses granted by the magistrates to grocers and confectioners, and also 8 licenses issued by the In- land Revenue authorities to dealers in spirits, wine and beer. The licenses may be described as fol- lows :—Fully licensed houses 44; beerhouses with licenses 4; beerliouses 47; provision shops with off beer licenses 2; grocers and confectioners 4; Inland Revenue licenses 8; total 109. div.head: FATAL OMNIBUS ACCIDENT.
div.p: FATAL OMNIBUS ACCIDENT.

Shortly before ten on Sunday night an omnibus pro- needing down Quay-st., Manchester, came into collision with a tramcar coming up towards Deangate. A pas- senger who was sitting next to the driver of the omnibus as thrown to the grown between the two vehicles. He was unconscious when taken up by the police, and died on the way to the Royal Infirmary. His name is William Henry Clegg, 27 years ef age, residing in Gerald-st., Pendleton.

div.head: PROFESSOR HIGGINS KILLED.
div.p: PROFESSOR HIGGINS KILLED.
THE INQUEST.

At the Star and Garter Hotel, near Leeds, an inquest was held on Monday relative to the death of Professor Higgins, who was killed on Saturday, when attempting 1 to make a baloon ascent. The first witness was Emily Higgins, known as Miss de Voy, who stated that the de- ceased was her husband, and lived at Marsh-lane, Liver- pool. At the Birkstall ascent deceased was responsible for the preparations. She attached no blame to him or to any one else. She was doubtful as to whether it was safe to ascend, owing to the boisterous weather. Her husband thought it was, and went up at his own wish. He would have been safe if he had cleared the telegraph wires. The wires caught his feet, and he was thrown to the ground with great violehie.—The medical evidence showed that the man's back was broken, and that death resulted in half an hour after the fall.—After other evi- dence had been given, the Coroner said it was only for the jury to be satisfied that there was no negligence. Higgins made all the arrangements and took all risks, knowing he was following a dangerous occupation.—A verdict of " Accidental death " was returned, a rider disapproving of such dangerous occupations not finding Support. Higgins was a publican at Crewe, where he was land- lord of the Lord Nelson Inn. He left Crewe a few weeks ago to fulfil balloon engagements in the North of Eng- land. He had made several parachute descents in Crewe and neighbourhood, and had had one or two marvellous escapes. He was some years previously a London cab- man. He held the gold medal of the Balloon Society for bringing down a balloon without grappling irons. Many a story illustrating the coolness, courage, and judgment of the unfortunate parachutist Higgins has been brought to the minds of his friends by his tragic end. On one occasion he lost his parachute entirely, but the fearless atronaut was in nowise disconcerted. He simply climbed into the netting of the balloon to which the parachute had been attached, and then, ripping up the silk, made it bring litin down parachute fashion till he alighted in perfect safety on the ground. The relater of this a,necdote was present at the fatal occurrence on Saturday last. It has been already stated that the wind was" very strong," and that there were doubts in the minds of many whether it was safe to ascend. Miss De Voy, it will be remembered, jumped from the bar before the balloon was released, so clear was it to her experi- enced eye that it was unmanageable; but poor Higgins had clearly made up his mind to ascend at any cost. As his friend says, " I put my hand on his shoulder just before he started and said, George, don't go.' But he would. He said, Let go,' and everybody must do as he tells them. He had that in his manner. He would not be led."

APPOINTMENT OF RELIEVING OFFICER FOR NEWTON. Sir,—l hope that after the unfortunate termination of their last appointment the Guardians have become wiser. I see that one of them has already declared his disap- proval of youthful candidates for the above appoint- ment. I trust the others will be equally wise, so that, while avoiding both extremes of age and youth, a trust- worthy servant of mature age will be selected to distri- bute the public money.—Yours truly, WATCHMAN.
THE BOROUGH ACCOUNTS: THE CEMETERY.

Sir,—ln touching this grave subject, I trust your readers will not think for a moment that I am actuated by any feeling of disrespect for the dead or for the living either. The only object is to draw attentioa to one or two points of interests in the cemetery accounts for the year ended on the 25th of March, 1891. According to pages 6 and 7 of the Borough Treasurer's financial state- ments for the period named, the total expenditure on the cemetery,
£ s d Including interest on the bonded debt, was 1,489 8 6 While the income from all sources was 1,072 10 6

Balance, being loss to the ratepayers 416 18 0 One item in the expenditure calls for more than a passing notice. On page 7we find that the Rector and others received for Church burial fees, and purchase and washing of vestments, the sum of £167 14s. 6,1., or fifteen per cent. of the entire revenue, and only £5B 6s. 6d. less than the total amount of wages paid to the gardeners and labourers for keeping the ground in order, and opening and filling up the graves. Believing, as I sincerely do, that " the clergy" are very much overpaid for the services which they render to the living, I think it is neither seemly nor Christ-like on their part to be found extending excessive claims to the dead. But if they will insist upon having" their dues," let them render a little more " service" for the money they receive. Instead of hurrying away from the graveside as soon as they have finished reading "the service," might they not, with advantage, linger a little while with the mourners, and speak a kindly word in season t) the weary and heavy laden. In thus "improving the occasion," as our Methodist friends would say, they might reach the ears of multitudes of their flock who seem to.wander about as sheep having no shepherd.—Yours faithfully,
OBSERVER.
TORY MISMANAGEMENT: PRIMROSE LEAGURES HUNGRY AND WET.

Sir,—Most of your readers will know from the nume- rous and varied advertisements that the Tory camp was all astir on Saturday last. It was a high day with the Primrose Leaguers of Stretton, Appleton, and Grappen- hall, and all were anticipating a fine treat in the visit to Tatton Park, the residence of Lord Egerton. The amalgamation of the leagues was a new departure from the usual course of procedure, and from the result I should say it is not likely to be repeated. The first whisper of anything being wrong originated in the fact that the Appleton League was to be conveyed to and from, and to be provided with tea, for the moderate sum of one shilling, whilst the Grappenhall League, who lived nearer the rendezvous by two miles. were charged for the ride and tea two shillings, or as much again as the Appleton League. Some of the more advanced of the members thought this was not right, and although talked of quietly, yet,for reasons too well known, it was fairly well kept from the public, none asking questions for conscience sake. I dare say the Appleton Leaguers thought one shilling was enough to pay for the convey- ance and the tea. They certainly had no room to com- plain on that account. I could not help asking myself why all this fuss and concern about the working classes? A few years since and we heard nothing of Primrose Leagues, and their fetes. No excursions and teas and amusements were provided by the Tories for the working-men and their wives and families. But as soon as it was seen that in voting power "Jack was as good as his master and a little bit better too," there was a rush to pet and fondle and to secure his vote at any price, or under any circumstance.

Who catered for the League I do not know, but it is evident the Executive made a serious mistake. The provisions soon ran short, and very many of the members had to return home without having anything to eat. This was not all nor the worst. 'the arrange- ments made concerning the return journey were sadly disregarded, and several to my knowledge were left behind through the buses starting before the stipulated time, and had to trust to Shanks' pony. Had the night been fine the journey would have been sufficiently long and tiresome, but, with such a down pour of rain as we had on Saturday, no one could be exposed for any length of tune without getting drenched. It must have been deplorable. Some of the disappointed were prisoners in their homes during Sunday, and there are now rumours of resip,nations, and threats of not going to fetes again from those who to-day, through Saturday's experience, are sadder, if not wiser men. NEMO.

The railway returns issued on Thursday show that during the year 1890, 1,076 persons were killed and 4,721 injured on railways in the Uroted Kingdom. One hun- dred and eighteen of those killed and 1,361 of the injured were passengers, the remainder being workers on rail- ways. Only 18 passengers were killed and 496 injured through accieents to trains. The proportion of passengers killed during the year from all causes was one in 930,034.

div.head: FAA 1 INER. SATURO 4.V, AUGUST 15, 1891.
div.p: FAA 1 INER. SATURO 4.V, AUGUST 15, 1891.
A VISITING DAY AT THE BLUE COAT SCHOOL.
BY BLUE-BOY.

Some years ago I was an inmate of the Warring- ton Blue Coat School. The manners and customs at that time seemed, as they do no doubt in all insti- tutions, as unchangeable as the laws of the Medes and Persians ; they are perhaps altered now; but my attempt at description may be interesting. The time of the year was November—a bleak, cold day,favourable to rheumatism or kindred kindnesses —influenza I should have mentioned, had it been fashionable at that particular season. It was the first Wednesday of the month, known to the school progeny as "mammy-day." How excited all the , small fry were! How eager that certain tin and wooden boxes should be cleared of bits of string, brace ends, buttons, pencils, nondescript articles of every species, and that certain variegated-coloured bags should be washed, oh! so clean, in hot water from the wash-house, and hung out on the fireguard •to dry! I remember that several came to an untimely end by slyly falling upon some hot cin- ders on the hearth. Studies progressed in an extra- ordinary manner that day—to the extent of nil minus something, and well they might; for did not each boy expect that some good friend might visit him shortly, and provide luxuries unafforded by the diet regime of the Institution? Fancy yourself a schoolboy again, reader, with a schoolboy's love for good things, conjure for yourself the constant expectations in which boys live, and are happy (oh! that we possessed them ever) and score on study's sheet a minus sign for the attention paid thereto. Six o'clock was the time fixed for the season of bliss; and at that time 25 boys were arrayed in their second-best suits on the forms in the schoolroom. Twenty-six boys should have been there, but of that hereafter. I remember that 1 had a coat-button, fastened on with a match-stalk; which consisted of piercing the coat, putting the button-shank through the hole, and the said match-stalk through the button-shank. Another boy was minus the two hinder buttons of his "unmentionables," k this term appeases my admiration of the present-day modesty of ladies), and appeared with his braces tied round his neck; another had his unmentionables back to front, to the eternal annoyance of his sense of humour—he presented an anomaly in figure; and yet another, the 26th, had lost his unmentionables altogether; and roamed around the bedrooms in a state of undignified dishabille, until a quarter of an hour afterwards, when he emerged in a pair of best "seat-and-leg-casings." For the said quarter of an hour there was unmitigated growling on the part of the others, and vows of visitation for the unfortu- nate offender, who had by far the most unpleasant part of the business. Boys know no justice—their code of honour is selfishness—yet they wist not. All is silence now, save the roaring of the huge school fire. "Gate," says the master,and a boy with a string and key fastened to his button-hole eagerly rises from his seat and rushes from the schoolroom. All eyes—large and small; brown, blue, gray; one set with a perpetual wink (a kind of parody on a former king of England), and one pair with a decided squint—are anxiously feasting on the door. A step is heard ; the eyes feast still more greedily (a Barmeeide feast for 25 pairs of them, for a cer- tainty)—the latch clicks; the door opens;. and in walks a portly female, carrying a large basket, out of which are temptingly peeping a 21b. pot of jam and a large home made currant cake. Half a dozen voices call out " carrots " (this being the nickname of a boy who asked his friends to bring him some carrots one visiting clay)—which boy comes for- ward to meet his mother, his face lightens up with smiles, and beaming with Sharratt's Carbolic Soap, which, like other soaps, makes the face shiny and sleet-looking, if not properly rinsed off before wiping. She kisses him, but his eyes are rivetted on the basket, from which he produces three black- puddings, the aforesaid cake and pot of jam, six oranges, a pound of sweets, half a pound of butter, two dough cakes, a large slab of Everton toffee Sin. x 6x 2 (home-made),and a set of,draugh ts. ( How parents do love their children when they see little of them!) The boy stays with his mother for a short time; then hurries off to his box in the lava- tory to hide his treasures from the covetous gaze and numerous requests of others in proximity. The said treasures all come under one denomination with the boys; they call them" stuff." Hence their amusement when the master read to them of Saul hiding among the stuff. Parents and friends now enter the schoolroom thick and fast—a motley assembly—all sorts and conditions of men and women. Widows and widowers meet here, and turned, their meetings to account—good, or bad, the "-twain made one" covered for for themselves after the event. A, young widow might perhaps be seen, whose love for her husband now descended on the smaller people of his flesh and blood—God-sent reminders of pain. Now observe this old woman, feeble with age, and feeling thankful that her orphan grandchild, "her boy," will be fed, clothed, and equipped to face the outer world and to make his way in it, though she may not live to see the day. It were hardly a wise, and certainly a weary task for her to come to-day. She is truly thankful; who would not be ? Oh, that I could be situated thus! to know that for the next year, two, three, fouv, all would be provided for me, and I only to turn it to advantage. Such blessings are few and far between; but youth is blinder than love.

But I digress. Two or more boys have agreed to " whack " their stuff, which merely means the put- ting of the said stuff together in a lump sum, each contributor to have an equal portion doled out to him so long as the stuff lasts. What a treasure-house that lavatory is ! Look at this little red-headed fel- low with a mouthful of ginger-breads, yet trying to persuade a square inch of Everton toffee to enter. How his eyes brighten as he surveys his eatables ! He ties his bag up go neatly (but very tightly) smooth- ing nis hands over it in a very loving manner, while it swings backwards and forwards jovially as it hangs, sharing in the general excitement. Another boy spreads some blackpudding upon some currant cake with his pocket knife; while another licks very sagaciously the paper which has contained his Eccles cakes. During this carnival the boys' friends are accounted almost as nought. The boys, are very fond of their kind friends who supply the stuff; but, how natural! they are infinitely, fond of the stuff which the said friends bring. Oh, boyhood, boyhood, thy sweetness is thoughtlessness, thy joy is unjustice ; be happy in thy ignorance ; in much wisdom is much grief. The hubbub has now ceased somewhat. A sound is heard. It is a trumpet sound. For half a minute a deep stillness reigns; several heads are turned to- wards the clock. It is half-past seven—visiting day is over for the visitors. The boys suddenly awaken to the fact that they are fond of their iriends. How often we find it out when they have to leave us! Kisses are audible everywhere, and the murmuring of "good-byes." The visitors troop through the playground and the outer gate—home- ward bound. The boys flock to the almighty stuff. In forgetfulness they awaken to their pleasures— would it were possible all through life. Reader, could you atone for a parent's presence by the beauties of a bag of sweets and biscuits? Envy boyhood, ye lone hearts. Notice this downcast lad, an orphan. No one has been to see him. A friend did once, twice, three times, when he first entered the school, and, boylike, he thought it would continue. But the friend came not. The boy watched, and hoped; and for a time found contentment in expectation. But half-past seven came round—oh ! pitiless, piti- less, time! and he, poor little fellow, could not rejoice with those who rejoiced, for he lacked wherewith to furnish the rejoicing; and boyhood is selfish. Boyhood had a system of political economy too. I remember one big lad who sported on a string around his neck a number of box-keys belonging to the smaller fry, and who extorted a toll of sweets or nuts each time the boxes needed open- ing. He haa his system—unlike Monte Carlo "sys- tems," this was certain every time—he was an absolute monarchy in himself—a sort of stuff mono- ply; the dearly-bought pleasures of the weaker afforded his pleasures; such is life. All that night the schoolboy community pre- sented itself in two factions—the Epicureans, who gormandised, and the Stoics,who looked stolidly on. Unlike the Stoics of old, they did not believe in the philosophy of negatives. One whispered to his neighbour "All my suet pudding next week for that orange." How they lived in the present Another bartered three pegtops for a gingerbread. "Nil desperandum." So the time fled, and work was forgotten; and a few pale-faced boys at the kitchen door the next morning, waiting to be dosed with that sweeping- benefactor "Salts and Senna," fully bore out the fact that nature wants paying well for the pleasures one gives hgr. Visiting day, many are thy Altributes :—kind- ness, selfishness ; pleasure, pain; contentment, dis- satisfaction; pros and cons every way. But all is over; " truditur dies die." Did I say all? Nay; for one little boy has carefully saved one nut in the corner of his pockethandkerchief—tied in a knot. Why? So he can boast in a week or two that he has
made his stuff last the longest. " MultUz in parvo."

div.head: MILDURA COLONIST.
div.p: A MILDURA COLONIST.
EXTRACTS FROM A LETTER.

Scvo of our readers will remember he description of a voe to Australia given six months ago by Mr. ve r, an ex-journalist on his way to the irrigation co.lony of Mildura. Fie has given up literary wcvkio take to fruit farming in the colony specially organieed for the purpose on the banks of of the River Murray at Mildura. It will be seen from the sub pined extracts, from a letter received by the editor of this puma), that Mr. Lever and his family thus far like the change of lite it makes one fedever so much younger to be out in glorious sunshbne day afterday, with feeling of freedom that cannot be properry understoodi with- out experience of it, One can gtpabout contimually feeling "I care for nobody, no not I!'" withouh add- ing" And nobody ceres for me !"'

We were within 15 miles of H.M.`A Serpent when she went on the rocks, but I don't think we speke her. There was a report• on board before we knew anything about the disaater that a tToopship.had,, been in the Bay of Biscay,with rudder damaged,but 1 understood that was on the Tuesday morning and the Serpent was lost on Monday night. Nbthing; was said on board about the Serpent utttil after, news of her loss was received, and then, of course; some passengers were anxious to make out that we had spoken to her. Thanks for papers received which we read with interest. The mail arrives three times a week, but the time of arrival varies, as the steamers do not keep, time even as well as Lancashire and Yorkshire trains,, and the coach is often many hours behind time when the roads are bad. "Waiting for the mail" is not a very exciting experience, and I.usu- ally go down to town, or send thither,. the day after the English mail is expected in order to avoid the waiting otherwise neceseary. For instancel was informed the mail was expected at six o'clock the other Saturday evening, and as I expected the Oruba would have enabled letters from home to reach here on Saturday, instead of on the Mom:lay night following, I went down specially'. I concluded that if I called at the post-office tent minutes-before closing time (eight o'clock) letters would only need to be asked for to be immediately forthcoming, but Mound the office crowded with patient settlers, and many others outside. I got in- side and waited until about 8.30, and then the de- livery, began. The postmaster and two youths had by that time got all the letters sorted into boxes alphabetically arranged, but a wheelbarrow load of newspapers- were scattered on the floor, to remain over for, sorting until Monday. The men nearest the counter called their names, and all letters in the box allotted to persons whose names began with the same initial were looked over, and the required missives handed over the, counter by the youths. The postmaster meanwhile brought over the "M's," as" Macs" • were numerous, and getting the names of half-a-dozen different 'Macs" soon disposed of them, after which he tried another series of names, fortunately taking" L'B" at an early stage of the proceedings, and. so releasing yours truly, with a gratified feeling at being made the possessor of letters from you and a couple of other friends be- yond the sea. Here we do not need to trouble ourselves much about the weather; Now that the hot season has passed, we have come to regard delightful days as a matter of course, and it is a pleasure to live. The dreary appearance that some views had in the dry season has been changed by the growth of grass after the first autumnal rains, and when S. and I were at the top of our block this afternoon we were both highly delighted with the charming landscape spread out before us. But even when the landscape is not attractive we can almost always view a beautiful picture by turning our eyes upward, for the sky is very nearly a constant delight. The sun- sets are indescribably lovely,and several nights each week we are drawn to the front of our house as the sun sinks in the west to watch the rapid change of glorious colouring which steals across the sky—not confined to the western horizonsbut ofttimes spread- ing almost to the eastern horizon as well. We were assured on landing here that we should enjoy the climate for eight or nine months in the year, and if the weather we have had is a fair sample the assur- ance is certain to be realised. The heat, too, was not unbearable, and, although the summer was de- clared to be a cold one,we do not look forward to the future with any dread on the score of the possible heat, as we had some days as hot as we are aver likely to experience.- We had Be touch of frost on a couple of nights lately, but the days are warm. In. fact on getting up in the morning when the young- sters felt the cold they opened the door to let in the sunshine to warm them while dressing, and to-day S. put her bread outside to "rise "in the tins, as it was not convenient to have the loaves near the stove at the time, and the sun was warm enough. We have only been kept indoors by rain about half- a-dozen days in our five months residence, and we take fine weather asu matter of course. I am not the only ex-journalist amoug the settlers. One of the land agents was formerly proprietor of a newspaper in the COlony, but sold out when it had become a good property, and then lost his money by purchasing a leather business. Another settler, now having a block prepared, was formerly proprietor of a newspaper either in Exeter or near that city, and subseqnently the founder of the "Vegetarian," the organ of the London vegetarians. He has one son approaching manhood with him, and his wife and another son will shortly follow them. He is at present engaged on the" Cultivator," but hopes in a little while to devote his energies to his horticul- tural block. lam kept very busy at present in effecting numerous little improvements about the place, as we hope to make our block a credit to the holders, and I am afraid I shall soon deteroriate in writing, as the use of the shovel and the hoe makes the finger joints stiffer than of yore. However, I know any kind of "copy" can be de- ciphered by "experts," and I can only hope that the " copy" sent in, although not so carefully pre- pared as it ought to be, may always prove interest- ing in the little circle of readers for which it is de- signed. All the youngsters are so delighted with their new home that I believe they would find it very difficult indeed to settle down again to their old life,and I am sure that S. and I would consider it an infliction to have again to submit to the shackles of life in our former sphere.

div.head: SUPPOSED CHILD MURDER AT WARRINUTON.
div.p: THE SUPPOSED CHILD MURDER AT WARRINUTON.

On Tuesday morning, at the Bull's Head Inn, Church-st., Warrington, Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy- coroner, for South-West Lancashire, held an inquiry concerning the death of an unknown infant, whose body was found in the Howley Brook, yesterday week, under circumstances previously made public. The inquiry had been fixed for Monday afternoon, at about three o'clock, and at Oiat hour the jury- men, witnessesond police officials, had assembled. The coroner, however, did not arrive, and a tele- gram was received from him stating that he was detained, and the inquest must be adjourned. This was accordingly done, though one or two of the jurymen protested, and fresh jurors were warned in cases where it was impossible for the original one to attend. On Tuesday, medical evidence show- ing that the child had not had a separate existence, the proceedings were over in the course of a few minutes. The following evidence was taken : Walter Johnson, a boy, deposed that at about 3.30 p.m. on Friday, the 6th inst., he and other b oys were playing " shinty " near Howley Brook, when the bung they were using rolled down the bank into the brook. Ile went to get it out, when he noticed in the water a brown paper parcel. On opening it at one end,, he found that it contained. the body of a child. He took the parcel to the Police station. Dr. Braide, Warrington, stated that he made a post-mortem examination of the body of the de- ceased on Sunday morning. The body was wrapped in brown paper, and inside this was an apron.. The The strings of the apron passed round the body be- low the arms, bat tied the left leg to the chest.. The body was that of a well-developed male child,. and was in an advanced stage of decomposition.. There were no external injuries,and no bones were broken. The child had been dead three or four weeks. The lungs had not been filled with air, and the child had not had an existence separate from its mother. The Coroner said that the doctor's evidence was clear to the effect that the child had, not had a .separate existence, and consequently it really did not matter how or where the body was found. Of course, it should have been putout of sight in some respectable way. He supposed that the verdict of the jury would be that the body was that of a still- born child.
The jury returned a verdict accordingly.
John Swindells, who recently killed a carter named James Henney during a prize fight, at Longsight, Man- chester, was, on Thursday,, committed for triAl, on a charge of manslaughter,

div.head: STRANGE DISCOVERY.
div.p: A STRANGE DISCOVERY.
TWO SKELETONS IN A. WALL.

PARi§, THURSDAY.—A strange discovery has been made at the Chateau Champlain, which cansed considerable Sehsation in the neighbourhood. A vine grower found that his vineyard was encum- bered by an old decayed wall, and obtained permis- sion to have it pulled down. His surprise may be imagined when in the interior of a sort of cavity he discovered two male skeletons with their necks,. hands and feet ri vetted together with iron fetters. Some remnants of clothes reduced to dust were found on the ground where the skeletons lay, as well as some rusty iron fragments. A docter expressed the opinion that the skeletons had been there seven or eight hundred years. They will be preserved in the position in which' they were found pending an inquiry, and finally sent to Bordeaux Museum.

SERIOUS, DAMAGE BY FLOOIS. DARWEN.

_ . Early yesterday morning a great storm burst, over Darwen and so swelled the river Darwen that it burst its banks and did considerable damage to a homse in Pilkington-st., and thereis danger of the whole row fall- ing. Damage estimated at £14,000 is done throughout the town. Many of the mills are stopped owing to being flooded.

CHORLEY. About four o'clock yesterday morning there waS a tremendous storm-of 'rain•in the Chorley district. The streams rose several feet in an hour and flooded the low lying parts. In some houses the furniture floated, and at Whittlewoods all the manufacturing and printing works were stopped, some being two feet deep in water., A railway bridge on the Blackburn branch was partially washed away. Traffic, was-stopped by landslips.

BOLTCN. The heaviest rain of (the .year in the Bolton district occurred. on Thursday night,. when nearly three inches fell in nine hours. The Way-oh reservior rose six feet, and the neighbourhood of Turton was flooded . The railway line was washed up at Springvale, and a 1: tndslip occurred at Heaney near Choriey. Mill fires were extin- guished by the inrush of water at ,Turton, ai id con- siderable damage has been caused throughou it the district.
SHOCKING PIT-SHAFT Accum, JIVT

div.head: AtTx WIGAN.
div.p: AtTx WIGAN.
TWO ,MEN KILLED.

On Thursday night a shocking accident happE med at the Norley Collieries,Wigan, resulting in the Joss of two lives, it appears that during the da y a number of workmen were engaged in the shaft of No. 5 pit, about 390' yards from the top, strengtheen- ing the sides of the shaft. In order that the altera- tions might be more easily undertaken, the rope ot one of the cages was -taken of the vertical, its env- tomary place, and fastened to the head gear. At six o'clock William Gaskell, 3%. a fireman, residing at Pemberton, and John Bradshaw, 52, a sinker of Orrell, decended to the scaffold which had been erected in the shaft, the other cage being used in lowering them. About two hours afterwards, and when operations were 6till proceeding, the rope which had been fastened to the head gear slipped and went down the shaft. Assistance was at once procured, and on the shaft being descended Brad- shaw was found on the scaffold with one of his legs broken and suffering from other severe injuries, whilst Gaskell had been precipitated to the bottom of the mine, some fifty yardsl and was discovered lying amongst a qutaatity of bricks and materials. He was quite dead, and Bradshaw succumbed to ' his injuries early yesterday morinng. How the accident actually• occurred ha fl not yet been ascertained, but it is thought the falling rope was the primary cause.
THE VISIT ' OF- THE FRENCH FLEET.
THE WEEK'S PROGRAMME.

Respecting the visit of the French Fleet to Ports- mouth the following is a summary of the order of events :—Wednesday: Arrival of the French squad- ron, saluting. Thursday: Official visit of French Admiral to English Commander-in- Chief. Lord Clanwilliam will immediately return the visit to Admiral Gervais on the Marengo, At eleven a.m., the Queen will receive the French officers at Os- borne House. At nine o'clock the same evening the senior alters dine with the Queen at Osborne. On Friday the Queen will review the combined squadrons at Spithead. The same even- ing Admiral the Earl of Clanwilliam entertains a grand dinner party at Admiralty House, covers being laid for sixty. The guests will include Admiral Gervais, the Duk of Connaught, and Prince George of Wales. lhe same night a grand ball will be held' in the Town Hall. On Saturday evening Mr. William Pink gives a dinner at the Town Hall to the English and French officers and the leading members of the”municipality. On Monday the French officers will visit the dockyard, after which they will be conveyed by train to the Gunnery School, at Whale island, where they will be entertained at luncheon in the Gymnasium. In the evening the Duke of Connaught gives a dinner at Government House to the senior officers, and the Mayor entertains a thousand men of 'le French Fleet to dinner at seven o'clock, preceded by an organ recital at the Town Hall. On Tuesday the French Fleet will leave for Cherbourg.

div.head: EXCITING SCENE ON THE MERSEY AT RUNCORN, A WOMAN DROWNED.
div.p: EXCITING SCENE ON THE MERSEY AT RUNCORN, A WOMAN DROWNED.

Mr. J. E. Worsley, the Coroner for the Fee of Hal- ton, held an inquest at Runcorn Burial Board en Tuesday, on the body of Elizabeth Ann Payton, wife of William Payton, an ironworker's labourer, em- ployed at West Gorton and living at Sale. On Mon- day two Ship Canal navvies found the dead body of a woman on the sandbank near Bridgewater Lock, near Runcorn, and the description of the body and clothing circulated by the police led to her identifi- cation as Mrs. Payton, who was about 25 years of age. The evidence disclosed the following facts. On Tuesday the 3rd inst., the flat Argyle was passing through Sale on the Bridgewater Canal, when the Captain, Joseph Evans was hailed by the•deceased who asked if he would give her a lift to Liverpool, where she wished to see her aunt. He grantedf her request and in due time Runcorn was reached. On Thursday the flat formed the last of a string of ten flats, which were being taken down the Mersey by the steam tug Queen of the Mersey, and when off Dungeon Point the coasting fiat, James in tacking across ran into the Argyle at the stern. Evens shouted to the mate and the deceased who were having their dinner in the cabin to look out and they rushed on deck and jumped for the James. As the Argyle was fast sinking, Evans also jumped overboard and grasped the anchor chains of the James, the mate meanwhile scrambled on board. The woman, became exhausted, and Evans put his arm round her waist and sustained her, but his arm become numb, and the strong current caused by the motion of the flag dragged her from his hold and she sank. He was becoming exhausted and felt himself being dragged under the water, when those on board threw a rope round his shoulders and hauled him up. There was a stiff breeze blowing at the.tirne and the tide was flowing fast. Evans said to the captain of the James ".Tha's done a nice. thing neaw,besna tha ? " and the captain replied. " Welt I could not help it,; she would not answer to her elm."—The inquest was adjourned for a fortnight in order that the captain of the James, and his bands I might be examined and also to see what was the result of the Board of Trade enquiry, to see if any , blame attached to anybody.

div.p: MR. WILLIAM O'BRIEN M.P.

At the Dublin Bankruptcy, yesterday, the case of Mr. William O'Brien was called on, but no person answered on his behalf; The case was not allowed to stand over for a second calling, but is expected no cause will be shown.
A later telegram from Dublin to the Exchange Tele- graph Company says it is stated that Mr. William O'Brien has paid Lard Salisbury's costs in the recent libel action. THE. SHOEBURYNESS MEETING.

The volunteera who have been competing at the Shoe- buryness Artillery Volunteer meeting during the week have left the camp to make room for those of the second division, who,will compete for similar prizes next week. Eighty-six detachments, numbering nearly SOO of all ranks, are expected. MR. PARN-ELL AND THE BANKRURTCY ORDER.

The "National Press" says :—Mr. Parnelrs solicitors have as yet taken no action towards lodgiUg an appeal against the bankruptcy order made against the co-respon- dent in the divorce canse celebre of last November. The period of grace will expire in a few days,and Mr. Parnell will have to bestir himself if he wishes-to escape being placed in an awkward‘position. If he relies upon his alleged counter-claim against Captain 01Shea to support his case he will be confronted in the witness box by CaptainsO'Shea himself, who will deny any and every such allegation. There are two alternatives now open to Mr. Parnell—to prosecute his appeal or pay up. The "Press" thinks he will pay up. LOVE, MURDER, AND ST.TICIDE. Brutsw‘ FRIDAT.—A dramatic murder and suicide occurred here yesterday morning. M.. Halle and widow , Kernaon were shortly to be married. The banns had.. been published three weeks. The widow, however, had, her daughters opposed to their, mother's marriage because Halle had behaved rudely.to them. Finding the. widow.still influenced by her daughters, Halle went to her room yesterday morning, threw her on the bed, fed,, threetimes into her mouth, theasent a bullet through, his own and fell dead at once on the victim, who had already succumbed. When oneof the daughters, hear- ing reports, came into the rooxn, she found the • two corpses on the bed, that of the murderer lying across- the body of his victim.

HALF-YEAULY MEETING.

The. half-yearly meeting of the shareholders of the London and North-Western Railway Company was held in the Board-room, Ruston Station, yesterday morning, under the presidency of Lord Stal- bridge. In moving the adoption of the report, and state- ment of accounts, his Lordship expressed hisregret that on the first occasion on which he presided ha had to meet them with a slightly falling dividend. Thcw. could not fight against the fates. They might fairly hope that the fall was only temporary, and one which. need not dis- courage or frighten them in any way. With the return of prosperity of trade. in the country,, their:prosperity would return also.

A MEETING Of all persons interested in Temperance work in Warrington, will be held in the CO-OPERATIVE HALL, SANKEY-STREET, ON THURSDAY EVENING NEXT, AUGUST 20TH, 1891. Doors open at 7,30. The Chair will be taken at eight o'clock by TTIE REV. JOHN YONGE. A resolution will be submitted in favour of respectfully requesting the Licensing Committee of the Borough Magistrates to take active and immediate steps to reduce the number of Licensed Houses in the Town. Hall, Mr. David Houghton, Mr. C. H. Pigott, Mr. Wm. Twiss, Mr. R. Wylie, and many others. COUNTY OF CHESTER. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that at the General Quarter Sessions of the Peace, holden at Chester Castle, in and for the County of Chester, on the 29th day of June, 1891. IT WAS ORDERED, pursuant to the provisions of "The Licensing Acts, 1872-1874," that the Meetings of the County Licensing Committee, relative to the confirmation of New Licenses be held as follows: viz. :—The Meeting of the Chester Licensing Committee on SATURDAY, the 3rd day of October next,at Chester Castle, at One o'clock in the afternoon; and of the Knutsford Licensing Com- mittee at the Court House, Nether Knutsford, on MONDAY, the sth day of October next, at Two o'clock in the afternoon. And notice is Hereby also Given,that the said Meetings on the 3rd and sth of October respectively will be especi- ally convened under the provision in that behalf con- tained in the 32nd section of "The Licensing Act, 1874," for the purpose of making (if deemed necessary) orders under that section with respect to towns and populous places. By the Court, REGINALD POTTS, Clerk of the Peace for the said County. 11th August, 1891. NOTE.-By the Rules applicable to the said Meetings it is directed that "Any person applying for the confirmation of a grant "of a new License by the Licensing Justices shall give "Notice to the Clerk of the Peace' of such application, "two days before the meeting of the Committee, within "the district to which the house in respect of which the "License has been granted is situate. "In case any person shall appear, either by himself, "his counsel, or attorney, before the Licensing Justices "and oppose the grant of a new License, he shall be at "liberty so to appear either by himself, his counsel, or "attorney, before the Licensing Committee for the dis- " trict, and oppose the confirmation of the grant of such "new License, upon giving to the applicant and to the "Clerk of the Peace notice in writing of his intention so "to do not less than two days before the meeting of such "committee, and "All applications for the addition to Towns adjacent "Collections of Houses, or for Declarations of Areas to "be Populous Places under the 32nd Section of the Act "of 1874, must, in every instance, be accompanied by a "plan of the proposed addition or area (as the case may be), which plan must, previously to the meeting of the "Licensing Committee, have been submitted to the "Magistrates sitting in Petty Sessions for the Division "within which the proposed addition or area shall be "situate, in order that such Magistrates may express "their opinion thereon for the information of the "Licensing Committees."

DAMAGE FROM LIGHTNING. A Marlborough telegram states states that during a thunderstorm on Monday, 47 sheep were killed by lightning at Overton. A Spalding telegram reports that during a thunderstorm, on Monday afternoon, two horses and several sheep were struck by lightning and killed on a farm near that talace. SUPPOSED WIFE MURDER IN LIVERPOOL. A cooper named George Grayson was committed for trial by the county magistrates at Islington, Liverpool, on Wednesday on a charge of manslaughter. It is alleged that he caused the death of his wife by kicking her, and at the coroner's inquiry the jury returned a verdict against him of " Wilful murder." ; SUICIDE AND ATTEMPTED MURDER. An attempted murder and suicide took place on Sun- day afternoon, at Maryhill, a suburb of Glasgow. David Gray, a rivetter, employed at Clydebank, fired at Nellie Murray, or Gabriel, aged twenty-two, the wife of a tra- velling showman, whilst she wis stepping over a puddle in the street. Seeing her fall, he shot himself, and fell beside her. Both were conveyed to the Western Infir- mary, where the man expired. The bullet has not yet been extracted from the woman, and her wound is con- sidered dangerous. QUEEN'S VISIT TO PORTSMOUTH. The Queen left Osborne on Wednesday in the Royal yacht Alberta, accompanied by Prince and Princess Henry of Battenberg, Princess Irene of Prussia, and the Duchess of Albany, for Portsmouth, where her Majesty was received by the Duke of Connaught. The Royal party drove to the Government House. The streets en route was crowded with spectators. The Queen took tea with the Duke and Duchess of Connaught and family. After planting a tree in commemoration of her visit the Queen returned to Osborne, being joined on the journey by Prince Henry of Prussia.
